# Backend Engineering for AI Engineers

### A complete, production-oriented path from "I know Python" to "I can design, build, secure, and operate the backend of a real AI product"

---

> **What this guide is.** This is the sequel to *Python Foundations for AI Engineers*. That guide taught you the language. This one teaches you the **machine you put the language inside**: the socket, the event loop, the ASGI server, the router, the dependency graph, the database session, the cache, the queue, the token stream, the load balancer, and the pager that wakes you at 3 a.m.
>
> Every concept is taught twice: once as **backend engineering** (the way it works in any REST API at Stripe, Uber, or Netflix), and once as **AI infrastructure** (the way it works when the thing behind your endpoint is a 70-billion-parameter model that takes 40 seconds to answer and costs money per token).
>
> **What this guide is not.** It is not a FastAPI feature tour. FastAPI is the *vehicle*, not the subject. The subject is backend engineering. If you finish this and later move to Go, Rust, or Node, 80% of what you learned transfers, because concurrency, caching, idempotency, backpressure, and observability are not framework features — they are physics.

---

## Who This Is For

You can write Python. You have used `requests`, maybe `pandas`, maybe `openai`. You can call an LLM in a script.

You cannot yet answer:

- Why does my API fall over at 50 concurrent users when the model server is only 10% utilised?
- Why does `time.sleep(1)` in an `async def` endpoint freeze every other request on the server?
- Where do I put the OpenAI client so I don't open a new TLS connection per request?
- How do I stream tokens to a browser through Nginx without them arriving all at once at the end?
- What happens to a 40-second LLM request when Kubernetes sends SIGTERM during a deploy?
- Why did my "retry on failure" logic charge the customer twice?

By the end of this guide, all six are routine.

Two facts about this diagram drive nearly every design decision in this guide:

1. **Your Python process is mostly waiting.** For a typical AI endpoint, 95–99% of wall-clock time is spent waiting on the network — the database, the vector store, and above all the LLM. This is why async matters more here than in almost any other kind of backend.
2. **The expensive resource is not your CPU.** It is GPU seconds and provider tokens. Backend engineering for AI is largely the art of *not doing the expensive thing twice* (caching, idempotency, deduplication) and *not letting one user consume everyone's share of it* (quotas, rate limits, fairness, backpressure).

## Prerequisites and Setup

**1. Python 3.11+** (3.12 or 3.13 recommended — `TaskGroup`, `asyncio.timeout`, and much better tracebacks all landed in 3.11).

```bash
python3 --version
# Output: Python 3.12.4
```

**2. A virtual environment and the core stack.**

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip

pip install "fastapi[standard]"    # fastapi + uvicorn + httpx + jinja2 + python-multipart
pip install "pydantic-settings"    # 12-factor configuration
pip install "sqlalchemy[asyncio]" asyncpg alembic
pip install redis                  # redis-py, async-capable since 4.2
pip install "python-jose[cryptography]" "passlib[bcrypt]" argon2-cffi
pip install pytest pytest-asyncio anyio
pip install structlog prometheus-client opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-sdk
pip install openai anthropic       # the two provider SDKs used in examples
```

Version floor assumed throughout: **FastAPI ≥ 0.115, Pydantic ≥ 2.7, SQLAlchemy ≥ 2.0, Uvicorn ≥ 0.30, Starlette ≥ 0.37.** Where behaviour changed between Pydantic v1 and v2, the guide says so explicitly, because half the blog posts you will find online are still v1.

**3. Docker.** You need Postgres and Redis locally. Do not install them on your host.

```bash
docker run -d --name pg   -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev -p 5432:5432 postgres:16
docker run -d --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine
```

**4. An HTTP client that is not a browser.** `curl` is fine; `httpie` is friendlier; `xh` is fast. You will need to send raw JSON, custom headers, and read streaming bodies. Browsers cannot do most of that.

```bash
# The three commands you will type a thousand times
curl -s localhost:8000/health | jq
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/v1/chat -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"message":"hi"}'
curl -N -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/stream        # -N = no buffering, essential for SSE
```

**5. Ruff, for formatting and linting.** Non-negotiable in a team.

```bash
pip install ruff
ruff check . && ruff format .
```

Do not read it end to end like a novel. The chapters are ordered as a *learning path*, but they are written as *reference*.

- **First pass (2–3 weeks):** Read chapters 0, 1, 2, 3, 7, 10 in order. Build the mini project at the end of each. That is the spine — routing, DI, validation, async. Everything else attaches to it.
- **Second pass:** Chapters 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 14 — the layers that make an API safe and interactive. By the end you can build a real ChatGPT-style backend.
- **Third pass:** Chapters 11, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18 — scale and correctness.
- **Fourth pass:** Chapters 12, 19, 20, 21 — depth, tooling, and operations. Chapter 21 is the one that separates "it works on my laptop" from "it works for 100,000 users."
- **Then:** Appendix B, the capstone. Build it. Reading backend engineering teaches recognition; running a system under load teaches everything else.

# Chapter 0 — Orientation: How a Request Actually Reaches Your Code

Before any framework, build the mental model. Almost every confusing backend behaviour you will ever meet — why `time.sleep` freezes the server, why streaming arrives all at once, why you get "connection reset" under load, why your worker count matters — falls out of this one picture.

## 0.1 The Physical Truth: It's All Sockets

A web server is a program that has told the operating system: *"I am interested in TCP port 8000. When someone connects, wake me up."*

That is the entire foundation. HTTP is just an agreed text format sent over that connection.

Here is a working HTTP server in pure Python, no framework. Read it once; you will never need to write it again, but you need to have seen it.

```python
# raw_server.py — a real HTTP server in 25 lines
import socket

# AF_INET = IPv4, SOCK_STREAM = TCP (ordered, reliable byte stream)
server = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)

# Without this, restarting the server fails for ~60s with "Address already in use"
# because the OS holds the port in TIME_WAIT. Every server sets this.
server.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)

server.bind(("127.0.0.1", 8000))   # claim the port
server.listen(128)                  # 128 = backlog: how many pending connections the
                                    # kernel will queue before refusing new ones
print("listening on http://127.0.0.1:8000")

while True:
    conn, addr = server.accept()    # BLOCKS here until a client connects
    raw = conn.recv(65536)          # BLOCKS until bytes arrive
    print(raw.decode(errors="replace"))

    body = b'{"message":"hello"}'
    response = (
        b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"
        b"content-type: application/json\r\n"
        b"content-length: " + str(len(body)).encode() + b"\r\n"
        b"\r\n" + body
    )
    conn.sendall(response)
    conn.close()
```

Run it and hit it with curl:

```bash
python raw_server.py &
curl -s localhost:8000/users/42?verbose=true
```

**Output from curl:**
```json
{"message":"hello"}
```

**Output printed by the server** — this is what an HTTP request *is*, literally:
```
GET /users/42?verbose=true HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8000
User-Agent: curl/8.4.0
Accept: */*

```

Four things to burn in:

1. **A request is a text blob** with a request line, headers, a blank line, then an optional body. Nothing more.
2. **`accept()` and `recv()` block.** While this process is waiting for one client, it cannot serve another. Client #2 waits in the kernel backlog queue. This single fact is the origin of every concurrency model that follows.
3. **`content-length` is mandatory** (or `transfer-encoding: chunked`). The client has no other way to know where the body ends. Chapter 9's streaming is precisely the art of *not* knowing the length in advance.
4. **Parsing that text into a useful object is tedious and security-sensitive.** Header injection, request smuggling, and malformed-body crashes all live here. This is why you use a battle-tested server (Uvicorn) and never write the above.

## 0.2 The Concurrency Problem, and the Four Answers

The blocking server above handles exactly one request at a time. If each request takes 100 ms, you serve 10 requests per second, forever, no matter how many CPU cores you own.

Backend engineering has produced four answers. You must know all four because you will meet all four in the same company, and choosing wrong is the most common architectural mistake in AI backends.

```
 MODEL              HOW IT WORKS                    COST PER CONNECTION   GOOD FOR
 ─────────────────  ──────────────────────────────  ────────────────────  ─────────────────
 1. Process-per-    fork() a new OS process         ~10–50 MB             isolation,
    request         per request                     very slow to start    CGI (dead)

 2. Thread-per-     OS thread per request;          ~8 MB stack (virtual) blocking I/O,
    request         kernel preempts them            ~1–10 µs switch       Flask/Django sync
                                                    dies at ~1–5k threads

 3. Event loop      ONE thread, non-blocking        ~10–50 KB             I/O-bound work,
    (async)         sockets, epoll/kqueue tells     ~0.1 µs switch        100k+ connections,
                    you which are ready             dies on CPU work      LLM/HTTP waiting

 4. Multi-process   N processes, each running       N × the above         using all cores
    + event loop    an event loop                                         PRODUCTION DEFAULT
```

**Why this matters for AI backends specifically.** Consider one chat request:

```
   TIME BUDGET OF A TYPICAL RAG CHAT REQUEST (total ≈ 4,200 ms)

   auth + parse       ▏ 2 ms      CPU
   db: load history   ██ 15 ms    WAITING on network
   embed the query    ████ 40 ms  WAITING on network
   vector search      ███ 25 ms   WAITING on network
   build prompt       ▏ 1 ms      CPU
   LLM generation     ████████████████████████████████████ 4,100 ms  WAITING
   db: save message   ██ 12 ms    WAITING on network
   serialise response ▏ 1 ms      CPU

   CPU time:      ~4 ms   (0.1%)
   Waiting time:  ~4,192 ms (99.9%)
```

With **thread-per-request**, serving 1,000 concurrent chats needs 1,000 OS threads — roughly 8 GB of virtual memory in stacks, heavy context-switching, and a scheduler under strain, all to do 4 seconds of *nothing*.

With an **event loop**, those same 1,000 chats are 1,000 coroutine objects — a few tens of megabytes total — parked on `await` while a single thread services whichever socket has data. One CPU core can hold tens of thousands of in-flight LLM calls.

That is the whole argument for async in AI backends, and it is why FastAPI exists in the form it does.

**The catch, stated now so it never surprises you:** the event loop is *one thread*. If any coroutine does 500 ms of CPU work — parsing a 40 MB PDF, computing embeddings locally, `json.dumps` on a huge object, or the classic `time.sleep()` — then for those 500 ms *every other request on that process is frozen*. Chapter 10 is dedicated to this.

## 0.3 WSGI and ASGI: The Contract Between Server and Framework

Someone has to own the socket, and someone has to own your business logic. The interface between them is a *specification*.

**WSGI (2003, PEP 333)** was the first. It defines a synchronous callable:

```python
def application(environ, start_response):
    """environ = dict of request data. start_response = function to send status+headers.
    Return an iterable of bytes = the body."""
    start_response("200 OK", [("content-type", "text/plain")])
    return [b"hello"]
```

WSGI unified the Python web world — any WSGI app (Flask, Django, Bottle) runs on any WSGI server (Gunicorn, uWSGI, mod_wsgi). It is one of the most successful specs in Python's history.

But look at its shape: **one call in, one complete response out.** It is structurally incapable of expressing:

- WebSockets (long-lived, bidirectional)
- Server-Sent Events efficiently (many messages over time)
- `async def` handlers (the callable is synchronous by definition)
- Background work during a request lifecycle
- HTTP/2 server push

By 2016 those were no longer exotic. **ASGI** (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) is the successor, designed by Andrew Godwin (of Django fame) for Django Channels, and now the foundation of Starlette, FastAPI, Litestar, Quart, and Django's async mode.

An ASGI application is an async callable of three arguments:

```python
async def app(scope, receive, send):
    """
    scope    : dict — metadata about this connection.
               scope["type"] is "http", "websocket", or "lifespan".
    receive  : async callable — await it to GET the next event from the client.
    send     : async callable — await it to SEND an event to the client.
    """
```

Here is a complete ASGI application. **This is what FastAPI is, underneath all the sugar.**

```python
# raw_asgi.py — run with: uvicorn raw_asgi:app
async def app(scope, receive, send):
    assert scope["type"] == "http"

    # 1. Drain the request body. The client may send it in several chunks.
    body = b""
    more_body = True
    while more_body:
        message = await receive()          # {"type": "http.request", "body": b"...", "more_body": bool}
        body += message.get("body", b"")
        more_body = message.get("more_body", False)

    # 2. Send the response head: status + headers (lowercase bytes, always).
    await send({
        "type": "http.response.start",
        "status": 200,
        "headers": [(b"content-type", b"application/json")],
    })

    # 3. Send the body. Multiple http.response.body events = streaming.
    await send({
        "type": "http.response.body",
        "body": b'{"path": "%s"}' % scope["path"].encode(),
        "more_body": False,
    })
```

```bash
uvicorn raw_asgi:app --port 8000
curl -s localhost:8000/hello
```
**Output:**
```json
{"path": "/hello"}
```

**Why the three-argument shape is the key insight.** Because `receive` and `send` are *awaitable and callable many times*, the same interface expresses:

| Pattern | How it's expressed in ASGI |
|---|---|
| Normal request/response | one `receive` loop, one `start`, one `body` |
| **Token streaming (LLM)** | one `start`, then **many** `body` events with `more_body=True` |
| Large upload | **many** `receive` calls, each a chunk |
| WebSocket | `scope["type"]=="websocket"`, then unbounded `receive`/`send` |
| App startup/shutdown | `scope["type"]=="lifespan"` — load your model here |

WSGI can express only the first. **This is the technical reason AI backends standardised on ASGI**: streaming LLM tokens is not an optional feature of an AI product, it is the product.

## 0.4 The Full Stack, Layer by Layer

```
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  YOUR CODE          @app.post("/v1/chat")                            │
 │                     async def chat(req: ChatRequest,                 │
 │                                    user: User = Depends(current_user)│
 └───────────────────────────────▲──────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │  typed objects, validated
 ┌───────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  FastAPI            • routing table (path -> handler)                │
 │  (~10k lines)       • dependency graph resolution & caching          │
 │                     • Pydantic validation in and out                 │
 │                     • OpenAPI schema generation                      │
 │                     • exception -> HTTP response mapping             │
 └───────────────────────────────▲──────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │  Request / Response objects
 ┌───────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  Starlette          • Request/Response/UploadFile abstractions       │
 │  (~5k lines)        • middleware stack, BackgroundTasks              │
 │                     • WebSocket, StreamingResponse, TestClient       │
 │                     • routing primitives, lifespan handling          │
 └───────────────────────────────▲──────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │  ASGI: (scope, receive, send)
 ┌───────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  Uvicorn            • owns the socket, accept() loop                 │
 │                     • HTTP/1.1 parsing (httptools, C) & WS (wsproto) │
 │                     • drives the asyncio event loop (uvloop, C)      │
 │                     • keep-alive, timeouts, graceful shutdown        │
 └───────────────────────────────▲──────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │  epoll / kqueue readiness events
 ┌───────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  OS kernel          TCP/IP stack, socket buffers, TLS (usually       │
 │                     terminated earlier at the load balancer)         │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Each layer is replaceable and each is worth knowing by name, because production incidents are almost always diagnosed by identifying *which layer* is at fault:

- Requests hang at exactly 30 s → a **timeout**, at the LB or Uvicorn layer.
- Streaming arrives in one lump → **buffering**, at the Nginx/CDN layer.
- 502 under load → the **app layer** died or the LB's health check failed.
- Memory grows forever → **your code** (an unbounded cache, or a leaked client).
- `ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` at high concurrency → **kernel backlog** exhausted.

## 0.5 The Complete Request Lifecycle

Memorise this diagram. Every chapter of this guide expands one of its boxes.

```
 CLIENT                                                              SERVER PROCESS
 ──────                                                              ──────────────
   │
   │ 1. DNS: api.example.com -> 34.120.x.x
   │ 2. TCP 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)          ~1 RTT
   │ 3. TLS 1.3 handshake                                ~1 RTT   [at load balancer]
   │ 4. HTTP request bytes ─────────────────────────────────────►
   │                                                             │
   │                                       ┌─────────────────────▼──────────────────┐
   │                                       │ Uvicorn: read socket, parse with       │
   │                                       │ httptools -> build `scope` dict         │
   │                                       │ create asyncio Task for this request   │
   │                                       └─────────────────────┬──────────────────┘
   │                                                             │ await app(scope, receive, send)
   │                                       ┌─────────────────────▼──────────────────┐
   │                                       │ MIDDLEWARE STACK (outermost first)     │
   │                                       │  ServerErrorMiddleware                 │
   │                                       │   └ CORSMiddleware                     │
   │                                       │      └ your RequestIDMiddleware        │
   │                                       │         └ your TimingMiddleware        │
   │                                       │            └ ExceptionMiddleware       │
   │                                       └─────────────────────┬──────────────────┘
   │                                       ┌─────────────────────▼──────────────────┐
   │                                       │ ROUTER: match method + path pattern    │
   │                                       │  extract path params as strings        │
   │                                       │  404 if no match, 405 if wrong method  │
   │                                       └─────────────────────┬──────────────────┘
   │                                       ┌─────────────────────▼──────────────────┐
   │                                       │ DEPENDENCY GRAPH (topological order)   │
   │                                       │  get_settings() -> cached              │
   │                                       │  get_db() -> yields AsyncSession       │
   │                                       │  current_user() -> decode JWT, fetch   │
   │                                       │  check_quota() -> Redis INCR           │
   │                                       └─────────────────────┬──────────────────┘
   │                                       ┌─────────────────────▼──────────────────┐
   │                                       │ VALIDATION: body/query/path -> Pydantic│
   │                                       │  on failure: 422 + field-level errors  │
   │                                       │  (handler never runs)                  │
   │                                       └─────────────────────┬──────────────────┘
   │                                       ┌─────────────────────▼──────────────────┐
   │                                       │ >>> YOUR HANDLER RUNS <<<              │
   │                                       │  async def -> on the event loop        │
   │                                       │  def       -> offloaded to threadpool  │
   │                                       │  every `await` = yield to other reqs   │
   │                                       └─────────────────────┬──────────────────┘
   │                                       ┌─────────────────────▼──────────────────┐
   │                                       │ RESPONSE: validate against             │
   │                                       │  response_model, serialise to JSON     │
   │                                       └─────────────────────┬──────────────────┘
   │                                       ┌─────────────────────▼──────────────────┐
   │                                       │ MIDDLEWARE UNWINDS (innermost first)   │
   │                                       │  add headers, record latency metric    │
   │                                       └─────────────────────┬──────────────────┘
   │                                       ┌─────────────────────▼──────────────────┐
   │                                       │ DEPENDENCY TEARDOWN (reverse order)    │
   │                                       │  code after `yield` in get_db():       │
   │                                       │  commit/rollback, return conn to pool  │
   │                                       └─────────────────────┬──────────────────┘
   │ ◄─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── send()
   │ 5. Response bytes
   │ 6. BackgroundTasks run (client already has the response)
   │ 7. Connection kept alive for reuse (keep-alive), or closed
```

Note steps 6 and 7 especially. **Background tasks run after the response is sent** — this is why a slow background task doesn't slow the user down, and also why an exception in one is invisible to the client. **Keep-alive** means the TCP+TLS handshake cost is amortised over many requests, which is why you always reuse an `httpx.AsyncClient` instead of creating one per request (Chapter 10).

## 0.6 Where the Time Actually Goes

Order-of-magnitude table. Print it. Every performance decision in this guide is an application of it.

```
 OPERATION                                    TIME          RELATIVE
 ───────────────────────────────────────────  ────────────  ───────────────────
 L1 cache reference                           0.5 ns        1×
 Python function call                         ~50 ns        100×
 Pydantic v2 model validation (small)         ~2 µs         4,000×
 JSON parse, 1 KB                             ~5 µs         10,000×
 Redis GET, same datacenter                   0.2 ms        400,000×
 Postgres indexed SELECT, same DC             0.5–2 ms      1–4 M×
 Vector search, 1M vectors, HNSW              5–30 ms       10–60 M×
 Embedding API call (OpenAI)                  20–80 ms      40–160 M×
 Cross-region network round trip              80 ms         160 M×
 LLM first token (TTFT), GPT-class            300–800 ms    600 M–1.6 B×
 LLM full response, 500 tokens                4,000–15,000 ms  8–30 B×
 ───────────────────────────────────────────  ────────────  ───────────────────
```

**The lesson, and it is the most important sentence in this chapter:**

> In an AI backend, your Python code is *never* the bottleneck. The LLM is 6–7 orders of magnitude slower than anything you write. Optimise for **concurrency** (how many waits you can overlap), **caching** (how often you can avoid the wait entirely), and **correctness under failure** — not for micro-optimising your handler.

A junior engineer rewrites a Pydantic model to save 2 µs. A senior engineer adds a semantic cache that avoids the 4,000 ms call 30% of the time. Same day of work; the second is a million times more valuable.
