# Chapter 5 — Authentication

> Authentication answers **"who are you?"**. Authorization (Chapter 6) answers **"what may you do?"**. Conflating them is the most common security design error in backend engineering.

## 5.1 Concept Overview

**What it is.** Authentication (authn) is the process of establishing an identity claim and verifying it. In HTTP, this means: the client presents a credential, the server verifies it, and the server binds an identity to the request.

```
   CREDENTIAL TYPES, from weakest to strongest
   ────────────────────────────────────────────
   Something you know    password, PIN
   Something you have    API key, phone (SMS/TOTP), hardware key
   Something you are     fingerprint, face
   Somewhere you are     IP/geo (weak, contextual only)

   MFA = two or more from DIFFERENT categories.
   Password + security question = still one category. Not MFA.
```

**Why it exists in the form it does.** HTTP is stateless: every request stands alone. So identity must be re-established on *every single request*. There are only two ways to do that:

```
 ┌──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
 │ STATEFUL (server-side sessions)  │ STATELESS (self-contained tokens)│
 ├──────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
 │ client sends an opaque session ID│ client sends a signed token that │
 │ server looks it up in Redis/DB   │ CONTAINS the identity claims     │
 │                                  │                                  │
 │ + instant revocation             │ + no lookup: zero latency        │
 │ + tiny cookie                    │ + scales horizontally trivially  │
 │ + can store unlimited data       │ + works across services/domains  │
 │ − a store lookup per request     │ − CANNOT be revoked before expiry│
 │ − shared state to operate        │ − claims go stale                │
 │ − harder across domains          │ − larger header on every request │
 └──────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘
```

Neither is "better". The correct production answer is usually **both**: a short-lived stateless access token for speed, plus a stateful refresh token for revocation. That hybrid is what this chapter builds.

**Why AI engineers must care.** An AI API's requests are expensive. A stolen credential doesn't just leak data — it spends money, at up to thousands of dollars per hour. Authentication in an AI backend is a *cost control* as much as a security control. It is also the foundation of everything else in the system: quotas, rate limits, tenancy, billing, and audit all key off the identity established here.

## 5.2 Historical Background

```
 1993 ─ HTTP Basic Auth. base64(user:pass) on EVERY request. Not encryption.
 1997 ─ HTTP Digest Auth. Challenge-response, avoids sending the password.
        Complex, poorly implemented, effectively dead.
 1994 ─ Cookies (Netscape). Server-side sessions become the web's default.
 2006 ─ OAuth 1.0. "Let app X act on my behalf at service Y, without my password."
        Request signing; painful to implement.
 2012 ─ OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749). Drops signing, relies on TLS. Becomes universal.
        Not an authentication protocol — an AUTHORIZATION DELEGATION protocol.
 2014 ─ OpenID Connect. An identity layer ON TOP of OAuth 2.0. THIS is
        "Sign in with Google". The distinction matters.
 2015 ─ JWT (RFC 7519). Self-contained signed claims. Explodes in popularity,
        then a decade of blog posts explaining when NOT to use it.
 2019 ─ WebAuthn / FIDO2. Public-key auth in the browser. Passkeys.
        Genuinely phishing-resistant — the first mechanism that is.
 2020s ─ OAuth 2.1 consolidates best practice: PKCE mandatory, implicit flow
         removed, refresh token rotation expected.
 2023+ ─ AI APIs standardise on `Authorization: Bearer sk-...` API keys for
         server-to-server, OIDC for user-facing apps.
```

**The single most important historical lesson:** OAuth 2.0 is *not* an authentication protocol. Using a raw OAuth access token as proof of identity is the "OAuth confused deputy" problem — the token proves an app has *access*, not that a particular *user is present*. OpenID Connect exists precisely to fix this by adding an `id_token` with verified identity claims. If you are implementing "Sign in with X", you want **OIDC**, not bare OAuth.

## 5.3 Internal Working

### 5.3.1 Anatomy of a JWT

A JWT is three base64url-encoded parts separated by dots:

```
 eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCIsImtpZCI6ImsxIn0 . eyJzdWIiOiJ1c2VyXzEy... . MEUCIQDf...
 └──────────── HEADER ────────────────────────────┘   └──── PAYLOAD ────┘   └─ SIGNATURE ─┘

 HEADER  {"alg": "RS256", "typ": "JWT", "kid": "k1"}
                  │                        └─ key ID: which key signed this (for rotation)
                  └─ algorithm

 PAYLOAD (the "claims") — REGISTERED claims from RFC 7519:
   {
     "iss": "https://api.example.com",   issuer      — who minted it
     "sub": "user_12345",                subject     — WHO IT IS ABOUT
     "aud": "https://api.example.com",   audience    — who it's FOR
     "exp": 1735689600,                  expiry      — Unix seconds
     "nbf": 1735686000,                  not before
     "iat": 1735686000,                  issued at
     "jti": "01HQ3M4...",                JWT ID      — for revocation lists

     // custom claims — keep them SMALL, they ride on every request
     "org": "org_789",
     "scopes": ["chat:write", "docs:read"],
     "plan": "pro"
   }

 SIGNATURE = Sign(base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload), key)
```

**⚠ THE PAYLOAD IS NOT ENCRYPTED.** It is base64 — *encoding*, not encryption. Anyone holding the token can read every claim. Paste one into jwt.io and see. Therefore:

```
 ❌ NEVER put in a JWT: passwords, API keys, PII beyond an ID, medical data,
                        internal hostnames, anything you wouldn't print in a log.
 ✔ DO put in a JWT: user ID, org ID, roles/scopes, expiry, issuer, audience.
```

If you genuinely need encrypted claims, that is JWE, and it is almost always the wrong answer — put the data server-side and reference it by ID.

### 5.3.2 Signing algorithms

| Algorithm | Type | Key | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `HS256` | HMAC-SHA256 | one shared secret | single service signs and verifies |
| `RS256` | RSA-SHA256 | private signs, public verifies | **multiple services verify** |
| `ES256` | ECDSA P-256 | private/public | same as RS256, smaller signatures |
| `EdDSA` | Ed25519 | private/public | modern, fast; prefer where supported |
| `none` | — | — | **ATTACK VECTOR. Never accept.** |

**Choose asymmetric (`RS256`/`ES256`) if more than one service verifies tokens.** With `HS256`, every verifier needs the signing secret — which means every verifier can also *mint* tokens. One compromised read-only microservice becomes a token factory.

### 5.3.3 The `alg: none` and algorithm-confusion attacks

Two classic JWT vulnerabilities that still appear in production code:

```
 ATTACK 1 — "alg": "none"
   Attacker sends:  header {"alg":"none"}, payload {"sub":"admin"}, empty signature
   Naive library:   "algorithm is none, so no signature to check" → ACCEPTED
   Fix:             pass an explicit algorithms allowlist to decode()

 ATTACK 2 — algorithm confusion (RS256 → HS256)
   Server verifies with an RSA PUBLIC key (which is, by definition, public).
   Attacker changes the header to {"alg":"HS256"} and signs the token using the
   PUBLIC KEY AS THE HMAC SECRET.
   Naive library:   reads alg from the header, does HMAC with the provided key → ACCEPTED
   Fix:             NEVER let the token's own header choose the algorithm.
```

```python
# ❌ CATASTROPHIC — the attacker controls `alg`
jwt.decode(token, key)
jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["RS256", "HS256"])   # also broken: allows confusion

# ✔ CORRECT — one algorithm, explicitly, plus audience and issuer verification
jwt.decode(
    token,
    settings.JWT_PUBLIC_KEY,
    algorithms=["RS256"],              # exactly one
    audience=settings.JWT_AUDIENCE,    # or an attacker replays a token from another service
    issuer=settings.JWT_ISSUER,
    options={"require": ["exp", "iat", "sub", "aud", "iss"]},
)
```

**Verifying `aud` is not optional.** Without it, a token issued by your identity provider for *service A* is accepted by *service B*. If service A is a low-privilege analytics tool and B is your billing API, that is a privilege escalation.

### 5.3.4 Password hashing

Passwords are never stored. They are hashed with a **slow, salted, memory-hard** function.

```
   WHY NOT SHA-256?
   A modern GPU computes ~10 BILLION SHA-256 hashes per second.
   An 8-character lowercase+digit password has 36^8 ≈ 2.8×10^12 combinations.
   → cracked in under 5 minutes.

   Argon2id at 64 MB memory cost: ~50 hashes/second/GPU-core-equivalent.
   → the same password takes ~1,800 years.

   The property you want is not "hard to compute once" but
   "expensive to compute BILLIONS of times, especially in parallel on a GPU".
```

| Function | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Argon2id** | ✔ current best (OWASP #1) | memory-hard, tunable, PHC winner 2015 |
| **bcrypt** | ✔ still fine | battle-tested; ⚠ 72-byte input limit |
| **scrypt** | ✔ acceptable | memory-hard, less common |
| PBKDF2 | acceptable if required | FIPS-approved; not memory-hard |
| SHA-256/MD5 | ❌ never | far too fast |

```python
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
from argon2.exceptions import VerifyMismatchError, VerificationError

# OWASP-recommended baseline: 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, 1 degree of parallelism
_ph = PasswordHasher(time_cost=2, memory_cost=19456, parallelism=1,
                     hash_len=32, salt_len=16)

def hash_password(plain: str) -> str:
    return _ph.hash(plain)          # salt is generated and embedded automatically

def verify_password(plain: str, stored: str) -> bool:
    try:
        _ph.verify(stored, plain)
    except (VerifyMismatchError, VerificationError):
        return False
    return True

def needs_rehash(stored: str) -> bool:
    """Parameters should increase as hardware improves. Rehash on successful login."""
    return _ph.check_needs_rehash(stored)
```

**The bcrypt 72-byte trap.** bcrypt silently truncates input at 72 bytes. A user with a 100-character passphrase has only the first 72 bytes checked — and worse, if you pre-hash with SHA-256 and hex-encode, you get 64 chars of hex which is fine, but base64 of SHA-512 is 88 chars and gets truncated. Either use Argon2id, or pre-hash to exactly ≤72 bytes.

**Timing attacks.** Always take the same amount of time whether the user exists or not:

```python
# ❌ LEAKS which emails are registered, via response timing
user = await repo.get_by_email(email)
if user is None:
    raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid credentials")     # returns in 2 ms
if not verify_password(password, user.hashed_password): # takes 50 ms
    raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid credentials")

# ✔ Constant-ish time: always run a verification
DUMMY_HASH = _ph.hash("dummy-password-for-timing-equalisation")

user = await repo.get_by_email(email)
stored = user.hashed_password if user else DUMMY_HASH
ok = verify_password(password, stored)
if user is None or not ok:
    raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid credentials")     # identical message AND timing
```

### 5.3.5 The complete token lifecycle

```
 ┌────────┐                                              ┌──────────┐
 │ CLIENT │                                              │   API    │
 └───┬────┘                                              └────┬─────┘
     │ POST /v1/auth/token {email, password}                  │
     │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────► │
     │                                       verify password  │
     │                                       (Argon2id ~50ms) │
     │                                       mint access JWT  │ 15 min
     │                                       mint refresh tok │ 30 days, STORED
     │ ◄───────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
     │ {access_token, token_type:"bearer", expires_in:900}    │
     │ Set-Cookie: refresh_token=...; HttpOnly; Secure;       │
     │             SameSite=Strict; Path=/v1/auth/refresh     │
     │                                                        │
     │ GET /v1/chat  Authorization: Bearer <access>           │
     │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────► │
     │                             verify signature (~0.1 ms) │ NO DB HIT
     │ ◄───────────────────────── 200 ─────────────────────── │
     │                                                        │
     │            ... 15 minutes pass, access token expires ...│
     │                                                        │
     │ GET /v1/chat  Authorization: Bearer <expired>          │
     │ ◄───────────────────────── 401 ─────────────────────── │
     │                                                        │
     │ POST /v1/auth/refresh   (cookie sent automatically)    │
     │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────► │
     │                       look up refresh token in Redis   │ DB HIT
     │                       ROTATE: invalidate old, mint new │
     │                       detect reuse → revoke the family │
     │ ◄───────── new access + new refresh ────────────────── │
```

**Refresh token rotation with reuse detection** — the mechanism that makes this design safe:

```
  Normal flow:      RT1 → (RT2, AT2), RT1 invalidated
                    RT2 → (RT3, AT3), RT2 invalidated

  Theft detected:   attacker steals RT2 and uses it → gets RT3
                    legitimate user later uses RT2 → ALREADY USED
                    → the server concludes the token family is compromised
                    → REVOKE THE ENTIRE FAMILY; both parties must log in again
```

Without rotation, a stolen refresh token grants 30 days of silent access. With rotation and reuse detection, theft is detected the next time either party refreshes.

## 5.4 Syntax — FastAPI Security Utilities

```python
from fastapi.security import (
    OAuth2PasswordBearer,        # extracts "Authorization: Bearer <token>"
    OAuth2PasswordRequestForm,   # parses the standard token-request form body
    HTTPBearer,                  # generic bearer, no OAuth2 flow in the docs
    HTTPBasic,                   # username/password header
    APIKeyHeader,                # e.g. "X-API-Key: ..."
    APIKeyQuery,                 # ?api_key=...  (⚠ leaks into logs — avoid)
    APIKeyCookie,
    SecurityScopes,              # scope-aware dependencies
)

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(
    tokenUrl="/v1/auth/token",   # documentation only — tells Swagger where to log in
    scopes={"chat:write": "Send chat messages",
            "docs:read": "Read documents"},
    auto_error=True,             # False -> returns None instead of raising 401
                                 # (use for endpoints with optional auth)
)

api_key_header = APIKeyHeader(name="X-API-Key", auto_error=False)
```

These classes do two things: extract the credential from the request, and declare the security scheme in the OpenAPI document (which is what makes the "Authorize" button appear in `/docs`). They do **not** verify anything — verification is your code.

## 5.5 Beginner Examples

### Example — password login returning a JWT

```python
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordRequestForm
from jose import jwt

router = APIRouter(prefix="/v1/auth", tags=["auth"])

def create_access_token(subject: str, scopes: list[str], expires_in: int = 900) -> str:
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    payload = {
        "sub": subject,
        "scopes": scopes,
        "iat": now,
        "exp": now + timedelta(seconds=expires_in),
        "iss": settings.JWT_ISSUER,
        "aud": settings.JWT_AUDIENCE,
        "jti": str(uuid4()),
        "typ": "access",                  # distinguish from refresh tokens
    }
    return jwt.encode(payload, settings.JWT_PRIVATE_KEY, algorithm="RS256",
                      headers={"kid": settings.JWT_KEY_ID})

@router.post("/token", response_model=TokenResponse)
async def login(
    form: Annotated[OAuth2PasswordRequestForm, Depends()],
    db: DBSession,
) -> TokenResponse:
    user = await user_repo.get_by_email(db, form.username)  # OAuth2 calls it "username"
    stored = user.hashed_password if user else DUMMY_HASH
    if not verify_password(form.password, stored) or user is None:
        raise HTTPException(
            status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
            detail="Incorrect email or password",           # NEVER say which one
            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
        )
    if not user.is_active:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN, "Account disabled")

    return TokenResponse(
        access_token=create_access_token(str(user.id), user.scopes),
        token_type="bearer",
        expires_in=900,
    )
```

```bash
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/v1/auth/token \
  -d "username=a@b.com&password=correct-horse-battery-staple"
```
**Output:**
```json
{"access_token":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6ImsxIn0...","token_type":"bearer","expires_in":900}
```

**Why `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` uses `username` for an email.** It implements RFC 6749's password grant, which specifies the field name `username`. Fighting it breaks Swagger's Authorize button and every standard OAuth client. Accept it.

## 5.6 Intermediate Examples

### API key authentication — for server-to-server

Human users get JWTs. Machines get API keys. Different threat model, different design.

```python
import secrets, hashlib

KEY_PREFIX = "sk_live_"

def generate_api_key() -> tuple[str, str, str]:
    """Returns (full_key_shown_once, lookup_id, hash_to_store)."""
    raw = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)              # 256 bits of entropy
    full = f"{KEY_PREFIX}{raw}"
    # A lookup ID lets us find the row with an indexed equality search
    # instead of hashing against every key in the table.
    lookup_id = full[:16]
    # API keys are HIGH-ENTROPY random strings, not passwords. SHA-256 is correct
    # here — Argon2 exists to slow down guessing of LOW-entropy secrets, and
    # would add 50 ms to every single request for no security benefit.
    key_hash = hashlib.sha256(full.encode()).hexdigest()
    return full, lookup_id, key_hash

async def verify_api_key(
    api_key: Annotated[str | None, Depends(api_key_header)],
    db: DBSession,
) -> ApiKeyRecord:
    if not api_key or not api_key.startswith(KEY_PREFIX):
        raise HTTPException(401, "Missing or malformed API key")

    record = await db.scalar(
        select(ApiKey).where(ApiKey.lookup_id == api_key[:16],
                             ApiKey.revoked_at.is_(None))
    )
    expected = hashlib.sha256(api_key.encode()).hexdigest()
    # Constant-time comparison — a byte-by-byte `==` leaks the prefix via timing
    if record is None or not secrets.compare_digest(record.key_hash, expected):
        raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid API key")
    if record.expires_at and record.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc):
        raise HTTPException(401, "API key expired")

    # Fire-and-forget last-used tracking; don't block the request on a write.
    asyncio.create_task(touch_last_used(record.id))
    return record
```

**API key design rules — every one of these is learned from a real incident:**

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| Prefix them (`sk_live_`, `sk_test_`) | scanners (GitHub secret scanning) can detect leaks automatically |
| Show the full key exactly once | if you can display it, an attacker with DB access can too |
| Store only a hash | a database dump must not yield working keys |
| Store a lookup ID separately | so verification is one indexed query, not a table scan |
| ≥256 bits of entropy | brute force must be infeasible |
| Support multiple live keys per account | otherwise rotation requires downtime |
| Support expiry and revocation | keys outlive employees |
| Track `last_used_at` | so you can find and kill dormant keys |
| Scope them (read-only, per-project) | limits blast radius |
| Never accept keys in query strings | they land in access logs, browser history, and referrers |

### Multiple authentication schemes on one endpoint

Real AI APIs accept both a user JWT (from the web app) and an API key (from a script):

```python
async def authenticate(
    bearer: Annotated[str | None, Depends(oauth2_scheme_optional)],
    api_key: Annotated[str | None, Depends(api_key_header)],
    db: DBSession,
) -> Principal:
    """A Principal is either a User or a ServiceAccount. Downstream code
    works with the abstraction, so it doesn't care which was used."""
    if bearer:
        payload = decode_access_token(bearer)
        user = await user_repo.get(db, payload.sub)
        if user is None or not user.is_active:
            raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid token")
        return Principal.from_user(user, scopes=payload.scopes)
    if api_key:
        record = await verify_api_key_value(api_key, db)
        return Principal.from_api_key(record)
    raise HTTPException(401, "Authentication required",
                        headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"})

CurrentPrincipal = Annotated[Principal, Depends(authenticate)]
```

**Why the `Principal` abstraction matters.** Without it, every downstream function needs `if isinstance(actor, User) ... elif isinstance(actor, ApiKey)`. With it, authorization, rate limiting, quota, and audit all work uniformly. Add a third auth method later (OIDC, mTLS) and nothing downstream changes.

## 5.7 Production Example — The Complete Auth Service

```python
# app/core/security.py
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
import secrets
from jose import jwt, JWTError

class TokenPair(BaseModel):
    access_token: str
    refresh_token: str
    token_type: Literal["bearer"] = "bearer"
    expires_in: int

class TokenService:
    def __init__(self, settings: Settings, redis: Redis):
        self._s, self._redis = settings, redis

    # ─────────── ACCESS TOKENS (stateless, short-lived) ───────────
    def create_access_token(self, *, user_id: str, org_id: str,
                            scopes: list[str]) -> str:
        now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        return jwt.encode(
            {
                "sub": user_id, "org": org_id, "scopes": scopes,
                "iat": now, "exp": now + timedelta(minutes=15),
                "iss": self._s.JWT_ISSUER, "aud": self._s.JWT_AUDIENCE,
                "jti": secrets.token_urlsafe(16), "typ": "access",
            },
            self._s.JWT_PRIVATE_KEY, algorithm="RS256",
            headers={"kid": self._s.JWT_KEY_ID},
        )

    async def decode_access_token(self, token: str) -> TokenPayload:
        try:
            raw = jwt.decode(
                token, self._s.JWT_PUBLIC_KEY,
                algorithms=["RS256"],                # exactly one; no confusion attack
                audience=self._s.JWT_AUDIENCE,
                issuer=self._s.JWT_ISSUER,
                options={"require": ["exp", "iat", "sub", "aud", "iss", "jti"]},
            )
        except JWTError as exc:
            raise HTTPException(401, "Could not validate credentials",
                                headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"}) from exc
        if raw.get("typ") != "access":
            # Prevents a refresh token being used as an access token.
            raise HTTPException(401, "Wrong token type")
        # Denylist: the escape hatch for "log out everywhere" and incident response.
        # One Redis GET; only meaningful for the 15-minute access window.
        if await self._redis.exists(f"denylist:{raw['jti']}"):
            raise HTTPException(401, "Token revoked")
        return TokenPayload(**raw)

    # ─────────── REFRESH TOKENS (stateful, rotating) ───────────
    async def create_refresh_token(self, *, user_id: str,
                                   family_id: str | None = None) -> str:
        token = secrets.token_urlsafe(48)
        family_id = family_id or secrets.token_urlsafe(16)
        await self._redis.hset(f"rt:{_sha(token)}", mapping={
            "user_id": user_id, "family": family_id,
            "created_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(), "used": "0",
        })
        await self._redis.expire(f"rt:{_sha(token)}", 30 * 24 * 3600)
        await self._redis.sadd(f"rtfam:{family_id}", _sha(token))
        await self._redis.expire(f"rtfam:{family_id}", 30 * 24 * 3600)
        return token

    async def rotate_refresh_token(self, presented: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
        key = f"rt:{_sha(presented)}"
        data = await self._redis.hgetall(key)
        if not data:
            raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid refresh token")

        if data[b"used"] == b"1":
            # ⚠ REUSE DETECTED — this token was already exchanged.
            # Either the user replayed it, or it was stolen. Assume theft.
            await self._revoke_family(data[b"family"].decode())
            log.warning("refresh_token_reuse_detected",
                        user_id=data[b"user_id"].decode())
            raise HTTPException(401, "Refresh token reuse detected; "
                                     "all sessions revoked")

        await self._redis.hset(key, "used", "1")
        user_id = data[b"user_id"].decode()
        new_refresh = await self.create_refresh_token(
            user_id=user_id, family_id=data[b"family"].decode())
        user = await self._load_user(user_id)     # re-read: roles may have changed
        new_access = self.create_access_token(
            user_id=user_id, org_id=str(user.org_id), scopes=user.scopes)
        return new_access, new_refresh

    async def _revoke_family(self, family_id: str) -> None:
        members = await self._redis.smembers(f"rtfam:{family_id}")
        if members:
            await self._redis.delete(*[f"rt:{m.decode()}" for m in members])
        await self._redis.delete(f"rtfam:{family_id}")
```

```python
# app/api/v1/auth.py
@router.post("/token", response_model=AccessTokenResponse)
async def login(response: Response,
                form: Annotated[OAuth2PasswordRequestForm, Depends()],
                db: DBSession, tokens: TokenSvc, redis: RedisDep):
    # Brute-force protection, keyed by BOTH account and IP
    await enforce_login_attempts(redis, email=form.username)

    user = await user_repo.get_by_email(db, form.username)
    stored = user.hashed_password if user else DUMMY_HASH
    ok = verify_password(form.password, stored)
    if user is None or not ok:
        await record_failed_attempt(redis, email=form.username)
        raise HTTPException(401, "Incorrect email or password",
                            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"})
    await clear_failed_attempts(redis, email=form.username)

    if needs_rehash(user.hashed_password):        # upgrade params transparently
        user.hashed_password = hash_password(form.password)
        await db.commit()

    access = tokens.create_access_token(user_id=str(user.id),
                                        org_id=str(user.org_id), scopes=user.scopes)
    refresh = await tokens.create_refresh_token(user_id=str(user.id))

    # Refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie — JS cannot read it, so XSS cannot steal it.
    response.set_cookie(
        "refresh_token", refresh,
        httponly=True,        # invisible to document.cookie
        secure=True,          # HTTPS only
        samesite="strict",    # not sent on cross-site requests -> CSRF defence
        max_age=30 * 24 * 3600,
        path="/v1/auth/refresh",   # sent ONLY to the refresh endpoint
    )
    return AccessTokenResponse(access_token=access, expires_in=900)
```

### Where to store tokens on the client — the decision table

```
 ┌─────────────────┬──────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
 │ Storage         │ XSS risk │ CSRF risk    │ Verdict                      │
 ├─────────────────┼──────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
 │ localStorage    │ HIGH     │ none         │ ❌ any XSS steals the token  │
 │ sessionStorage  │ HIGH     │ none         │ ❌ same                      │
 │ JS-readable     │ HIGH     │ HIGH         │ ❌ worst of both             │
 │   cookie        │          │              │                              │
 │ HttpOnly cookie │ LOW      │ HIGH*        │ ✔ *mitigated by SameSite     │
 │ In memory (JS   │ MEDIUM   │ none         │ ✔ BEST for the access token  │
 │   variable)     │          │              │   — gone on refresh, which   │
 │                 │          │              │   is why you need the        │
 │                 │          │              │   refresh cookie             │
 └─────────────────┴──────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

 THE RECOMMENDED PATTERN:
   access token  → JavaScript memory (never persisted)
   refresh token → HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Strict cookie, scoped to /auth/refresh
   on page load  → call /auth/refresh to get a fresh access token
```

### Brute-force protection

```python
async def enforce_login_attempts(redis: Redis, *, email: str,
                                 max_attempts: int = 5, window: int = 900) -> None:
    key = f"login_fail:{email.lower()}"
    attempts = int(await redis.get(key) or 0)
    if attempts >= max_attempts:
        ttl = await redis.ttl(key)
        raise HTTPException(429, f"Too many failed attempts. Try again in {ttl}s.",
                            headers={"Retry-After": str(max(ttl, 1))})
```

**Lock the account or lock the IP?** Locking by account enables a denial-of-service: an attacker locks out any user by guessing wrong five times. Locking by IP is evaded with a botnet. The production answer is **both, with different thresholds**, plus exponential backoff, plus a CAPTCHA after N failures, plus alerting on distributed patterns. Never lock an account permanently on failed logins.

## 5.8 AI Engineering Perspective

**How the major AI providers authenticate, and why:**

| Provider | Mechanism | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| OpenAI | `Authorization: Bearer sk-...` | plus `OpenAI-Organization` and `OpenAI-Project` headers for scoping |
| Anthropic | `x-api-key: sk-ant-...` | plus a required `anthropic-version` header |
| Google Vertex | OAuth 2.0 service account / ADC | Google Cloud IAM |
| AWS Bedrock | SigV4 request signing | IAM roles; no long-lived keys needed on EC2/EKS |
| Hugging Face | `Authorization: Bearer hf_...` | fine-grained token scopes |

**Build your AI API to accept the pattern your users already know.** A `Bearer sk-...` key means the `openai` SDK works against your service with only a `base_url` change.

**AI-specific authentication concerns:**

**1. Keys are money.** A leaked key on GitHub is drained within minutes by automated scanners. Mitigations: prefixes for secret scanners, per-key spend limits, anomaly detection (a key that has done 10 req/day suddenly doing 10,000), and instant revocation.

```python
async def enforce_key_spend_limit(key: ApiKeyRecord, redis: Redis) -> None:
    spent = float(await redis.get(f"spend:{key.id}:{today()}") or 0)
    if key.daily_spend_limit and spent >= key.daily_spend_limit:
        raise HTTPException(402, "Daily spend limit reached for this API key")
```

**2. Streaming connections outlive tokens.** A 15-minute access token and a 20-minute agent stream are incompatible if you re-check on every chunk. **Authenticate once at connection establishment**; the connection is the session. For very long connections, send a periodic control event asking the client to re-authenticate, or cap connection duration.

**3. WebSocket authentication is different.** Browsers cannot set custom headers on a WebSocket handshake. Your options, in order of preference:

```
 ✔ BEST     — cookie-based auth (sent automatically on the handshake), plus
              an origin check to prevent Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking
 ✔ GOOD     — connect unauthenticated, then require an auth message as the
              first frame, with a 5-second deadline before disconnecting
 ⚠ WEAK     — token in the query string: it lands in access logs and proxy logs
 ✔ ALSO OK  — a short-lived (30 s) single-use ticket obtained over HTTPS first
```

**4. Agent and MCP server authentication.** When an AI agent calls your API on a user's behalf, you need delegated authority with a *reduced* scope — the agent should not inherit everything the user can do. This is exactly what OAuth was designed for, and the emerging pattern for MCP servers:

```python
# Mint a narrowly-scoped, short-lived token for an agent session
def create_agent_token(user_id: str, agent_id: str,
                       allowed_scopes: list[str], ttl_s: int = 3600) -> str:
    return jwt.encode({
        "sub": user_id,
        "act": {"sub": agent_id},          # RFC 8693 "actor" claim: delegation
        "scopes": allowed_scopes,          # a SUBSET of the user's scopes
        "exp": now() + ttl_s,
        "typ": "agent",
    }, ...)
```

The `act` claim records that the agent acted on behalf of the user — which is what your audit log needs when someone asks "why did this document get deleted?"

## 5.9 Backend Engineering Perspective

**Build vs buy.** Authentication is a solved problem with high stakes and low differentiation. Consider:

| Option | When |
|---|---|
| Build it | you need full control, have security expertise, or have unusual requirements |
| Auth0 / Okta / Clerk / WorkOS | you want SSO, SAML, MFA, and compliance without building them |
| Keycloak / Ory (self-hosted) | you need control *and* standards compliance |
| AWS Cognito / Firebase Auth | you're already deep in that cloud |
| Supabase Auth | small teams, Postgres-native |

**The honest recommendation:** build it if you're doing API keys for a developer product (simple, and you need custom scoping). Buy it the moment you need enterprise SSO, SAML, or SCIM — those are months of work and a compliance surface you don't want.

**Session vs token, revisited at scale:**

```
                   1 service        10 services       100 services
 Sessions          simple           needs shared      shared session store
 (stateful)        Redis lookup     Redis; fine       becomes a bottleneck
                                                      and a SPOF

 JWT               overkill         good              excellent — each
 (stateless)                        (public key       service verifies with
                                    distribution)      a cached JWKS

 Hybrid            ✔ recommended at every scale: short JWT + stateful refresh
```

**JWKS and key rotation.** In production, don't hardcode public keys. Publish a JWKS endpoint and have verifiers fetch and cache it:

```python
@app.get("/.well-known/jwks.json")
async def jwks():
    return {"keys": [
        {"kty": "RSA", "kid": "k2", "use": "sig", "alg": "RS256", "n": ..., "e": "AQAB"},
        {"kty": "RSA", "kid": "k1", "use": "sig", "alg": "RS256", "n": ..., "e": "AQAB"},
    ]}
```

Rotation procedure: publish the new key alongside the old, wait for caches to refresh (one TTL), start signing with the new key, keep the old published until every token signed with it has expired, then remove it. The `kid` header is what makes this work.

## 5.10 Performance

```
 JWT verify (RS256)                    ~0.1–0.3 ms   CPU only, no I/O
 JWT verify (HS256)                    ~0.02 ms      faster, but shared secret
 Session lookup in Redis               ~0.2–1 ms     network round trip
 Argon2id verify (19 MiB, t=2)         ~40–60 ms     BY DESIGN
 bcrypt verify (cost 12)               ~250 ms       BY DESIGN
 API key SHA-256 + indexed lookup      ~0.5 ms       one query
```

**Password hashing is intentionally slow, and that has architectural consequences:**

```python
# ❌ 50 ms of pure CPU inside an async endpoint = the event loop is FROZEN
@router.post("/token")
async def login(form: ...):
    verify_password(form.password, user.hashed_password)   # blocks EVERYTHING

# ✔ Offload to the thread pool — the loop stays free for other requests
@router.post("/token")
async def login(form: ...):
    ok = await run_in_threadpool(verify_password, form.password, user.hashed_password)

# ✔ Or make the whole endpoint sync so FastAPI does the offloading for you
@router.post("/token")
def login(form: ...):
    ok = verify_password(...)
```

At 100 logins/second with 50 ms hashing, you need 5 CPU-seconds per second — five cores dedicated to hashing alone. That's a real capacity line item. It's also why login endpoints deserve their own rate limits: they're your most expensive endpoint per request.

**Caching authentication:**
```python
# JWT: nothing to cache; verification is pure CPU. But the USER LOOKUP is I/O.
async def current_user(payload: TokenPayload, db: DBSession, redis: RedisDep) -> User:
    cached = await redis.get(f"user:{payload.sub}")
    if cached:
        return User.model_validate_json(cached)
    user = await user_repo.get(db, payload.sub)
    await redis.setex(f"user:{payload.sub}", 60, user.model_dump_json())
    return user
# ⚠ A 60-second cache means a deactivated user keeps access for up to 60 seconds.
#   Explicitly invalidate on deactivation, and keep the TTL short.
```

## 5.11 Security

**The authentication security checklist, ordered by how often each is violated:**

```
 ❌ 1.  Storing passwords with SHA-256 or MD5
 ❌ 2.  jwt.decode() without an explicit `algorithms` list
 ❌ 3.  Not verifying `aud` and `iss`
 ❌ 4.  Long-lived access tokens (hours or days) with no revocation path
 ❌ 5.  Tokens in localStorage
 ❌ 6.  Distinguishing "user not found" from "wrong password"
 ❌ 7.  No rate limit on the login endpoint
 ❌ 8.  API keys stored in plaintext
 ❌ 9.  Secrets in source control or in the container image
 ❌ 10. No TLS, or TLS terminated but internal traffic unencrypted
 ❌ 11. Password reset tokens that don't expire or aren't single-use
 ❌ 12. Email enumeration via the signup or reset flow
 ❌ 13. No MFA option for privileged accounts
 ❌ 14. Session fixation: not issuing a NEW session on privilege change
 ❌ 15. Timing-unsafe comparison of secrets (`==` instead of compare_digest)
```

**Password reset — the flow everyone gets wrong:**

```python
@router.post("/password-reset/request", status_code=202)
async def request_reset(payload: EmailIn, db: DBSession, redis: RedisDep,
                        bg: BackgroundTasks):
    user = await user_repo.get_by_email(db, payload.email)
    if user:                                  # note: no `else` branch
        token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
        await redis.setex(f"pwreset:{_sha(token)}", 900, str(user.id))  # 15 min
        bg.add_task(send_reset_email, user.email, token)
    # ALWAYS the same response, whether or not the account exists.
    return {"message": "If that email is registered, a reset link has been sent."}

@router.post("/password-reset/confirm")
async def confirm_reset(payload: ResetConfirm, db: DBSession, redis: RedisDep,
                        tokens: TokenSvc):
    key = f"pwreset:{_sha(payload.token)}"
    user_id = await redis.get(key)
    if not user_id:
        raise HTTPException(400, "Invalid or expired reset token")
    await redis.delete(key)                   # SINGLE USE — delete before proceeding

    user = await user_repo.get(db, user_id.decode())
    user.hashed_password = hash_password(payload.new_password)
    await db.commit()

    # CRITICAL: a password reset must invalidate every existing session.
    # Otherwise an attacker who already has a session keeps it after the
    # victim "secures" their account.
    await tokens.revoke_all_sessions(user.id)
    bg.add_task(send_security_alert_email, user.email, "Your password was changed")
    return {"message": "Password updated"}
```

Five things there are load-bearing: identical responses (no enumeration), hashed token storage (a DB leak doesn't grant resets), short expiry, single use, and **session invalidation on reset**.

**OWASP API2:2023 — Broken Authentication.** The most common real-world instances: no rate limiting on login/OTP endpoints, weak or missing token validation, tokens in URLs, and password reset flows that can be brute-forced (a 6-digit code with no attempt limit is 10^6 guesses — trivially exhausted in minutes without a limiter).

## 5.12 Best Practices

```
✔ Argon2id for passwords; bcrypt if you must; never a fast hash
✔ 15-minute access tokens; 30-day rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection
✔ RS256/ES256 if more than one service verifies; explicit `algorithms=[...]`
✔ Always verify exp, aud, iss, and a `typ` claim
✔ Access token in memory; refresh token in an HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite cookie
✔ API keys: prefixed, hashed, shown once, scoped, expiring, revocable, spend-limited
✔ Constant-time comparison for every secret
✔ Identical responses and timing for "user not found" and "wrong password"
✔ Rate limit login, refresh, reset, and OTP endpoints aggressively
✔ Revoke all sessions on password change, email change, and MFA change
✔ Log every auth event (success and failure) with IP, user agent, and request ID
✔ MFA available, and mandatory for admin roles
✔ Publish JWKS; rotate keys with `kid`; never hardcode
```

## 5.13 Common Mistakes

```python
# ❌ 1. Algorithm chosen by the attacker
jwt.decode(token, key)
# ✔ jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["RS256"], audience=..., issuer=...)

# ❌ 2. Fast hashes
hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()
# ✔ argon2 PasswordHasher().hash(password)

# ❌ 3. Revealing which field was wrong
raise HTTPException(401, "User not found")
raise HTTPException(401, "Incorrect password")
# ✔ one message for both: "Incorrect email or password"

# ❌ 4. `==` on secrets (timing leak)
if provided_key == stored_key:
# ✔ if secrets.compare_digest(provided_key, stored_key):

# ❌ 5. Long-lived access tokens as the only mechanism
exp = now + timedelta(days=30)     # a stolen token works for a month
# ✔ 15 minutes + refresh rotation

# ❌ 6. Blocking the event loop with password hashing
async def login(...): verify_password(...)
# ✔ await run_in_threadpool(verify_password, ...) — or make the endpoint sync

# ❌ 7. Sensitive claims in the JWT
{"sub": "u1", "email": "...", "ssn": "...", "internal_notes": "..."}
# ✔ {"sub": "u1", "org": "o1", "scopes": [...]} — an ID and authorisation data only

# ❌ 8. Not invalidating sessions on password reset

# ❌ 9. API keys in query strings
GET /v1/chat?api_key=sk_live_...      # logged everywhere, forever
# ✔ Authorization or X-API-Key header

# ❌ 10. Rolling your own crypto
def sign(data): return hashlib.md5(data + SECRET).hexdigest()
# ✔ Use a vetted library. Always.
```

## 5.14 Interview Questions

1. **Authentication vs authorization?** Authn establishes identity ("who are you"); authz decides permissions ("what may you do"). 401 means unauthenticated; 403 means authenticated but not permitted.

2. **What are a JWT's three parts?** Header (algorithm, key ID), payload (claims), signature. Header and payload are base64url-encoded, not encrypted — anyone can read them.

3. **Can you put a password in a JWT?** No. The payload is readable by anyone holding the token.

4. **Why is `algorithms=[...]` mandatory?** Without it, the token's own header selects the algorithm, enabling `alg: none` and RS256→HS256 confusion attacks where the public key is used as an HMAC secret.

5. **Why verify `aud`?** So a token minted for one service can't be replayed against another. Without it, a low-privilege service's token works on your billing API.

6. **Why Argon2id over SHA-256?** SHA-256 is designed to be fast; a GPU does billions per second. Argon2id is deliberately slow and memory-hard, making massively parallel guessing impractical.

7. **What is a salt and why is it per-password?** Random data mixed into the hash so identical passwords produce different hashes, defeating rainbow tables and preventing an attacker from cracking many accounts at once. Modern libraries generate and embed it automatically.

8. **How do you revoke a stateless JWT?** You can't, directly. Options: short expiry (the standard answer), a `jti` denylist in Redis until the token would have expired, or a per-user `tokens_valid_after` timestamp checked at verification.

9. **What is refresh token rotation?** Each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old. If an already-used token is presented, you infer theft and revoke the whole token family.

10. **Where should a browser store tokens?** Access token in JavaScript memory; refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to the refresh path. Never localStorage.

11. **What is CSRF and how does SameSite help?** CSRF tricks a browser into sending an authenticated request from another site. `SameSite=Strict` stops the cookie being sent on cross-site requests, which removes the vector for cookie-based auth. Bearer-token APIs aren't CSRF-vulnerable because the token isn't sent automatically.

12. **Why do API keys use SHA-256 rather than Argon2?** API keys are high-entropy random values; there's nothing to guess. Argon2's slowness exists to frustrate guessing of low-entropy human passwords, and would add 50 ms to every request for no benefit.

13. **How do you prevent user enumeration?** Identical responses and timing for existing and non-existing accounts, on login, signup, and password reset. Run a dummy hash when the user doesn't exist.

14. **How do you rate-limit login safely?** Limit by account and by IP with different thresholds, use exponential backoff, add a CAPTCHA after repeated failures, and never permanently lock accounts (that's a DoS vector).

15. **Why must a password reset invalidate sessions?** Otherwise an attacker who already holds a session keeps it after the victim resets their password, which is exactly the moment the victim believes they are safe.

16. **What is OAuth 2.0 actually for?** Delegated authorization — letting an app act on a user's behalf without their password. It is not an authentication protocol; OpenID Connect adds that layer.

17. **What is PKCE and why is it mandatory now?** Proof Key for Code Exchange: the client sends a hashed random verifier when starting the flow and the raw verifier when exchanging the code, so an intercepted authorization code is useless. OAuth 2.1 requires it for all clients.

18. **How do you authenticate a WebSocket from a browser?** Cookies (sent on the handshake) plus a strict origin check, or an auth message as the first frame with a short deadline, or a single-use short-lived ticket fetched over HTTPS. Avoid tokens in the query string.

19. **How do you handle a 20-minute streaming connection with a 15-minute token?** Authenticate once at connection time and treat the connection as the session, with a maximum duration. Re-validating per chunk breaks long streams and adds latency for no real gain.

20. **How would you design API keys for an AI product?** Prefixed for secret scanners, ≥256 bits, hashed at rest with a separate indexed lookup ID, shown once, multiple live keys per account, per-key scopes, expiry, revocation, `last_used_at`, per-key spend limits, and anomaly alerting.

21. **What does JWKS solve?** Public key distribution and rotation. Verifiers fetch and cache the key set; the `kid` header selects the key, so you can publish a new key, migrate signing, and retire the old one without downtime.

22. **How do you authenticate an AI agent acting for a user?** Mint a short-lived token with an `act` (actor) claim identifying the agent and a *subset* of the user's scopes. Audit logs then record both the principal and the actor.

23. **Session vs JWT for a 100-service architecture?** JWTs, verified locally against a cached JWKS, avoid a shared session store becoming a bottleneck and SPOF. Keep them short-lived and pair them with stateful refresh for revocation.

24. **How do you detect a compromised API key?** Baseline per-key behaviour (request rate, endpoints, geography, spend) and alert on deviation; watch for keys appearing in public code (GitHub secret scanning notifies you if your prefix is registered); enforce spend limits so the damage is bounded even before detection.

25. **Design authentication for a multi-tenant AI SaaS.** OIDC via an identity provider for human users, with SSO/SAML for enterprise tenants; short JWTs carrying `sub`, `org`, and `scopes`, verified against JWKS; rotating refresh tokens in HttpOnly cookies; API keys for programmatic access, scoped per project with spend limits; org membership verified server-side per request (never trusted from a client-supplied header); MFA enforced for admin roles; full audit logging of every auth event.

## 5.15 Exercises

**Easy**
1. Hash a password with Argon2id, verify it, and time both operations.
2. Mint a JWT and decode it at jwt.io to confirm the payload is readable.
3. Build `POST /v1/auth/token` returning a JWT, and a protected endpoint that requires it.

**Medium**
4. Add `aud`, `iss`, and `typ` claims and enforce all three at verification. Write tests proving a token with the wrong audience is rejected.
5. Implement API key generation and verification with a lookup ID, hashed storage, and constant-time comparison.
6. Implement login rate limiting by email with `Retry-After`.
7. Make login timing-constant for existing and non-existing users; measure both paths to prove it.

**Hard**
8. Implement refresh token rotation with families and reuse detection. Write a test simulating theft: use RT2 twice and assert the family is revoked.
9. Implement a JWT denylist with `jti` and a "log out everywhere" endpoint that revokes all of a user's tokens.
10. Implement the complete password reset flow with all five properties from §5.11, plus tests for enumeration and replay.

**Production**
11. Build a complete auth service supporting both user JWTs and API keys behind a single `Principal` abstraction, with MFA (TOTP), audit logging, JWKS publication with key rotation, and a test suite covering every attack in §5.13.

## 5.16 Solutions

**Solution 8 — rotation with reuse detection.**
```python
# tests/test_refresh_rotation.py
async def test_refresh_reuse_revokes_family(client, tokens, user):
    rt1 = await tokens.create_refresh_token(user_id=str(user.id))
    access2, rt2 = await tokens.rotate_refresh_token(rt1)
    access3, rt3 = await tokens.rotate_refresh_token(rt2)

    # Attacker replays rt2, which was already exchanged.
    with pytest.raises(HTTPException) as exc:
        await tokens.rotate_refresh_token(rt2)
    assert exc.value.status_code == 401
    assert "reuse detected" in exc.value.detail.lower()

    # The whole family is now dead — even rt3, which was legitimate.
    with pytest.raises(HTTPException):
        await tokens.rotate_refresh_token(rt3)
```
**Reasoning:** revoking the entire family (not just the reused token) is the point. You cannot tell whether the legitimate user or the attacker holds the newest token, so you invalidate everything and force a fresh login. The user experiences one unexpected logout; the attacker loses persistent access. That trade is correct.

**Solution 9 — logout everywhere.**
```python
@router.post("/logout-all", status_code=204)
async def logout_everywhere(user: CurrentUser, redis: RedisDep, db: DBSession):
    # 1. Kill all refresh tokens (stateful — immediate).
    await revoke_all_refresh_tokens(redis, user.id)
    # 2. Access tokens are stateless. Set a watermark instead of listing jtis.
    now_ts = int(time.time())
    await redis.setex(f"tokens_valid_after:{user.id}", 900, now_ts)
    await db.execute(update(User).where(User.id == user.id)
                     .values(tokens_valid_after=now_ts))

# In decode_access_token, after signature verification:
watermark = await redis.get(f"tokens_valid_after:{payload.sub}")
if watermark and payload.iat < int(watermark):
    raise HTTPException(401, "Token revoked")
```
**Reasoning:** a per-user watermark is O(1) storage and one Redis GET, versus a denylist entry per token. The Redis TTL matches the access token lifetime, because after 15 minutes every affected token has expired anyway. The database column is the durable fallback if Redis is flushed.

## 5.17 Mini Project — A Production Authentication Service

**Goal.** A complete, standalone auth service you can drop into any FastAPI project.

**Endpoints:**
```
POST   /v1/auth/register           create account, send verification email
POST   /v1/auth/verify-email       confirm with a single-use token
POST   /v1/auth/token              login → access + refresh (cookie)
POST   /v1/auth/refresh            rotate → new access + refresh
POST   /v1/auth/logout             revoke this session
POST   /v1/auth/logout-all         revoke every session
POST   /v1/auth/password-reset/request
POST   /v1/auth/password-reset/confirm
POST   /v1/auth/mfa/enroll         TOTP secret + QR
POST   /v1/auth/mfa/verify         confirm enrolment
GET    /v1/auth/me                 current principal
POST   /v1/api-keys                create (returns the key ONCE)
GET    /v1/api-keys                list (prefix + metadata only)
DELETE /v1/api-keys/{id}           revoke
GET    /.well-known/jwks.json      public keys
```

**Requirements:**
1. Argon2id with rehash-on-login.
2. RS256 with `kid`, JWKS publication, and a documented rotation procedure.
3. 15-minute access tokens, 30-day rotating refresh tokens with family revocation.
4. TOTP MFA, with single-use recovery codes.
5. API keys: prefixed, hashed, lookup ID, scopes, expiry, spend limits, `last_used_at`.
6. Rate limiting on every credential endpoint.
7. Audit log of every auth event: actor, IP, user agent, outcome, request ID.
8. A `Principal` abstraction unifying users and API keys.
9. Password hashing offloaded from the event loop.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- Every attack in §5.13 has a test proving it fails.
- Login p99 under 150 ms with hashing offloaded, under concurrent load.
- Reused refresh token revokes the family, with an alert emitted.
- Password reset invalidates all sessions.
- No timing difference (within noise) between existing and non-existing users.
- Key rotation demonstrated with zero downtime and no token rejections.

## Chapter 5 Summary

| Idea | The one-line version |
|---|---|
| Authn ≠ authz | who you are vs what you may do; 401 vs 403 |
| Stateless vs stateful | speed vs revocability — production uses both |
| JWT payload is public | base64, not encryption; IDs and scopes only |
| Always pin the algorithm | `algorithms=["RS256"]`, plus `aud` and `iss` |
| Argon2id for passwords | slow and memory-hard by design; offload it from the loop |
| SHA-256 for API keys | high-entropy secrets need speed, not stretching |
| Rotation + reuse detection | turns a stolen refresh token into a detected incident |
| HttpOnly cookie + memory | the only client storage combination that resists XSS |
| Reset invalidates sessions | otherwise "securing" the account changes nothing |
| Keys are money in AI APIs | prefix, scope, limit spend, and alert on anomalies |

### Cheat Sheet

```python
# Password
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher(time_cost=2, memory_cost=19456, parallelism=1)
h = ph.hash(pw);  ph.verify(h, pw);  ph.check_needs_rehash(h)

# JWT
jwt.encode(claims, PRIVATE_KEY, algorithm="RS256", headers={"kid": KID})
jwt.decode(tok, PUBLIC_KEY, algorithms=["RS256"], audience=AUD, issuer=ISS,
           options={"require": ["exp","iat","sub","aud","iss"]})

# Secrets
secrets.token_urlsafe(32)            # 256-bit random token
secrets.compare_digest(a, b)         # constant-time comparison

# FastAPI
OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="/v1/auth/token")
OAuth2PasswordRequestForm             # form with `username` + `password`
APIKeyHeader(name="X-API-Key")

# Cookie
response.set_cookie("refresh_token", tok, httponly=True, secure=True,
                    samesite="strict", path="/v1/auth/refresh", max_age=2592000)
```

### Production Checklist
- [ ] Argon2id (or bcrypt) with rehash-on-login
- [ ] Access tokens ≤ 15 minutes; rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection
- [ ] RS256 + JWKS + `kid`, with a rehearsed rotation procedure
- [ ] Hashing offloaded from the event loop; capacity budgeted for it
- [ ] Rate limits on login, refresh, reset, MFA, and registration
- [ ] Audit log for every auth event, retained and queryable
- [ ] MFA available; mandatory for admins
- [ ] "Log out everywhere" implemented and tested

### Security Checklist
- [ ] `algorithms=[...]` explicit; `aud`, `iss`, `exp`, `typ` all verified
- [ ] Constant-time comparisons for all secrets
- [ ] No enumeration via response content or timing
- [ ] Tokens never in URLs, logs, or localStorage
- [ ] API keys hashed at rest, shown once, prefixed, scoped, spend-limited
- [ ] Sessions revoked on password/email/MFA change
- [ ] Reset tokens: hashed, short-lived, single-use
- [ ] TLS everywhere, including internal service-to-service traffic

### Performance Checklist
- [ ] Password verification not on the event loop
- [ ] User lookups cached with a short TTL and explicit invalidation
- [ ] JWT verification local (no network call per request)
- [ ] JWKS cached with a sane TTL
- [ ] Login endpoint capacity planned separately (it's your most expensive route)
