# Chapter 9 — Streaming

> A 20-second wait with a blank screen feels broken. The same 20 seconds with text appearing word by word feels fast. Streaming is not a performance optimisation — the total time is identical or slightly worse — it is a *perception* optimisation, and it is the single biggest UX difference between an AI product that feels alive and one that feels dead.

## 9.1 Concept Overview

**What it is.** Streaming means sending a response in pieces as they become available, rather than buffering the whole thing and sending it at the end.

```
   NON-STREAMING                          STREAMING
   ─────────────                          ─────────
   t=0.0  request sent                    t=0.0  request sent
   t=0.4  model starts generating         t=0.4  ┐
   ...    (client sees NOTHING)           t=0.5  │ "The"
   ...                                    t=0.6  │ " capital"
   t=8.2  generation completes            t=0.7  │ " of"
   t=8.2  ENTIRE response arrives         ...    │ (user is reading already)
                                          t=8.2  ┘ done

   Same 8.2 s total.
   Perceived latency: 8.2 s  vs  0.5 s.  A 16× difference in felt speed.
```

**Why it exists at the protocol level.** HTTP/1.1 needs to know where a response body ends. Normally that's `Content-Length`. But you cannot know the length of an LLM's answer before generating it. **Chunked transfer encoding** (RFC 7230) solves this: send `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and then a sequence of length-prefixed chunks, terminated by a zero-length chunk.

```
 HTTP/1.1 200 OK
 Content-Type: text/event-stream
 Transfer-Encoding: chunked

 1a\r\n                        ← 0x1a = 26 bytes follow
 data: {"delta":"The"}\n\n\r\n
 1f\r\n
 data: {"delta":" capital"}\n\n\r\n
 0\r\n                         ← zero-length chunk = end of body
 \r\n
```

HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 handle this natively with DATA frames — no chunked encoding needed — but the application-level model is the same.

**Why it changes your architecture, not just your handler.** This is the part people underestimate:

```
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ WHAT STREAMING BREAKS                                                     │
 ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ Status codes    the 200 is sent BEFORE generation. An error at token 400  │
 │                 cannot become a 500 — the client already has a 200.       │
 │ Caching         HTTP caches store complete responses. Streams aren't.     │
 │ Compression     gzip buffers to fill blocks → defeats incremental delivery│
 │ Proxies         Nginx buffers responses by default → all-at-once delivery │
 │ Middleware      anything reading the body iterator serialises the stream  │
 │ Retries         you cannot retry a half-delivered response                │
 │ Timeouts        a legitimate stream may last 10 minutes                   │
 │ Capacity        you plan by CONCURRENT CONNECTIONS, not requests/second   │
 │ Load balancing  connections are long-lived → least-connections, not RR    │
 │ Deployments     SIGTERM mid-stream cuts the user off mid-sentence         │
 │ Billing         you must count tokens as they pass, not from a final total│
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Every one of those has a solution in this chapter.

## 9.2 Historical Background

```
 1999 ─ HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer encoding (RFC 2616).
 2000s ─ "Comet" / long polling: hold a request open, respond when there's news,
         client immediately reconnects. Hacky but universal.
 2006 ─ Server-Sent Events drafted; a standard one-way server→client stream
        over plain HTTP, with automatic reconnection.
 2011 ─ WebSockets standardised (RFC 6455). Full duplex, but a separate protocol.
 2015 ─ HTTP/2: multiplexed streams; no head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer.
 2018 ─ ASGI makes streaming natural in Python — `send` can be called many times.
 2023 ─ **ChatGPT ships with token streaming and makes it the expectation.**
        OpenAI's `stream: true` + SSE + `data: [DONE]` becomes the de-facto
        standard that every provider and every client library now implements.
 2024+ ─ Streaming structured output, streaming tool calls, and streamed
         agent traces (thinking → tool call → result → answer) become common.
```

**Why SSE won for LLM streaming, over WebSockets.** The data flow is one-directional: the client sends a prompt, the server sends tokens. WebSockets give you bidirectionality you don't need, in exchange for: a separate protocol, no automatic reconnection, no standard auth headers, more complex proxy configuration, and no HTTP caching/middleware compatibility. SSE is *just an HTTP response with a specific content type*. Chapter 14 covers SSE in depth; this chapter covers the streaming mechanism underneath it.

## 9.3 Internal Working

### 9.3.1 How `StreamingResponse` works

```python
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

async def generate():
    for i in range(5):
        yield f"chunk {i}\n"
        await asyncio.sleep(0.5)

@app.get("/stream")
async def stream():
    return StreamingResponse(generate(), media_type="text/plain")
```

At the ASGI level:

```
 StreamingResponse.__call__(scope, receive, send)
    │
    ├─► await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200,
    │               "headers": [...]})                    ← HEADERS GO NOW
    │                                                        (status is committed)
    ├─► async for chunk in self.body_iterator:
    │       await send({"type": "http.response.body",
    │                   "body": chunk.encode(),
    │                   "more_body": True})               ← one send per chunk
    │
    └─► await send({"type": "http.response.body",
                    "body": b"", "more_body": False})     ← terminator
```

**The critical consequence, stated once so it sticks:** `http.response.start` is sent before the first chunk. The status code and headers are *committed* at that moment. If your generator raises at token 400, you cannot go back and send a 500. The client has a 200 and a truncated body.

```python
# ❌ This does NOT produce a 500. The client gets 200 + partial content.
async def generate():
    yield "The capital of France is "
    raise RuntimeError("model exploded")

# ✔ Errors must be sent IN-BAND, as part of the stream's own protocol
async def generate():
    try:
        async for token in llm.stream(prompt):
            yield f"data: {json.dumps({'delta': token})}\n\n"
    except Exception as exc:
        log.exception("stream_failed")
        yield f"data: {json.dumps({'error': {'code': 'upstream_error', 'message': 'Generation failed', 'request_id': rid}})}\n\n"
    finally:
        yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
```

**Clients must be written to check for an in-band error object.** This is why every serious streaming API documents an error event type. A client that only looks at the HTTP status will silently treat a failed generation as a successful short answer.

### 9.3.2 Where buffering happens (and ruins everything)

```
 ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐
 │   LLM    │──►│   Your   │──►│  Uvicorn │──►│  Nginx / │──►│  Browser │
 │ provider │   │   app    │   │          │   │   CDN    │   │          │
 └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘
       │              │              │              │              │
   buffer?        buffer?        buffer?        BUFFER!        buffer?
   provider       ← YOUR         no, sends       ← THE          browsers
   SDK may        MIDDLEWARE     each chunk      #1 CAUSE       may buffer
   batch          may buffer     immediately     OF "MY         until a
                  (Ch. 4)                        STREAMING      newline or
                                                 DOESN'T        4KB for
                                                 WORK"          text/plain
```

**Fixing each layer:**

```nginx
# nginx.conf — the four directives that matter
location /v1/chat/completions {
    proxy_pass http://api_backend;
    proxy_buffering off;            # ← THE critical one: don't accumulate
    proxy_cache off;
    proxy_read_timeout 300s;        # a long generation must not be cut off
    proxy_http_version 1.1;         # chunked encoding requires 1.1
    proxy_set_header Connection ''; # don't send "Connection: close" upstream
    chunked_transfer_encoding on;
}
```

```python
# Application-side: an escape hatch that works even without nginx access
return StreamingResponse(
    generate(),
    media_type="text/event-stream",
    headers={
        "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",  # no-transform stops CDN rewriting
        "Connection": "keep-alive",
        "X-Accel-Buffering": "no",   # ← Nginx reads this and disables buffering
                                     #   for THIS response. Works when you can't
                                     #   edit nginx.conf. Also honoured by some CDNs.
    },
)
```

**`X-Accel-Buffering: no` is the single most useful header in this chapter.** Memorise it. It is the fix for "streaming works locally but not in production" roughly 70% of the time.

**Browser buffering.** For `text/plain`, some browsers buffer until 1 KB. `text/event-stream` is never buffered — another reason to use SSE rather than raw text streaming.

**Your own middleware.** Covered in Chapter 4: `BaseHTTPMiddleware` that touches `response.body_iterator` will collect the whole stream. Audit for it.

### 9.3.3 Backpressure

```
 The LLM generates at 50 tokens/s. The client reads at 5 tokens/s
 (slow mobile connection).  Where do the extra tokens go?

 ┌────────┐  fast   ┌──────────┐  slow   ┌────────┐
 │  LLM   │────────►│ your app │────────►│ client │
 └────────┘         └──────────┘         └────────┘
                          │
                    tokens accumulate HERE
                    in the OS socket buffer, then in your generator's
                    suspended state

 asyncio HANDLES this correctly: `await send(...)` does not return until the
 transport accepts the data. So your generator naturally SLOWS DOWN to the
 client's pace. This is backpressure, and it works for free.

 ⚠ It works for free ONLY if you don't defeat it:
   ❌ pre-collecting all tokens into a list, then yielding them
   ❌ an unbounded asyncio.Queue between the provider and the response
   ✔ yielding directly from the provider's async iterator
```

**But there is a cost you must handle:** if the client is slow or has disconnected, your generator stays suspended, holding the provider connection open and continuing to be billed. Detect disconnection:

```python
@app.post("/v1/chat/stream")
async def chat_stream(payload: ChatRequest, request: Request):
    async def generate():
        async for token in llm.stream(payload):
            if await request.is_disconnected():     # cheap check per token
                log.info("client_disconnected_mid_stream")
                break                                # stop generating; stop paying
            yield f"data: {json.dumps({'delta': token})}\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(generate(), media_type="text/event-stream")
```

## 9.4 Syntax

```python
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse, FileResponse

StreamingResponse(
    content,                        # sync or async generator/iterator of str|bytes
    status_code=200,
    headers={"X-Accel-Buffering": "no"},
    media_type="text/event-stream",
    background=BackgroundTask(fn),  # runs AFTER the stream completes
)
```

**The content iterator can be:**

```python
# async generator (the normal case)
async def gen():
    async for chunk in upstream:
        yield chunk

# sync generator (runs in a threadpool — acceptable for file reads)
def gen():
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        while chunk := f.read(64 * 1024):
            yield chunk

# any async iterable
StreamingResponse(response.aiter_bytes())     # httpx streaming response
```

**The SSE wire format** (full details in Chapter 14):

```
 data: <payload>\n\n              ← the message; double newline terminates it
 event: <name>\n                  ← optional event type
 id: <id>\n                       ← optional; used for reconnection
 retry: <ms>\n                    ← optional; reconnection delay hint
 : this is a comment\n\n          ← keep-alive ping (ignored by clients)
```

## 9.5 Beginner Examples

```python
import asyncio, json
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/stream/text")
async def stream_text():
    async def gen():
        for word in "Streaming makes an AI product feel alive".split():
            yield word + " "
            await asyncio.sleep(0.3)
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/plain")

@app.get("/stream/sse")
async def stream_sse():
    async def gen():
        for i, word in enumerate("Hello from a server sent event".split()):
            yield f"data: {json.dumps({'index': i, 'token': word})}\n\n"
            await asyncio.sleep(0.3)
        yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream",
                             headers={"X-Accel-Buffering": "no"})
```

```bash
curl -N localhost:8000/stream/sse
```
**Output (arriving one line every 0.3 s):**
```
data: {"index": 0, "token": "Hello"}

data: {"index": 1, "token": "from"}
...
data: [DONE]
```

**`curl -N` disables curl's own buffering.** Without it you will see everything at once and conclude your server is broken. This wastes an hour of someone's life about once a week somewhere in the world.

## 9.6 Intermediate Examples

### A real LLM streaming endpoint

```python
# app/api/v1/chat.py
import json, time
from fastapi import APIRouter, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

router = APIRouter(prefix="/v1/chat", tags=["chat"])

@router.post("/completions/stream")
async def stream_completion(
    payload: ChatRequest,
    request: Request,
    user: CurrentUser,
    svc: ChatSvc,
    _rl: RateLimited,
    _q: QuotaChecked,
):
    request_id = get_request_id()
    started = time.perf_counter()

    async def event_stream():
        prompt_tokens = 0
        completion_tokens = 0
        first_token_at: float | None = None
        finish_reason = "stop"

        try:
            # Emit metadata FIRST so the client can render a header immediately.
            yield _sse({"type": "start", "id": request_id, "model": payload.model})

            async for event in svc.stream(payload, user=user):
                if await request.is_disconnected():
                    finish_reason = "client_disconnect"
                    break

                if event.type == "token":
                    if first_token_at is None:
                        first_token_at = time.perf_counter()
                        TTFT.labels(model=payload.model).observe(
                            first_token_at - started)
                    completion_tokens += 1
                    yield _sse({"type": "delta", "content": event.text})

                elif event.type == "tool_call":
                    yield _sse({"type": "tool_call", "name": event.name,
                                "arguments": event.arguments})

                elif event.type == "usage":
                    prompt_tokens = event.prompt_tokens

            # Final frame carries usage so the client can display cost.
            yield _sse({
                "type": "done",
                "finish_reason": finish_reason,
                "usage": {"prompt_tokens": prompt_tokens,
                          "completion_tokens": completion_tokens,
                          "total_tokens": prompt_tokens + completion_tokens},
                "latency_ms": int((time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000),
            })

        except ContextLengthExceededError as exc:
            yield _sse({"type": "error", "code": "context_length_exceeded",
                        "message": str(exc), "request_id": request_id})
        except Exception:
            log.exception("stream_failed", request_id=request_id)
            yield _sse({"type": "error", "code": "internal_error",
                        "message": "Generation failed", "request_id": request_id})
        finally:
            # ⚠ ALWAYS runs — including on client disconnect and on error.
            # This is where billing and metrics MUST happen, because the
            # normal "after the response" hooks may never fire.
            yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
            await svc.record_usage(
                user_id=user.id, model=payload.model,
                prompt_tokens=prompt_tokens, completion_tokens=completion_tokens,
                finish_reason=finish_reason,
            )

    return StreamingResponse(
        event_stream(),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={
            "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
            "Connection": "keep-alive",
            "X-Accel-Buffering": "no",
            "X-Request-ID": request_id,
        },
    )

def _sse(obj: dict) -> str:
    return f"data: {json.dumps(obj, ensure_ascii=False)}\n\n"
```

**Six design decisions in that code, each deliberate:**

1. **A `start` event first.** The client can render the model name and a spinner immediately, and it proves the connection works before the first token arrives (which may take 800 ms).
2. **Typed events**, not bare text. You will need to stream tool calls, citations, and errors later; a `{"type": ...}` envelope makes that additive rather than breaking.
3. **TTFT measured separately from total latency.** Time-to-first-token is the metric users actually feel. Total latency is what you bill on. They need separate histograms.
4. **Disconnect checked every token.** Stops generation, stops billing.
5. **Usage recorded in `finally`.** If the client disconnects at token 300, you were still charged for 300 tokens. Recording usage only on the success path means systematically under-billing and losing the data you need to debug abandonment.
6. **`[DONE]` sentinel.** OpenAI-compatible; tells clients the stream ended normally rather than being cut.

### Proxying a provider's stream

The most common real implementation: pass the provider's stream through, translating the format.

```python
async def stream_openai(payload: ChatRequest, http: httpx.AsyncClient,
                        api_key: str) -> AsyncIterator[StreamEvent]:
    body = payload.to_openai_payload() | {"stream": True,
                                          "stream_options": {"include_usage": True}}
    async with http.stream(
        "POST", "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",
        json=body, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
        timeout=httpx.Timeout(connect=5.0, read=300.0, write=10.0, pool=5.0),
    ) as response:
        if response.status_code != 200:
            await response.aread()               # must read before accessing .text
            raise map_provider_error(response)

        async for line in response.aiter_lines():
            if not line.startswith("data: "):
                continue
            data = line[6:]
            if data == "[DONE]":
                break
            chunk = json.loads(data)

            if usage := chunk.get("usage"):      # final chunk with include_usage
                yield StreamEvent(type="usage",
                                  prompt_tokens=usage["prompt_tokens"],
                                  completion_tokens=usage["completion_tokens"])
                continue

            choice = chunk["choices"][0]
            delta = choice.get("delta", {})
            if content := delta.get("content"):
                yield StreamEvent(type="token", text=content)
            if tool_calls := delta.get("tool_calls"):
                yield StreamEvent(type="tool_call_delta", tool_calls=tool_calls)
            if reason := choice.get("finish_reason"):
                yield StreamEvent(type="finish", finish_reason=reason)
```

**Three things that bite people here:**

- **`read=300.0`, not the default.** The default httpx read timeout applies *between chunks*; a model thinking hard before its first token can exceed a 30 s default and kill the stream.
- **`stream_options: {"include_usage": true}`** — without it, OpenAI's streaming responses contain **no token counts at all**, and you have to estimate them for billing. Estimation drift is a real revenue problem.
- **Tool calls arrive as deltas** with fragments of a JSON string spread across chunks. You must accumulate them per index before parsing.

```python
# Accumulating streamed tool calls — a fiddly detail worth getting right
tool_buffers: dict[int, dict] = {}

async for event in stream:
    if event.type == "tool_call_delta":
        for tc in event.tool_calls:
            idx = tc["index"]
            buf = tool_buffers.setdefault(idx, {"id": "", "name": "", "arguments": ""})
            buf["id"] += tc.get("id", "")
            fn = tc.get("function", {})
            buf["name"] += fn.get("name", "")
            buf["arguments"] += fn.get("arguments", "")   # JSON string, in FRAGMENTS

# Only parse once the stream finishes — mid-stream JSON is invalid.
for idx, buf in tool_buffers.items():
    args = ToolSchemas[buf["name"]].model_validate_json(buf["arguments"])
```

## 9.7 Production Example — A Complete Streaming Architecture

### The event protocol

Define and publish it. Clients depend on it.

```python
# app/schemas/streaming.py
from typing import Literal, Annotated, Union
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class StartEvent(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["start"] = "start"
    id: str
    model: str
    created: int

class DeltaEvent(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["delta"] = "delta"
    content: str

class ThinkingEvent(BaseModel):
    """Reasoning traces, shown in a collapsible UI section."""
    type: Literal["thinking"] = "thinking"
    content: str

class ToolCallEvent(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["tool_call"] = "tool_call"
    id: str
    name: str
    arguments: dict

class ToolResultEvent(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["tool_result"] = "tool_result"
    tool_call_id: str
    content: str
    is_error: bool = False

class CitationEvent(BaseModel):
    """Emitted as sources are used, so the UI can render them inline."""
    type: Literal["citation"] = "citation"
    document_id: str
    chunk_id: str
    title: str
    url: str | None = None
    score: float

class ErrorEvent(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["error"] = "error"
    code: str
    message: str
    request_id: str
    retryable: bool = False

class DoneEvent(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["done"] = "done"
    finish_reason: Literal["stop", "length", "tool_calls", "content_filter",
                           "client_disconnect", "error"]
    usage: Usage
    latency_ms: int

StreamEvent = Annotated[
    Union[StartEvent, DeltaEvent, ThinkingEvent, ToolCallEvent, ToolResultEvent,
          CitationEvent, ErrorEvent, DoneEvent],
    Field(discriminator="type"),
]
```

Publish this as part of your API documentation. A typed event protocol is the difference between clients that work and clients that guess.

### Keep-alive for slow starts

A RAG pipeline may take 3 seconds before the first token (embed → search → rerank → prompt → model TTFT). Proxies and browsers may time out an idle connection:

```python
async def with_keepalive(source: AsyncIterator[str],
                         interval_s: float = 15.0) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
    """Emit an SSE comment every `interval_s` while waiting, so intermediaries
    see traffic and don't close the connection."""
    iterator = source.__aiter__()
    while True:
        try:
            chunk = await asyncio.wait_for(iterator.__anext__(), timeout=interval_s)
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            yield ": keep-alive\n\n"        # a COMMENT — clients ignore it
            continue
        except StopAsyncIteration:
            return
        yield chunk
```

### Resumable streams

A mobile client that loses connectivity mid-answer should be able to resume rather than regenerate (which costs money and produces a different answer).

```python
class StreamBuffer:
    """Persist emitted events so a reconnecting client can replay from an offset."""

    def __init__(self, redis: Redis, ttl_s: int = 3600):
        self._redis, self._ttl = redis, ttl_s

    async def append(self, stream_id: str, index: int, event: str) -> None:
        await self._redis.rpush(f"stream:{stream_id}", event)
        await self._redis.expire(f"stream:{stream_id}", self._ttl)

    async def replay(self, stream_id: str, from_index: int) -> list[str]:
        return await self._redis.lrange(f"stream:{stream_id}", from_index, -1)

@router.post("/completions/stream")
async def stream_completion(payload: ChatRequest, request: Request,
                            last_event_id: Annotated[str | None, Header()] = None):
    stream_id = payload.stream_id or str(uuid4())

    async def generate():
        start_index = 0
        if last_event_id:                       # SSE reconnection: replay first
            replayed = await buffer.replay(stream_id, int(last_event_id) + 1)
            for i, event in enumerate(replayed, start=int(last_event_id) + 1):
                yield f"id: {i}\n{event}"
            start_index = int(last_event_id) + 1 + len(replayed)

        async for i, event in aenumerate(generate_events(payload), start=start_index):
            payload_str = _sse_body(event)
            await buffer.append(stream_id, i, payload_str)
            yield f"id: {i}\n{payload_str}"     # `id:` is what the browser sends back
```

The browser's `EventSource` automatically sends `Last-Event-ID` on reconnect. Emitting `id:` on every event is what makes resumption possible, and it costs almost nothing.

### Graceful shutdown with active streams

```python
# The problem: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM. Uvicorn stops accepting new connections
# and waits for in-flight requests. A 5-minute agent stream blocks the shutdown
# until terminationGracePeriodSeconds expires, then SIGKILL cuts it mid-sentence.

class StreamRegistry:
    """Track active streams so shutdown can notify them."""
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._active: set[asyncio.Event] = set()
        self.draining = False

    @contextlib.contextmanager
    def track(self):
        stop = asyncio.Event()
        self._active.add(stop)
        try:
            yield stop
        finally:
            self._active.discard(stop)

    async def drain(self, grace_s: float = 30.0) -> None:
        self.draining = True
        for stop in self._active:
            stop.set()                       # ask every stream to finish early
        deadline = time.monotonic() + grace_s
        while self._active and time.monotonic() < deadline:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.25)

# In the generator:
with registry.track() as stop_requested:
    async for token in llm.stream(payload):
        if stop_requested.is_set():
            yield _sse({"type": "done", "finish_reason": "server_shutdown",
                        "resume_token": stream_id})
            break
        yield _sse({"type": "delta", "content": token})

# In lifespan:
@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    yield
    await app.state.stream_registry.drain(grace_s=30)
```

And in Kubernetes:
```yaml
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120   # MUST exceed your longest expected stream
```

## 9.8 AI Engineering Perspective

### The metrics that actually matter for streaming AI

```
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ TTFT — Time To First Token                                             │
 │   What the user perceives as "did it work?"                            │
 │   Target: < 1 s. Above 2 s feels broken.                               │
 │   Dominated by: prompt length, model, queue depth at the provider,      │
 │                 and (for RAG) retrieval time BEFORE generation starts.  │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ TPS — Tokens Per Second (inter-token latency)                          │
 │   What the user perceives as "reading speed".                          │
 │   Human reading is ~5–8 words/s ≈ 7–11 tokens/s.                       │
 │   Above ~20 tok/s, faster is imperceptible. Below 10 it feels slow.    │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ E2E — total wall clock                                                 │
 │   What you bill on and what capacity planning uses.                    │
 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ ABANDONMENT RATE — fraction of streams the client disconnects early    │
 │   The most under-instrumented metric in AI products. A rising rate     │
 │   means slow TTFT, bad answers, or a broken client. Track it.          │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

```python
TTFT = Histogram("llm_ttft_seconds", "Time to first token", ["model"],
                 buckets=(.1, .25, .5, .75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5, 10, 30))
TPS = Histogram("llm_tokens_per_second", "Generation speed", ["model"],
                buckets=(1, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200))
STREAM_ABANDONED = Counter("llm_streams_abandoned_total", "Client disconnects",
                           ["model"])
```

### Streaming a full RAG pipeline

Users should see progress during the 3 seconds *before* generation starts:

```python
async def stream_rag(query: str, kb_id: UUID, org: Organization):
    yield _sse({"type": "status", "stage": "embedding"})
    embedding = await embedder.embed(query)

    yield _sse({"type": "status", "stage": "searching"})
    hits = await vector_store.search(embedding, kb_id=kb_id, top_k=20)

    yield _sse({"type": "status", "stage": "reranking"})
    top = await reranker.rerank(query, hits, top_k=5)

    # Emit citations BEFORE generation — the UI renders sources while the
    # answer is still being written. This is a large perceived-quality win.
    for hit in top:
        yield _sse(CitationEvent(document_id=str(hit.doc_id), chunk_id=str(hit.id),
                                 title=hit.title, score=hit.score).model_dump())

    yield _sse({"type": "status", "stage": "generating"})
    async for token in llm.stream(build_prompt(query, top)):
        yield _sse({"type": "delta", "content": token})
```

The user sees: *embedding → searching → reranking → [5 source cards appear] → answer streams in.* Every stage transition is proof the system is working. Perceived latency collapses even though total time is unchanged.

### Streaming agent execution

```
   AGENT LOOP, STREAMED

   {"type":"thinking","content":"I need to look up the user's recent orders"}
   {"type":"tool_call","name":"search_orders","arguments":{"user_id":"u_1"}}
   {"type":"tool_result","tool_call_id":"tc_1","content":"[3 orders found]"}
   {"type":"thinking","content":"The most recent order was delayed"}
   {"type":"delta","content":"Your"}
   {"type":"delta","content":" order"}
   ...
   {"type":"done","finish_reason":"stop","usage":{...}}
```

Streaming the agent's *reasoning and tool use*, not just its final text, is now a product expectation. It turns a 45-second opaque wait into a legible process. It also has a real support benefit: when the agent does something wrong, the user can see *where* it went wrong.

**⚠ Streamed tool calls must still pass full authorization.** Chapter 6 §6.8: the model proposes, your authorization layer disposes. Streaming does not change that — if anything it increases the temptation to execute eagerly, which is exactly the wrong instinct.

### Cost control during streaming

```python
async def stream_with_budget(source, *, max_tokens: int, max_cost_usd: float,
                             cost_per_token: float):
    tokens = 0
    async for event in source:
        if event.type == "token":
            tokens += 1
            if tokens >= max_tokens:
                yield DoneEvent(finish_reason="length", ...)
                return
            if tokens * cost_per_token >= max_cost_usd:
                yield ErrorEvent(code="budget_exceeded",
                                 message="Response budget reached")
                return
        yield event
```

A runaway generation (a model that starts repeating itself) can produce tens of thousands of tokens. A hard stop in the stream loop is your last line of defence after `max_tokens`.

## 9.9 Backend Engineering Perspective

**Capacity planning changes completely.**

```
 NON-STREAMING API                    STREAMING API
 ─────────────────                    ─────────────
 metric: requests/second              metric: CONCURRENT CONNECTIONS
 a request occupies a worker          a connection occupies memory + a file
   slot for 200 ms                      descriptor for 30 SECONDS
 1000 rps × 0.2 s = 200 concurrent    1000 streams × 30 s = 30,000 concurrent

 Limits you will hit, in order:
   1. file descriptors      (ulimit -n; default 1024 — raise to 65536)
   2. ephemeral ports on the LB
   3. memory per connection (~10-50 KB for asyncio; fine)
   4. the PROVIDER's concurrency limit (usually the real ceiling)
```

**Load balancer configuration:**

```
 ❌ Round-robin       long-lived connections accumulate unevenly; one pod
                      ends up with 3× the streams
 ✔ Least-connections  the correct algorithm for long-lived connections
 ✔ Long idle timeout  ALB default is 60 s — will kill a 90 s generation
 ✔ Sticky sessions    NOT needed if streams are stateless (they should be)
```

**HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 for streaming.** Browsers limit HTTP/1.1 to ~6 connections per origin. If a user opens 7 tabs of your chat app, the seventh hangs. HTTP/2 multiplexes hundreds of streams over one connection and eliminates the problem entirely. **Enable HTTP/2 at your load balancer** — it's usually one setting, and it's the fix for a bug class that's very hard to diagnose from the server side.

## 9.10 Performance

```
 Per-chunk ASGI send overhead              ~10 µs
 SSE framing (f-string + encode)           ~2 µs
 json.dumps per event, small               ~3 µs
 Per-token overhead, total                 ~15 µs
 → at 50 tokens/s that is 0.075% CPU. Negligible.

 Memory per idle streaming connection      ~10–50 KB
 10,000 concurrent streams                 ~200–500 MB. Fine.
```

**Optimisations:**

1. **Batch small tokens.** Emitting one SSE frame per token at 100 tok/s means 100 syscalls/s per stream. Coalescing every ~30 ms is invisible to users and cuts overhead substantially:
```python
async def coalesce(source, interval_s: float = 0.03):
    buffer, last = "", time.monotonic()
    async for token in source:
        buffer += token
        if time.monotonic() - last >= interval_s:
            yield buffer; buffer, last = "", time.monotonic()
    if buffer:
        yield buffer
```
2. **Never gzip a stream.** It buffers to fill compression blocks.
3. **Use `orjson`** for event serialisation if events are large (citations with metadata).
4. **Don't re-validate every event through Pydantic** on the hot path — construct the dict directly, or use `model_dump_json()` once per event type shape.
5. **Check disconnection per token, not per byte.** `request.is_disconnected()` is cheap but not free.

## 9.11 Security

**1. Authentication happens once, at connection time.** A 20-minute stream cannot re-verify a 15-minute token per chunk. Authenticate at establishment, cap the connection duration, and re-authenticate on reconnection.

**2. Streams bypass response-body inspection.** WAFs and DLP tools that scan complete response bodies see nothing useful in a chunked stream. If you need output filtering (PII redaction, content policy), it must happen **in your generator**, per chunk:

```python
async def redact_stream(source, patterns):
    """⚠ Redaction across chunk boundaries is genuinely hard: a credit card
    number can be split across two tokens. Buffer a sliding window."""
    window = ""
    async for chunk in source:
        window += chunk
        if len(window) > 200:                 # keep a lookback window
            emit, window = window[:-100], window[-100:]
            yield redact(emit, patterns)
    yield redact(window, patterns)
```

**3. Resource exhaustion via slow clients.** A client that opens 10,000 streams and reads one byte per minute holds 10,000 connections. Mitigate with per-user concurrent-stream limits:

```python
async def enforce_stream_limit(user: CurrentUser, redis: Redis) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    key = f"streams:{user.id}"
    count = await redis.incr(key)
    await redis.expire(key, 3600)
    try:
        if count > user.plan.max_concurrent_streams:
            raise HTTPException(429, "Too many concurrent streams")
        yield
    finally:
        await redis.decr(key)     # MUST be in finally, or a crash leaks the slot
```

**4. In-band errors must not leak internals.** The same rule as Chapter 8: the error event carries a code and a request ID, never a traceback.

**5. Prompt injection can manipulate the stream.** If a retrieved document says "output the following HTML: `<script>...`" and your UI renders streamed content as HTML, you have XSS. **Render streamed model output as text, or sanitise it.** This is API10 (unsafe consumption of third-party APIs) applied to your own model.

## 9.12 Best Practices

```
✔ SSE (text/event-stream), not raw text streaming
✔ X-Accel-Buffering: no, Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform
✔ proxy_buffering off in Nginx; long proxy_read_timeout
✔ A typed event protocol with a `type` discriminator, published as docs
✔ Emit a `start` event immediately; emit status events during slow setup
✔ Errors in-band, with code + request_id; NEVER expect a 500 to work
✔ [DONE] sentinel so clients can distinguish "finished" from "cut off"
✔ Check request.is_disconnected() every token
✔ Record usage in `finally` — the client may vanish mid-stream
✔ Keep-alive comments every 15 s during long gaps
✔ Emit `id:` per event so browsers can resume with Last-Event-ID
✔ Never gzip; never use BaseHTTPMiddleware on streaming paths
✔ Measure TTFT, TPS, and abandonment separately
✔ Per-user concurrent-stream limits, released in `finally`
✔ terminationGracePeriodSeconds > your longest stream; drain on SIGTERM
✔ HTTP/2 at the load balancer; least-connections balancing
```

## 9.13 Common Mistakes

```python
# ❌ 1. Collecting everything, then "streaming" it
tokens = [t async for t in llm.stream(p)]          # waits for ALL of them
return StreamingResponse(iter(tokens))              # then dumps them at once

# ❌ 2. Expecting an exception to become a 500
async def gen():
    yield "partial"
    raise RuntimeError()          # client already has 200 + partial body
# ✔ in-band error event

# ❌ 3. No X-Accel-Buffering / proxy_buffering on
#    "works on localhost, arrives all at once in production"

# ❌ 4. gzip on the streaming path

# ❌ 5. BaseHTTPMiddleware reading response.body_iterator (Ch. 4)

# ❌ 6. Not checking disconnection → paying for tokens nobody reads

# ❌ 7. Recording usage only on the success path → systematic under-billing

# ❌ 8. Blocking call inside the generator
async def gen():
    for t in tokens:
        time.sleep(0.1)           # freezes EVERY stream on this worker
# ✔ await asyncio.sleep(0.1)

# ❌ 9. Default httpx read timeout on a provider stream → cut off before TTFT
# ✔ timeout=httpx.Timeout(connect=5, read=300)

# ❌ 10. Forgetting stream_options: {"include_usage": true} → no token counts

# ❌ 11. Parsing accumulated tool-call JSON mid-stream → it's incomplete

# ❌ 12. Rendering streamed model output as HTML → XSS via prompt injection

# ❌ 13. No concurrent-stream limit → one user holds every connection

# ❌ 14. terminationGracePeriodSeconds shorter than a stream → cut mid-sentence

# ❌ 15. Round-robin load balancing for long-lived connections → uneven load
```

## 9.14 Interview Questions

1. **Why stream LLM responses?** Perceived latency. Total time is unchanged, but TTFT drops from seconds to sub-second, which is the difference between feeling instant and feeling broken.

2. **How does HTTP stream without a Content-Length?** Chunked transfer encoding in HTTP/1.1 (length-prefixed chunks, zero-length terminator) or DATA frames in HTTP/2.

3. **Why can't you return a 500 from a failed stream?** `http.response.start` — status and headers — is sent before the first chunk. The status is committed. Errors must be delivered in-band as part of the stream protocol.

4. **What's the most common cause of "streaming doesn't work in production"?** Nginx `proxy_buffering on` (the default). Fix with `proxy_buffering off` or by sending `X-Accel-Buffering: no`.

5. **Why SSE rather than WebSockets for LLM output?** The flow is one-directional. SSE is plain HTTP — it works with existing auth, middleware, proxies, and load balancers, and it reconnects automatically. WebSockets add a protocol and complexity you don't need.

6. **What is backpressure and does asyncio handle it?** Yes: `await send(...)` doesn't return until the transport accepts the data, so a slow client naturally slows the generator. You defeat it by buffering into an unbounded queue or pre-collecting tokens.

7. **How do you detect a disconnected client?** `await request.is_disconnected()` inside the generator loop. Break out to stop generating and stop paying.

8. **Where must you record usage for a stream?** In a `finally` block. The client can vanish at token 300 and you were still billed for 300 tokens; recording only on success systematically under-bills and hides abandonment.

9. **What is TTFT and why measure it separately?** Time to first token — what users perceive as responsiveness. Total latency is what you bill on. They have different distributions and different causes; a single latency histogram hides both.

10. **How do you keep a connection alive during a slow RAG setup?** Emit SSE comments (`: keep-alive\n\n`) every ~15 s, and better, emit real status events so the user sees progress.

11. **How do resumable streams work?** Emit `id:` with each event; browsers send `Last-Event-ID` on reconnect; the server replays buffered events from that index (from Redis) and continues.

12. **Why does streaming change capacity planning?** You plan by concurrent connections, not requests per second. 1,000 streams lasting 30 s is 30,000 simultaneous connections, and you'll hit file descriptor limits before CPU.

13. **What load balancing algorithm should you use?** Least-connections. Round-robin distributes *connections* evenly at creation, but long-lived streams accumulate unevenly.

14. **Why enable HTTP/2 for a streaming API?** Browsers cap HTTP/1.1 at ~6 connections per origin, so a user with several tabs open gets hangs. HTTP/2 multiplexes and removes the limit.

15. **How do you handle SIGTERM with a 5-minute stream active?** Fail readiness immediately, notify active streams to finish early with a `finish_reason` and a resume token, drain with a grace period, and set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` above your longest expected stream.

16. **How do you accumulate streamed tool calls?** Buffer per index, concatenating `id`, `name`, and the `arguments` JSON *fragments*; only parse and validate after the stream completes, since mid-stream JSON is invalid.

17. **What does `stream_options: {"include_usage": true}` do and why does it matter?** It makes OpenAI emit a final chunk containing token counts. Without it, streaming responses carry no usage data and you must estimate — which drifts from actual billing.

18. **How do you cap runaway generation?** `max_tokens` on the request, plus a hard token and cost counter in the streaming loop that terminates with `finish_reason: "length"` or a budget error.

19. **What are the security implications of streaming?** Output-inspection tools see nothing useful, so filtering must happen in your generator (with a sliding window across chunk boundaries); slow clients can exhaust connections, so per-user stream limits are needed; and streamed model output rendered as HTML is an XSS vector.

20. **Why must the stream-limit decrement be in a `finally`?** Otherwise a crash or disconnect leaks a slot permanently, and the user is locked out until the key expires.

21. **How do you stream a whole RAG pipeline?** Emit status events for each stage (embedding, searching, reranking), emit citations before generation so sources render early, then stream tokens. The user sees continuous progress instead of three silent seconds.

22. **Should you batch tokens before sending?** Yes, coalescing over ~30 ms windows. It's imperceptible to users and materially reduces syscall and framing overhead at high token rates.

23. **How do you test a streaming endpoint?** Assert on *timing*, not just content: collect chunks with arrival timestamps and assert the first arrives within X ms and that inter-chunk gaps exist. A test that only checks the concatenated body passes even when buffering has broken streaming entirely.

24. **What's the `[DONE]` sentinel for?** It lets a client distinguish a completed stream from a truncated one. Without it, a connection drop and a normal ending look identical.

25. **Design the streaming layer for a production AI chat product.** SSE with a typed, discriminated event protocol (start, status, citation, thinking, tool_call, delta, error, done); `X-Accel-Buffering: no` plus `proxy_buffering off`; keep-alives during setup; per-event `id:` with Redis-backed replay for resumption; disconnect detection and usage recorded in `finally`; per-user concurrent-stream limits; TTFT/TPS/abandonment metrics; HTTP/2 and least-connections at the LB; graceful drain on SIGTERM with resume tokens; and in-band errors carrying a request ID.

## 9.15 Exercises

**Easy**
1. Build a `/stream` endpoint emitting a word every 0.3 s. Verify with `curl -N` that chunks arrive incrementally.
2. Convert it to SSE with a JSON payload and a `[DONE]` sentinel.
3. Add `X-Accel-Buffering: no` and the correct cache headers.

**Medium**
4. Build a streaming endpoint that proxies a real (or stubbed) provider stream, translating the format.
5. Add disconnect detection and prove with a test that generation stops when the client goes away.
6. Add usage accounting in `finally` and assert it records correctly on normal completion, on error, and on disconnect.
7. Implement token coalescing over 30 ms and measure the reduction in send calls.

**Hard**
8. Implement the full typed event protocol and stream a complete RAG pipeline with status events and early citations.
9. Implement resumable streams with `id:`, `Last-Event-ID`, and Redis-backed replay; test by killing and reconnecting a client mid-stream.
10. Implement graceful shutdown: a stream registry, SIGTERM draining, resume tokens, and a test that no stream is cut without a `done` event.

**Production**
11. Build a complete streaming chat backend with everything above, plus per-user concurrency limits, TTFT/TPS/abandonment metrics, cost caps in-stream, and a timing-based test suite that fails if buffering is ever reintroduced anywhere in the stack.

## 9.16 Solutions

**Solution 11 (partial) — the timing test that catches buffering regressions.**
```python
import time, pytest, httpx

@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_stream_is_actually_incremental(app):
    """The test that matters. A content-only assertion passes even when a
    middleware has silently buffered the entire response."""
    timings: list[tuple[float, str]] = []
    start = time.perf_counter()

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(app=app, base_url="http://test") as client:
        async with client.stream("POST", "/v1/chat/completions/stream",
                                 json={"messages": [{"role": "user",
                                                     "content": "count to five"}]},
                                 headers=AUTH) as response:
            assert response.status_code == 200
            assert response.headers["content-type"].startswith("text/event-stream")
            assert response.headers.get("x-accel-buffering") == "no"
            async for line in response.aiter_lines():
                if line.startswith("data: "):
                    timings.append((time.perf_counter() - start, line))

    assert len(timings) >= 5, "expected multiple events"
    # 1. The first event must arrive quickly.
    assert timings[0][0] < 0.5, f"TTFB was {timings[0][0]:.2f}s — buffering?"
    # 2. Events must be SPREAD OVER TIME, not all at the end.
    spread = timings[-1][0] - timings[0][0]
    assert spread > 0.3, f"all events arrived within {spread:.3f}s — buffered"
    # 3. The stream must terminate properly.
    assert timings[-1][1] == "data: [DONE]"
```
**Reasoning:** assertion 2 is the one that earns its keep. Someone adds a logging middleware six months from now, it buffers the body, and every content-based test still passes — the user-visible behaviour is destroyed and CI is green. Asserting that events are *spread over time* is the only way to test the property you actually care about.

**Solution 6 — usage accounting across all three exit paths.**
```python
async def event_stream():
    tokens = 0
    reason = "stop"
    try:
        async for token in svc.stream(payload):
            if await request.is_disconnected():
                reason = "client_disconnect"; break
            tokens += 1
            yield _sse({"type": "delta", "content": token})
    except Exception:
        reason = "error"
        log.exception("stream_failed")
        yield _sse({"type": "error", "code": "internal_error",
                    "request_id": rid})
        raise
    finally:
        # Runs on: normal completion, exception, client disconnect, AND
        # GeneratorExit if the response is closed early.
        await usage_repo.record(user_id=user.id, model=payload.model,
                                completion_tokens=tokens, finish_reason=reason)

# tests
async def test_usage_recorded_on_disconnect(client, usage_repo):
    async with client.stream("POST", "/v1/chat/completions/stream", json=BODY) as r:
        async for _ in r.aiter_lines():
            break                              # disconnect after one event
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    record = await usage_repo.latest()
    assert record.finish_reason == "client_disconnect"
    assert record.completion_tokens > 0        # we WERE billed for these
```
**Reasoning:** the `finally` also catches `GeneratorExit`, which is what Python raises into a suspended generator when the response is closed. Without it, every abandoned stream is invisible in your billing data — and abandonment is exactly the signal you need to diagnose a slow TTFT problem.

## 9.17 Mini Project — A Production Streaming Chat Backend

**Goal.** The streaming layer of a ChatGPT-style product.

**Requirements:**
1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with a `stream` flag, and `/stream` as an explicit alias.
2. Typed event protocol (§9.7) published in the OpenAPI docs.
3. Full RAG streaming: status events, early citations, then tokens.
4. Provider proxying with format translation and `include_usage`.
5. Keep-alive comments during gaps > 15 s.
6. Disconnect detection; usage recorded in `finally`.
7. Resumable streams with `id:` + `Last-Event-ID` + Redis replay (1 h TTL).
8. Per-user concurrent-stream limits, released in `finally`.
9. In-stream token and cost caps.
10. TTFT, TPS, E2E, and abandonment metrics.
11. Graceful shutdown with stream draining and resume tokens.
12. Nginx config with `proxy_buffering off` and a 300 s read timeout.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- TTFT p95 under 1 s for a cached-embedding query.
- The timing test from §9.16 passes through the *full* production middleware stack.
- Killing a client mid-stream stops provider billing within one token.
- Reconnecting with `Last-Event-ID` resumes without regenerating.
- SIGTERM during 50 active streams: every one receives a `done` event; none is cut.
- A 100-tab load test (HTTP/2) shows no connection starvation.

## Chapter 9 Summary

| Idea | The one-line version |
|---|---|
| Streaming is perception, not speed | same total time; 16× better felt latency |
| The status code is committed early | errors must be in-band, never a 500 |
| Nginx buffers by default | `proxy_buffering off` / `X-Accel-Buffering: no` |
| Never gzip a stream | compression buffers, defeating the entire point |
| asyncio gives backpressure free | unless you pre-collect or use an unbounded queue |
| Check disconnection per token | it stops generation and stops the bill |
| Record usage in `finally` | clients vanish mid-stream and you were still charged |
| Type your events | `{"type": ...}` makes tool calls and citations additive |
| Plan capacity by connections | 1,000 streams × 30 s = 30,000 concurrent |
| Drain on SIGTERM | with grace period > longest stream, and resume tokens |
| Test timing, not just content | a content-only test passes when buffering breaks streaming |

### Cheat Sheet

```python
StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream", headers={
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
    "Connection": "keep-alive",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": "no",
})

# SSE frame
f"id: {n}\nevent: {name}\ndata: {json.dumps(obj)}\n\n"
": keep-alive\n\n"        # comment / heartbeat
"data: [DONE]\n\n"        # sentinel

# Disconnect
if await request.is_disconnected(): break

# Provider stream
async with http.stream("POST", url, json=body,
                       timeout=httpx.Timeout(connect=5, read=300)) as r:
    async for line in r.aiter_lines(): ...
```
```nginx
proxy_buffering off; proxy_cache off; proxy_read_timeout 300s;
proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection '';
```

### Production Checklist
- [ ] `X-Accel-Buffering: no` + `proxy_buffering off` verified end-to-end
- [ ] No gzip and no `BaseHTTPMiddleware` on streaming paths
- [ ] Typed event protocol, documented, with `[DONE]`
- [ ] Keep-alives during long setup phases
- [ ] Disconnect detection; usage in `finally`
- [ ] Resumption via `id:` / `Last-Event-ID`
- [ ] Per-user concurrent-stream limits
- [ ] `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` > longest stream; drain implemented
- [ ] HTTP/2 + least-connections at the LB; file descriptor limits raised
- [ ] Timing-based tests in CI

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Authenticate at connection establishment; cap connection duration
- [ ] Output filtering inside the generator, with a cross-chunk window
- [ ] In-band errors carry a code and request ID only
- [ ] Streamed model output rendered as text or sanitised (XSS via injection)
- [ ] Stream slots released in `finally`
- [ ] Streamed tool calls fully authorized and schema-validated

### Performance Checklist
- [ ] Tokens coalesced over ~30 ms
- [ ] Provider read timeout raised (300 s), connect timeout kept short
- [ ] No blocking calls inside generators
- [ ] TTFT, TPS, E2E, and abandonment measured separately
- [ ] In-stream token and cost caps enforced
