# Chapter 10 — Async Programming

> If you learn one chapter of this guide deeply, make it this one. Every serious FastAPI performance problem, every mysterious "the server hangs under load", and every "why is my API slower than the model" traces back to a misunderstanding of the event loop.

## 10.1 Concept Overview

**The core insight.** A CPU executes instructions. Waiting for a network response is not an instruction — it is *nothing at all*. Traditional concurrency uses one OS thread per concurrent operation, so 1,000 waits cost 1,000 threads. Async concurrency notices that a waiting operation needs no thread, and uses one thread to manage thousands of waits.

```
   THREE REQUESTS, EACH: 10 ms CPU + 1,000 ms WAITING

   SEQUENTIAL (1 thread, blocking)
   ├──R1: [CPU]▓[═══════ waiting 1000ms ═══════]
   │                                            ├──R2: [CPU]▓[══════ 1000ms ══════]
   │                                                                               ├──R3...
   Total: 3,030 ms

   THREADED (3 threads, blocking)
   ├──R1: [CPU]▓[═══════ waiting 1000ms ═══════]
   ├──R2: [CPU]▓[═══════ waiting 1000ms ═══════]
   ├──R3: [CPU]▓[═══════ waiting 1000ms ═══════]
   Total: ~1,010 ms.  Cost: 3 OS threads (~24 MB of stack), kernel scheduling.

   ASYNC (1 thread, event loop)
   ├─R1:[CPU]▓──await──────────────────────────┐
   ├─R2:  [CPU]▓──await────────────────────────┼┐
   ├─R3:    [CPU]▓──await──────────────────────┼┼┐
   │        ↑ the single thread runs each      │││
   │          CPU segment, then parks the      ▼▼▼
   │          coroutine and moves on         all three resume as data arrives
   Total: ~1,030 ms.  Cost: 3 coroutine objects (~3 KB total).

   At 10,000 concurrent: threads = 80 GB of stacks (impossible).
                         async   = ~100 MB (routine).
```

**Why this dominates AI backends.** From Chapter 0: an LLM request is 99.9% waiting. Async is not a nice-to-have here; it is the difference between 250 req/s and 40 req/s on identical hardware.

**The one rule.** The event loop is a **single thread**. While your code runs, nothing else on that worker runs. `await` is the only place another coroutine can be scheduled. Therefore:

> **Any operation that takes meaningful CPU time or blocks without awaiting freezes every concurrent request on that worker.**

Everything else in this chapter is a consequence of that sentence.

## 10.2 Historical Background

```
 2001 ─ Twisted: callback-based async in Python. Powerful, and famous for
        "callback hell" — deeply nested inversion of control.
 2012 ─ Tulip / PEP 3156: Guido designs a standard async framework.
 2014 ─ `asyncio` ships in Python 3.4, using generators + `yield from`.
 2015 ─ PEP 492: `async`/`await` keywords (Python 3.5). Async code finally
        reads like sequential code. This is the change that made it usable.
 2016 ─ `async for`, `async with` (3.6). uvloop released (libuv, 2–4× faster).
 2018 ─ ASGI; Starlette; async database drivers mature (asyncpg, aiohttp).
 2019 ─ `asyncio.run()`, and `curio`/`trio` popularise STRUCTURED CONCURRENCY —
        the idea that tasks should have clear lifetimes tied to a scope.
 2021 ─ AnyIO unifies asyncio and trio. Starlette adopts it.
 2022 ─ Python 3.11: `TaskGroup` (structured concurrency in the stdlib),
        `asyncio.timeout()`, and exception groups. Big correctness improvements.
 2023+ ─ Async becomes mandatory for LLM serving. Python 3.12/3.13 continue
         improving; free-threaded builds (PEP 703) begin to change the GIL story.
```

**The `TaskGroup` change is worth calling out** because most tutorials still teach the older, more error-prone `gather` pattern. `TaskGroup` guarantees that no task outlives its scope and that failures cancel siblings — properties you had to build by hand before 3.11.

## 10.3 Internal Working

### 10.3.1 What a coroutine actually is

```python
async def fetch():
    return 42

c = fetch()
print(type(c))          # <class 'coroutine'>
print(c)                # <coroutine object fetch at 0x...>
# NOTHING HAS RUN YET.
```

**Calling an async function does not execute it.** It creates a coroutine object — a paused, resumable frame. It only runs when awaited (or scheduled as a task).

```python
# The classic bug this causes:
async def main():
    result = fetch()           # ❌ a coroutine object, not 42
    print(result + 1)          # TypeError: unsupported operand type(s)
    # RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'fetch' was never awaited
```

Under the hood, a coroutine is a generator with a different protocol:

```python
async def demo():
    print("A")
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    print("B")

c = demo()
c.send(None)        # prints "A", then SUSPENDS at the await
# The suspension yields control back to whoever called send().
```

`await` compiles to (essentially) "yield from" — the coroutine hands control up the stack to the event loop, along with a description of what it's waiting for.

### 10.3.2 The event loop

```
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                        THE EVENT LOOP, ONE ITERATION                     │
 │                                                                          │
 │  ┌─────────────────┐                                                     │
 │  │ 1. READY QUEUE  │  callbacks/tasks ready to run RIGHT NOW             │
 │  │   [T1, T2, T3]  │  → pop each and run it until it awaits or returns   │
 │  └────────┬────────┘     ⚠ THIS IS WHERE YOUR CODE RUNS.                 │
 │           │                Nothing else happens while it runs.           │
 │           ▼                                                              │
 │  ┌─────────────────┐                                                     │
 │  │ 2. TIMERS       │  a min-heap of (deadline, callback)                 │
 │  │   heap by time  │  → move any expired timers to the ready queue       │
 │  └────────┬────────┘                                                     │
 │           ▼                                                              │
 │  ┌─────────────────┐                                                     │
 │  │ 3. I/O POLL     │  epoll (Linux) / kqueue (BSD) / IOCP (Windows)      │
 │  │  select(timeout)│  timeout = time until the next timer                │
 │  │                 │  → the KERNEL tells us which sockets are ready      │
 │  │                 │  → move their callbacks to the ready queue          │
 │  └────────┬────────┘                                                     │
 │           └──────────────► back to 1                                     │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The kernel does the hard part. `epoll` monitors 100,000 file descriptors and returns only the ready ones — in O(ready), not O(total). That is the mechanism that makes 100k connections on one thread possible.

**What blocking does to this picture:**

```
   NORMAL:                          BLOCKED:
   ready queue: [T1]                ready queue: [T1, T2, T3, ..., T500]
   run T1 → awaits after 50 µs      run T1 → time.sleep(2) ...
   run T2 → awaits after 30 µs      ... 2 seconds of NOTHING ...
   poll I/O → 40 sockets ready      ... T2..T500 wait ...
   ...                              ... incoming data sits in kernel buffers ...
                                    ... /health times out ...
                                    ... Kubernetes restarts the pod ...
```

### 10.3.3 Tasks vs coroutines

```python
# A coroutine runs only when awaited — sequentially.
await fetch_a()      # 1 s
await fetch_b()      # 1 s
# total: 2 s

# A Task is a coroutine WRAPPED and SCHEDULED on the loop — it runs concurrently.
ta = asyncio.create_task(fetch_a())     # starts running at the next await point
tb = asyncio.create_task(fetch_b())
await ta; await tb
# total: 1 s
```

```
 coroutine ──create_task()──► Task ──► scheduled on the loop
                               │
                               ├─ has its own lifecycle: PENDING → RUNNING →
                               │  DONE / CANCELLED
                               ├─ can be cancelled: task.cancel()
                               ├─ holds its result or exception
                               └─ ⚠ if nobody awaits it and it raises, the
                                  exception may be silently swallowed until GC
```

**The fire-and-forget trap:**
```python
# ❌ Two bugs in one line
asyncio.create_task(background_work())
# 1. Nothing holds a reference → the task may be garbage-collected mid-execution.
# 2. If it raises, the exception surfaces only at GC time, as a warning.

# ✔ Hold a reference and attach an error handler
_background: set[asyncio.Task] = set()

def spawn(coro) -> asyncio.Task:
    task = asyncio.create_task(coro)
    _background.add(task)
    task.add_done_callback(_background.discard)
    task.add_done_callback(_log_if_failed)
    return task

def _log_if_failed(task: asyncio.Task) -> None:
    if task.cancelled():
        return
    if exc := task.exception():
        log.error("background_task_failed", exc_info=exc)
```

### 10.3.4 The GIL, and what async does and doesn't fix

```
 THE GIL (Global Interpreter Lock): only ONE thread executes Python
 bytecode at a time, per process.

 ┌────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ WORKLOAD               │ WHAT HELPS                                      │
 ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ I/O-bound              │ ✔ async (best), ✔ threads (ok)                  │
 │ (network, disk)        │   the GIL is RELEASED during I/O syscalls        │
 ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ CPU-bound, pure Python │ ✘ async, ✘ threads (GIL serialises them)        │
 │ (parsing, loops)       │ ✔ multiprocessing / ProcessPoolExecutor          │
 │                        │ ✔ multiple worker processes                      │
 ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ CPU-bound, C extension │ ✔ threads — NumPy, torch, and cryptography       │
 │ (numpy, torch, bcrypt) │   RELEASE the GIL during their C work            │
 └────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Async does not make CPU-bound work faster. It makes waiting free.** These are different problems with different solutions, and conflating them is the second-most-common async mistake after blocking the loop.

### 10.3.5 How FastAPI dispatches your handler

```
 @app.get("/x")
 async def handler(): ...          → awaited on the event loop thread
                                     ZERO handoff cost
                                     ⚠ you promise not to block

 @app.get("/y")
 def handler(): ...                → await run_in_threadpool(handler)
                                     AnyIO's thread pool, default 40 threads
                                     ~50–100 µs handoff
                                     ✔ safe to block
                                     ⚠ request 41 queues
```

Raising the thread pool limit:

```python
import anyio
@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    limiter = anyio.to_thread.current_default_thread_limiter()
    limiter.total_tokens = 100        # default 40
    yield
```
Only do this if you have measured thread-pool saturation. More threads means more memory and more GIL contention; it is a bandage over "we're using blocking libraries", not a fix.

## 10.4 Syntax

```python
import asyncio

# ── Definitions ──
async def f(): ...                       # coroutine function
async def g():
    async with resource() as r: ...      # async context manager
    async for item in stream(): ...      # async iterator
    return [x async for x in stream()]   # async comprehension

# ── Awaiting ──
result = await f()

# ── Concurrency: TaskGroup (Python 3.11+, PREFERRED) ──
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    t1 = tg.create_task(fetch_user(uid))
    t2 = tg.create_task(fetch_orders(uid))
# On exit: all tasks are complete. If ANY raised, the others are CANCELLED
# and an ExceptionGroup is raised. No task can outlive this block.
user, orders = t1.result(), t2.result()

# ── Concurrency: gather (older, still common) ──
user, orders = await asyncio.gather(fetch_user(uid), fetch_orders(uid))
results = await asyncio.gather(*coros, return_exceptions=True)  # errors as values

# ── First to finish ──
done, pending = await asyncio.wait(tasks, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)
for t in pending:
    t.cancel()

# ── Streaming results as they complete ──
for coro in asyncio.as_completed(coros):
    result = await coro                  # yields in COMPLETION order

# ── Timeouts (3.11+) ──
async with asyncio.timeout(5.0):
    await slow()
# older / alternative:
result = await asyncio.wait_for(slow(), timeout=5.0)

# ── Offloading ──
await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_fn, arg)          # 3.9+, thread pool
await run_in_threadpool(blocking_fn, arg)          # starlette equivalent
loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, cpu_fn)   # PROCESS pool for CPU work

# ── Synchronisation (asyncio versions — NOT threading's!) ──
lock = asyncio.Lock()
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)
event = asyncio.Event()
queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100)       # maxsize gives you backpressure
```

**`TaskGroup` vs `gather` — the difference that matters:**

```python
# gather: if fetch_a raises, fetch_b KEEPS RUNNING as an orphan.
#         You get one exception; the other task's failure may be swallowed.
await asyncio.gather(fetch_a(), fetch_b())

# TaskGroup: if fetch_a raises, fetch_b is CANCELLED, the block waits for
#            cleanup, and you get an ExceptionGroup with everything that failed.
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    tg.create_task(fetch_a())
    tg.create_task(fetch_b())
```

**Use `TaskGroup`** on Python 3.11+. Orphaned tasks are a genuine source of resource leaks and confusing production behaviour — a cancelled parent request whose child task keeps calling the LLM and burning money.

## 10.5 Beginner Examples

```python
import asyncio, time

async def fake_llm(prompt: str, delay: float = 1.0) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return f"answer to {prompt}"

# ❌ SEQUENTIAL — 3 seconds
async def sequential():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    a = await fake_llm("q1")
    b = await fake_llm("q2")
    c = await fake_llm("q3")
    print(f"sequential: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")

# ✔ CONCURRENT — 1 second
async def concurrent():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        t1 = tg.create_task(fake_llm("q1"))
        t2 = tg.create_task(fake_llm("q2"))
        t3 = tg.create_task(fake_llm("q3"))
    print(f"concurrent: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")

asyncio.run(sequential())    # sequential: 3.00s
asyncio.run(concurrent())    # concurrent: 1.00s
```

**The `await` in a loop trap** — the single most common performance bug in AI backends:

```python
# ❌ 100 documents × 200 ms = 20 SECONDS
embeddings = []
for doc in documents:
    embeddings.append(await embed(doc))

# ✔ ~200 ms (plus provider rate limits)
embeddings = await asyncio.gather(*[embed(d) for d in documents])

# ✔✔ Bounded concurrency — what you ACTUALLY want in production
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(20)
async def embed_limited(doc):
    async with sem:
        return await embed(doc)
embeddings = await asyncio.gather(*[embed_limited(d) for d in documents])
```

**Why the third version, not the second.** `gather` over 10,000 documents opens 10,000 simultaneous connections: you'll exhaust your connection pool, hit the provider's rate limit, get 429s on everything, and possibly run out of file descriptors. A semaphore is not an optimisation — it is a correctness requirement.

## 10.6 Intermediate Examples

### Blocking, demonstrated

```python
import time, asyncio
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/blocking")
async def blocking():
    time.sleep(1)                # ❌ blocks the ENTIRE worker
    return {"ok": True}

@app.get("/nonblocking")
async def nonblocking():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)       # ✔ yields to the loop
    return {"ok": True}

@app.get("/sync")
def sync_endpoint():
    time.sleep(1)                # ✔ acceptable — runs in the thread pool
    return {"ok": True}

@app.get("/health")
async def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}
```

```bash
# 20 concurrent requests, single worker
$ hey -n 20 -c 20 http://localhost:8000/blocking      # Total: 20.1s  ← serialised!
$ hey -n 20 -c 20 http://localhost:8000/nonblocking   # Total:  1.1s
$ hey -n 20 -c 20 http://localhost:8000/sync          # Total:  1.1s  (≤40 threads)

# And the killer demonstration:
$ curl localhost:8000/blocking &        # start a blocking request
$ time curl localhost:8000/health       # 1.02s — HEALTH CHECK BLOCKED
$ curl localhost:8000/nonblocking &
$ time curl localhost:8000/health       # 0.003s — fine
```

**That last pair is the production failure mode.** A blocking endpoint makes your health check time out, Kubernetes marks the pod unhealthy, it gets restarted, traffic shifts to other pods, which now have more blocking requests, and the whole fleet cascades. One `time.sleep` or one `requests.get` can take down a service.

### Finding blocking calls

```python
# 1. asyncio debug mode — logs any callback taking > 100 ms
import asyncio
asyncio.get_event_loop().set_debug(True)
# or: PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 uvicorn app.main:app
# Output: Executing <Task ...> took 1.003 seconds

# 2. A watchdog that detects loop stalls in production
async def loop_monitor(threshold_s: float = 0.25):
    """If the loop is healthy, this wakes every 100 ms. If a wake-up is late,
    something blocked the loop for the difference."""
    while True:
        start = time.perf_counter()
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        lag = time.perf_counter() - start - 0.1
        EVENT_LOOP_LAG.observe(lag)
        if lag > threshold_s:
            log.warning("event_loop_blocked", lag_seconds=round(lag, 3))

# 3. Static detection — the libraries to grep for
BLOCKING_IMPORTS = ["requests", "urllib.request", "psycopg2", "pymongo",
                    "boto3", "time.sleep", "open(", "subprocess.run"]
```

**`EVENT_LOOP_LAG` should be a permanent dashboard panel.** It is the single most diagnostic metric for an async service: when p99 lag rises above ~50 ms, something is blocking, and everything else you're seeing (latency spikes, health check failures) is downstream of that.

### Handling blocking libraries correctly

```python
# The situation: you must use a sync-only SDK (boto3, a legacy client, pypdf).

# ── OPTION 1: sync endpoint (simplest) ──
@app.post("/upload")
def upload(file: UploadFile):
    s3.upload_fileobj(file.file, bucket, key)      # boto3 is sync
    return {"ok": True}
# FastAPI runs the whole thing in the thread pool. Limited to ~40 concurrent.

# ── OPTION 2: async endpoint + explicit offload (mixed workloads) ──
@app.post("/process")
async def process(file: UploadFile, db: DBSession):
    content = await file.read()                             # async
    text = await asyncio.to_thread(extract_pdf_text, content)  # blocking → thread
    embedding = await embed_client.embed(text)              # async
    await db.execute(insert(Doc).values(text=text))         # async
    return {"ok": True}
# Only the blocking part uses a thread; the awaits stay concurrent.

# ── OPTION 3: process pool for CPU-bound work (threads don't escape the GIL) ──
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    app.state.pool = ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4)
    yield
    app.state.pool.shutdown(wait=True)

@app.post("/heavy")
async def heavy(request: Request, payload: Data):
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    result = await loop.run_in_executor(request.app.state.pool,
                                        cpu_intensive_fn, payload.data)
    return result
# ⚠ Arguments and results must be picklable, and there's ~1 ms IPC overhead.
# ⚠ For anything longer than a few seconds, use a real task queue (Ch. 11).
```

### Timeouts and cancellation

```python
# ── Timeout ──
try:
    async with asyncio.timeout(30):
        result = await llm.complete(prompt)
except TimeoutError:
    raise UpstreamTimeoutError()

# ── Cancellation is delivered as an EXCEPTION into the coroutine ──
async def work():
    try:
        await long_operation()
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        await cleanup()        # ✔ clean up
        raise                  # ⚠ ALWAYS RE-RAISE. Swallowing it breaks
                               #   cancellation for everything above you.
```

**The cancellation rules, which are subtle and important:**

```python
# ❌ 1. Swallowing CancelledError
try:
    await work()
except asyncio.CancelledError:
    pass                     # the task now can't be cancelled — a hang bug

# ❌ 2. Bare `except Exception` catching cancellation
#    (In 3.8+, CancelledError inherits from BaseException, not Exception,
#     specifically to prevent this. But `except BaseException` still catches it.)

# ✔ 3. Shielding critical cleanup from cancellation
async def handler():
    try:
        return await do_work()
    finally:
        # Without shield, a cancellation during cleanup aborts the cleanup.
        await asyncio.shield(record_usage())

# ✔ 4. Cancellation is COOPERATIVE — it only takes effect at an await point.
#    A blocking call cannot be cancelled. Another reason not to block.
```

## 10.7 Production Example — Async Patterns for AI Backends

### The shared HTTP client

```python
@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.http = httpx.AsyncClient(
        timeout=httpx.Timeout(connect=5.0, read=120.0, write=10.0, pool=5.0),
        limits=httpx.Limits(
            max_connections=200,           # total across all hosts
            max_keepalive_connections=50,  # kept warm for reuse
            keepalive_expiry=30.0,
        ),
        http2=True,                        # multiplexing to providers that support it
        follow_redirects=False,            # SSRF hygiene (Ch. 3)
    )
    yield
    await app.state.http.aclose()
```

```
   COST OF NOT DOING THIS

   New AsyncClient per request:
     DNS lookup          ~20 ms (usually cached)
     TCP handshake       ~30 ms (1 RTT)
     TLS 1.3 handshake   ~30 ms (1 RTT)
     ─────────────────────────
     ~80 ms of pure overhead per call, plus socket churn and, under load,
     ephemeral port exhaustion (TIME_WAIT sockets accumulate for 60 s).

   Reused pooled client: ~0 ms. The connection is already open.
```

### Bounded parallel fan-out

```python
class BoundedExecutor:
    """Run many coroutines with a concurrency cap and per-item timeouts."""

    def __init__(self, max_concurrency: int = 20, timeout_s: float = 60.0):
        self._sem = asyncio.Semaphore(max_concurrency)
        self._timeout = timeout_s

    async def run(self, coros: list[Coroutine]) -> list[Any | Exception]:
        async def guarded(coro):
            async with self._sem:
                try:
                    async with asyncio.timeout(self._timeout):
                        return await coro
                except Exception as exc:
                    return exc
        return await asyncio.gather(*(guarded(c) for c in coros))

# Usage: embed 5,000 chunks without melting anything
executor = BoundedExecutor(max_concurrency=20, timeout_s=30)
results = await executor.run([embed(chunk) for chunk in chunks])
succeeded = [r for r in results if not isinstance(r, Exception)]
failed = [r for r in results if isinstance(r, Exception)]
log.info("embedding_batch", ok=len(succeeded), failed=len(failed))
```

### Parallel RAG retrieval

```python
async def hybrid_retrieve(query: str, kb_id: UUID, org: Organization) -> list[Chunk]:
    """Run three retrieval strategies concurrently, then fuse.
    Sequentially this is ~120 ms; concurrently it's ~50 ms."""
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        dense_task = tg.create_task(vector_search(query, kb_id, top_k=20))
        sparse_task = tg.create_task(bm25_search(query, kb_id, top_k=20))
        meta_task = tg.create_task(metadata_filter_search(query, kb_id, top_k=20))

    fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion([dense_task.result(), sparse_task.result(),
                                    meta_task.result()])
    return await reranker.rerank(query, fused, top_k=5)
```

### Racing providers for lowest latency

```python
async def race_providers(prompt: str, clients: list[LLMClient]) -> str:
    """Send to several providers; take the first success; cancel the rest.
    ⚠ You pay for ALL of them. Use only where latency is worth 3× the cost
    (interactive UX-critical paths), never for batch work."""
    tasks = [asyncio.create_task(c.complete(prompt)) for c in clients]
    try:
        done, pending = await asyncio.wait(tasks, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)
        for task in pending:
            task.cancel()
        await asyncio.gather(*pending, return_exceptions=True)  # let cancellation land
        return done.pop().result()
    finally:
        for t in tasks:
            if not t.done():
                t.cancel()
```

### Async database with SQLAlchemy 2.0

```python
engine = create_async_engine(
    settings.DATABASE_URL,           # postgresql+asyncpg://...
    pool_size=20, max_overflow=10,
    pool_pre_ping=True, pool_recycle=1800,
    echo=False,
)
SessionLocal = async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)

async def get_user_with_orders(db: AsyncSession, uid: UUID) -> User:
    # ✔ Eager loading in ONE query — avoids the async lazy-load trap below
    return await db.scalar(
        select(User).options(selectinload(User.orders)).where(User.id == uid)
    )
```

**The `MissingGreenlet` error — the async-SQLAlchemy rite of passage:**

```python
# ❌ Lazy loading cannot work in async: accessing user.orders would need to
#    issue I/O from a plain attribute access, which can't await.
user = await db.get(User, uid)
for order in user.orders:          # sqlalchemy.exc.MissingGreenlet
    ...

# ✔ Three fixes:
# 1. Eager load:      .options(selectinload(User.orders))
# 2. Explicit await:  await db.refresh(user, ["orders"])
# 3. Configure the relationship: lazy="selectin" on the model
```

**Connection pool arithmetic — the scaling wall everyone hits:**

```
   pool_size=20, max_overflow=10  →  up to 30 connections PER WORKER PROCESS
   × 4 workers per pod            =  120 per pod
   × 10 pods                      =  1,200 connections

   Postgres default max_connections = 100.
   → "FATAL: sorry, too many clients already" under any real load.

   FIXES:
   1. Shrink the pool (pool_size=5 is often plenty for async — connections are
      held only during a query, not during the LLM call)
   2. PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode (the standard answer)
      ⚠ transaction mode breaks prepared statements: for asyncpg set
        `prepared_statement_cache_size=0` or use `statement_cache_size=0`
   3. Raise max_connections (last resort — each connection costs ~10 MB in PG)
```

## 10.8 AI Engineering Perspective

**The async patterns that define an AI backend:**

```python
# ── 1. Parallel multi-model calls (ensembles, comparisons, judges) ──
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    gpt = tg.create_task(openai.complete(prompt))
    claude = tg.create_task(anthropic.complete(prompt))
best = await judge(gpt.result(), claude.result())

# ── 2. Streaming with concurrent side effects ──
async def stream_and_persist(prompt):
    buffer = []
    async for token in llm.stream(prompt):
        buffer.append(token)
        yield token                                   # to the user, immediately
    # persist AFTER, without delaying the user
    spawn(save_message("".join(buffer)))

# ── 3. Pipeline parallelism: overlap retrieval with prompt preparation ──
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    retrieval = tg.create_task(retrieve(query))
    history = tg.create_task(load_conversation(conv_id))
    profile = tg.create_task(load_user_context(user_id))
prompt = build(retrieval.result(), history.result(), profile.result())

# ── 4. Batched embedding with a time window ──
class BatchedEmbedder:
    """Collect embedding requests for up to 50 ms or 100 items, then send one
    batched API call. Cuts cost and latency dramatically under load."""

    def __init__(self, client, max_batch: int = 100, max_wait_s: float = 0.05):
        self._client, self._max_batch, self._max_wait = client, max_batch, max_wait_s
        self._pending: list[tuple[str, asyncio.Future]] = []
        self._flush_task: asyncio.Task | None = None
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def embed(self, text: str) -> list[float]:
        future: asyncio.Future = asyncio.get_running_loop().create_future()
        async with self._lock:
            self._pending.append((text, future))
            if len(self._pending) >= self._max_batch:
                await self._flush()
            elif self._flush_task is None:
                self._flush_task = asyncio.create_task(self._flush_after_delay())
        return await future

    async def _flush_after_delay(self) -> None:
        await asyncio.sleep(self._max_wait)
        async with self._lock:
            await self._flush()

    async def _flush(self) -> None:
        if not self._pending:
            return
        batch, self._pending = self._pending, []
        if self._flush_task:
            self._flush_task.cancel()
            self._flush_task = None
        texts = [t for t, _ in batch]
        try:
            vectors = await self._client.embed_batch(texts)
            for (_, fut), vec in zip(batch, vectors):
                if not fut.done():
                    fut.set_result(vec)
        except Exception as exc:
            for _, fut in batch:
                if not fut.done():
                    fut.set_exception(exc)
```

**Why batching matters so much for embeddings.** OpenAI's embedding endpoint charges per token but has significant per-request overhead. 100 separate calls of one text each: ~100 × 40 ms = 4 s of wall clock and 100 requests against your rate limit. One call of 100 texts: ~120 ms and 1 request. **A 30× improvement for ~50 lines of code**, and it's the difference between a document-ingestion pipeline that takes an hour and one that takes two minutes.

**Rate limiting your own outbound calls.** Providers enforce requests-per-minute *and* tokens-per-minute. Exceeding either gets you 429s that cost latency:

```python
class TokenBucket:
    """Async token bucket for outbound provider rate limiting."""

    def __init__(self, rate_per_s: float, capacity: float):
        self._rate, self._capacity = rate_per_s, capacity
        self._tokens = capacity
        self._last = time.monotonic()
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def acquire(self, amount: float = 1.0) -> None:
        async with self._lock:
            while True:
                now = time.monotonic()
                self._tokens = min(self._capacity,
                                   self._tokens + (now - self._last) * self._rate)
                self._last = now
                if self._tokens >= amount:
                    self._tokens -= amount
                    return
                wait = (amount - self._tokens) / self._rate
                await asyncio.sleep(wait)

# One bucket for requests, one for tokens — providers limit both.
rpm_bucket = TokenBucket(rate_per_s=500 / 60, capacity=500)
tpm_bucket = TokenBucket(rate_per_s=200_000 / 60, capacity=200_000)

async def call_llm(prompt: str, estimated_tokens: int):
    await rpm_bucket.acquire(1)
    await tpm_bucket.acquire(estimated_tokens)
    return await client.complete(prompt)
```

**⚠ This is per-process.** With 4 workers × 10 pods you have 40 independent buckets and your effective rate is 40× the configured one. For accurate global limiting, use a Redis-backed distributed limiter — or divide your quota by the number of processes and accept the inefficiency.

## 10.9 Backend Engineering Perspective

**When async is the wrong choice:**

| Situation | Why async doesn't help |
|---|---|
| Pure CPU-bound work | one thread; the GIL blocks parallelism anyway |
| Very low concurrency (< 10) | thread overhead was never the bottleneck |
| Your whole stack is sync | mixing costs more than it saves |
| The team has no async experience | one blocking call anywhere destroys the benefit |

**The async/sync split in a real codebase.** A pragmatic rule that scales:

```
 async: everything touching the network — HTTP clients, database, cache,
        vector store, message queue, object storage
 sync:  everything pure — prompt building, token counting, parsing, scoring,
        business rules, data transformation

 Pure functions are trivially testable and can be called from either world.
 Push I/O to the edges; keep the middle synchronous and pure.
```

**Structured concurrency as a design principle.** The rule is: *a task's lifetime never exceeds the scope that created it*. This eliminates a whole class of bugs — orphaned tasks, leaked resources, work continuing after a cancelled request, exceptions surfacing in unrelated code. `TaskGroup` gives you this in the stdlib. Prefer it over `create_task` + manual bookkeeping everywhere you can.

## 10.10 Performance

```
 Coroutine creation                       ~0.3 µs
 await on an already-complete future      ~0.1 µs
 Context switch between coroutines        ~0.1 µs
 OS thread context switch                 ~1–10 µs      (10–100×)
 create_task overhead                     ~2 µs
 asyncio.sleep(0) — yield to the loop     ~1 µs
 Thread pool handoff (run_in_threadpool)  ~50–100 µs
 Process pool handoff (pickle + IPC)      ~1–5 ms

 Memory per coroutine                     ~1–3 KB
 Memory per OS thread                     ~8 MB virtual (~64 KB resident)
 → 10,000 coroutines ≈ 30 MB. 10,000 threads ≈ impossible.
```

**The optimisation checklist, in order of impact:**

1. **Eliminate blocking calls.** Worth more than everything else combined. Monitor `EVENT_LOOP_LAG`.
2. **Reuse clients and pools.** Saves ~80 ms per outbound call.
3. **Parallelise independent I/O.** Sequential awaits are the #1 latency bug.
4. **Bound concurrency with semaphores.** Unbounded fan-out causes 429s and pool exhaustion, which are *slower* than bounded concurrency.
5. **Batch where the API supports it.** 30× for embeddings.
6. **Install `uvloop`.** 2–4× faster loop, one line.
7. **Right-size the thread pool** only after measuring saturation.
8. **Avoid `create_task` for work you immediately await** — it adds 2 µs and a scheduling round trip for nothing.

**Measuring properly:**

```python
# ❌ Meaningless — measures one request with no contention
start = time.perf_counter(); await endpoint(); print(time.perf_counter() - start)

# ✔ Load test with realistic concurrency
# hey -n 1000 -c 100 -m POST -D body.json http://localhost:8000/v1/chat
# locust, k6, or vegeta for anything more complex.
#
# The number that matters is p99 UNDER CONCURRENCY, not p50 in isolation.
# A blocking call has almost no effect at concurrency 1 and catastrophic
# effect at concurrency 100 — which is exactly why it survives code review
# and fails in production.
```

## 10.11 Security

**1. Unbounded concurrency is a self-inflicted DoS.**
```python
# ❌ A request with 10,000 URLs opens 10,000 connections
await asyncio.gather(*[fetch(u) for u in payload.urls])
# ✔ Cap the input AND the concurrency
urls: list[HttpUrl] = Field(max_length=50)
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)
```

**2. Missing timeouts are a resource exhaustion vector.** An attacker who controls a slow endpoint you call can hold your workers indefinitely. Every outbound call needs a deadline.

**3. Cancellation must not skip security-relevant cleanup.** Use `asyncio.shield` for audit logging and usage recording so a cancelled request still leaves a trail.

**4. Race conditions in async code are real, despite the single thread.**
```python
# ❌ Not atomic — the await creates a window for interleaving
balance = await get_balance(user_id)          # ← another coroutine can run here
if balance >= amount:
    await set_balance(user_id, balance - amount)   # lost update

# ✔ Atomic at the storage layer
new_balance = await redis.decrby(f"balance:{user_id}", amount)
if new_balance < 0:
    await redis.incrby(f"balance:{user_id}", amount)
    raise InsufficientCreditsError()

# ✔ Or a database-level atomic update
await db.execute(
    update(Account).where(Account.id == uid, Account.balance >= amount)
                   .values(balance=Account.balance - amount)
)
```
**Single-threaded does not mean atomic.** Any sequence spanning an `await` can interleave with other requests. If you find yourself thinking "this is fine, it's single-threaded", check whether there's an `await` in the middle.

**5. `asyncio.Lock` is not `threading.Lock`.** Using the wrong one either blocks the loop (threading lock in async code) or provides no protection (asyncio lock across threads).

## 10.12 Best Practices

```
✔ async def for I/O; def for blocking libraries; process pool for CPU
✔ NEVER block the event loop — monitor loop lag as a first-class metric
✔ TaskGroup over gather (3.11+); never bare create_task without a reference
✔ Semaphores on every fan-out — bounded concurrency is correctness, not tuning
✔ Timeouts on every await that touches the network
✔ Re-raise CancelledError, always
✔ shield() critical cleanup (billing, audit)
✔ One shared HTTP client and one DB engine per process, created in lifespan
✔ Eager-load ORM relationships; lazy loading doesn't work in async
✔ Batch API calls where the provider supports it
✔ Do the connection-pool arithmetic before you scale
✔ Push I/O to the edges; keep business logic pure and synchronous
✔ Load test at realistic concurrency; p99 under load is the only honest number
```

## 10.13 Common Mistakes

```python
# ❌ 1. Blocking in async
async def h(): time.sleep(1); requests.get(url); open(f).read()

# ❌ 2. Sequential awaits for independent work
a = await fetch_a(); b = await fetch_b()
# ✔ async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: ...

# ❌ 3. Forgetting await
result = fetch()          # a coroutine object; RuntimeWarning at GC

# ❌ 4. Unbounded gather
await asyncio.gather(*[f(x) for x in ten_thousand_items])

# ❌ 5. create_task with no reference → may be GC'd mid-flight; errors swallowed

# ❌ 6. Swallowing CancelledError → the task becomes uncancellable

# ❌ 7. Client per request → +80 ms and port exhaustion

# ❌ 8. Lazy-loading ORM relationships in async → MissingGreenlet

# ❌ 9. Assuming single-threaded means atomic → lost updates across awaits

# ❌ 10. threading.Lock in async code → blocks the whole loop

# ❌ 11. Pool size × workers × pods > max_connections → "too many clients"

# ❌ 12. No timeout → one hung upstream fills every worker slot

# ❌ 13. asyncio.run() inside a running loop → RuntimeError
#     (happens when porting sync code that called asyncio.run internally)

# ❌ 14. CPU work in a thread pool expecting parallelism → the GIL serialises it

# ❌ 15. Measuring performance at concurrency 1 → blocking bugs are invisible
```

## 10.14 Interview Questions

1. **What is the event loop?** A single-threaded scheduler that runs ready callbacks, fires expired timers, and polls the OS for I/O readiness — repeatedly. Your code runs in the first phase, and nothing else happens while it does.

2. **What does `await` actually do?** Suspends the current coroutine, returns control to the loop, and registers a callback to resume when the awaited thing completes. It is the *only* place another coroutine can be scheduled.

3. **Why does one blocking call break the whole server?** Because there's one thread. A blocking call means the loop cannot run any other coroutine, poll for I/O, or fire timers — every concurrent request, including health checks, is frozen.

4. **`async def` vs `def` endpoints in FastAPI?** `async def` is awaited on the loop (fast, but you must not block). `def` is dispatched to a 40-thread pool (safe for blocking code, but limited concurrency plus a handoff cost).

5. **Does async make code faster?** It makes *waiting* concurrent. CPU-bound code gets no benefit — often slightly worse, from scheduling overhead.

6. **What is the GIL and does async avoid it?** One thread executes Python bytecode at a time per process. Async doesn't avoid it; it makes it irrelevant for I/O, because the GIL is released during I/O syscalls. CPU parallelism needs processes.

7. **Coroutine vs task?** A coroutine is a suspended function that runs only when awaited. A task wraps a coroutine and schedules it on the loop so it runs concurrently, with its own cancellation and result handling.

8. **`TaskGroup` vs `gather`?** `TaskGroup` guarantees no task outlives the block, cancels siblings on failure, and raises an ExceptionGroup. `gather` leaves orphans running when one task fails.

9. **Why must you keep a reference to `create_task` results?** The loop holds only a weak reference; without a strong one the task can be garbage-collected mid-execution, and its exceptions surface only as GC warnings.

10. **What happens on cancellation?** `CancelledError` is raised *into* the coroutine at its next await point. You may catch it to clean up, but you must re-raise — swallowing it makes the task uncancellable.

11. **How do you protect cleanup from cancellation?** `await asyncio.shield(cleanup())`, so the cleanup completes even though the outer task is being cancelled.

12. **Is async code free of race conditions?** No. Any sequence spanning an `await` can interleave with other coroutines. Read-modify-write patterns need atomic storage operations or locks.

13. **How do you handle a blocking library?** Sync endpoint (framework offloads it), `asyncio.to_thread` for the blocking part only, or a process pool for CPU-bound work. For anything long-running, a task queue.

14. **Why doesn't a thread pool help CPU-bound Python?** The GIL serialises bytecode execution, so threads take turns. Only C extensions that release the GIL (NumPy, torch, bcrypt) get real parallelism from threads.

15. **What is `MissingGreenlet`?** SQLAlchemy's async error when you trigger lazy loading — an attribute access that needs I/O but can't await. Fix with eager loading, explicit refresh, or `lazy="selectin"`.

16. **Explain the connection pool math problem.** `pool_size × workers × pods` easily exceeds Postgres's `max_connections`. Fix with smaller pools (async holds connections briefly), PgBouncer in transaction mode, or raising the limit.

17. **Why bound concurrency with a semaphore?** Unbounded fan-out exhausts your connection pool, trips provider rate limits (429s on everything), and can exhaust file descriptors. Bounded concurrency is usually *faster* as well as safer.

18. **How do you find blocking calls in production?** An event-loop lag monitor (sleep 100 ms, measure the overshoot), `PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1` in staging, and grepping for known-sync libraries.

19. **When would you batch requests, and how?** When the provider supports batch endpoints and per-request overhead dominates — embeddings especially. Collect for a short window (~50 ms) or until a max batch size, then send one call. Often 30× throughput.

20. **How do you rate-limit your outbound provider calls?** A token bucket per limit type (RPM and TPM). Note it's per-process, so with N processes your effective rate is N×; use Redis for accurate global limiting.

21. **What's the correct timeout strategy?** Separate connect/read/write/pool timeouts, with read timeouts long enough for slow generation (300 s for streams) and connect timeouts short (5 s). Budgets must decrease from client inward.

22. **How do you measure async performance honestly?** Load testing at realistic concurrency, reporting p99. A blocking bug is invisible at concurrency 1 and catastrophic at concurrency 100.

23. **What is structured concurrency and why does it matter?** The principle that a task's lifetime is bounded by the scope that created it. It eliminates orphaned tasks, leaked resources, and work continuing after a cancelled request. `TaskGroup` implements it.

24. **How would you race two LLM providers for latency?** `asyncio.wait(..., return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)`, cancel the losers, and await their cancellation. Only worth it where latency justifies paying N× the cost.

25. **Design the async architecture for a RAG API.** Async everywhere I/O happens; one shared httpx client and DB engine per process from lifespan; retrieval strategies fanned out with `TaskGroup`; embeddings batched with a time window; semaphores bounding all fan-out; token buckets for provider limits; timeouts on every call; CPU work (PDF parsing, tokenisation of large documents) offloaded to a process pool or a queue; event-loop lag monitored as a first-class metric; and pool sizing verified against the database's connection limit.

## 10.15 Exercises

**Easy**
1. Write three async functions that sleep 1 s each; run them sequentially, then with `TaskGroup`, and compare.
2. Create a blocking endpoint and a non-blocking one; use `hey` at concurrency 20 and explain the difference.
3. Demonstrate that a blocking endpoint delays `/health`.

**Medium**
4. Convert a sequential `for ... await` loop over 100 items into bounded parallel execution with a semaphore; measure at concurrency 1, 10, and 100.
5. Implement an event-loop lag monitor and prove it detects a deliberate 500 ms block.
6. Implement `to_thread` offloading for a sync PDF parser inside an otherwise-async endpoint.
7. Implement a timeout with cleanup, proving that `CancelledError` propagates and the cleanup runs.

**Hard**
8. Implement `BatchedEmbedder` with a time window and size cap; test that 100 concurrent calls produce exactly one batch request.
9. Implement a `TokenBucket` and prove it holds an outbound rate within 5% over 60 seconds.
10. Demonstrate an async race condition (concurrent balance decrements losing updates), then fix it with an atomic database update and prove the fix with a 100-way concurrent test.

**Production**
11. Take a synchronous FastAPI service (requests + psycopg2 + boto3) and convert it fully to async: httpx, asyncpg/SQLAlchemy async, aioboto3 or threaded offload. Measure p99 at concurrency 100 before and after, and document the connection pool arithmetic.

## 10.16 Solutions

**Solution 5 — the loop lag monitor.**
```python
EVENT_LOOP_LAG = Histogram(
    "event_loop_lag_seconds", "Delay beyond the requested sleep",
    buckets=(.001, .005, .01, .025, .05, .1, .25, .5, 1, 5))

async def monitor_event_loop(interval_s: float = 0.1,
                             warn_threshold_s: float = 0.25) -> None:
    while True:
        start = time.perf_counter()
        await asyncio.sleep(interval_s)
        lag = time.perf_counter() - start - interval_s
        EVENT_LOOP_LAG.observe(max(0.0, lag))
        if lag > warn_threshold_s:
            log.warning("event_loop_blocked", lag_s=round(lag, 3),
                        task_count=len(asyncio.all_tasks()))

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    monitor = asyncio.create_task(monitor_event_loop())
    yield
    monitor.cancel()
    with contextlib.suppress(asyncio.CancelledError):
        await monitor
```
**Reasoning:** the measurement is the *overshoot*. If the loop is healthy, `sleep(0.1)` returns after ~0.1005 s and lag is ~0.5 ms. If a coroutine blocks for 800 ms, the timer callback can't run until it finishes, so lag is ~800 ms. This gives you a direct, continuous measurement of the property that matters most in an async service — and it costs one coroutine and ten wake-ups per second.

**Solution 10 — the async race, demonstrated and fixed.**
```python
# ❌ The bug
async def spend_credits_racy(db, user_id: UUID, amount: int) -> None:
    user = await db.get(User, user_id)         # read
    if user.credits < amount:                   # ← another coroutine runs HERE
        raise InsufficientCreditsError()
    user.credits -= amount                      # write based on a stale read
    await db.commit()

async def test_race_loses_updates(db, user):
    user.credits = 100
    await db.commit()
    await asyncio.gather(*[spend_credits_racy(db, user.id, 10) for _ in range(10)],
                         return_exceptions=True)
    await db.refresh(user)
    assert user.credits == 0        # FAILS: often 90 — nine updates lost

# ✔ The fix: one atomic statement; the database arbitrates
async def spend_credits(db, user_id: UUID, amount: int) -> None:
    result = await db.execute(
        update(User)
        .where(User.id == user_id, User.credits >= amount)   # guard IN the WHERE
        .values(credits=User.credits - amount)               # expression, not a value
        .returning(User.credits)
    )
    row = result.first()
    if row is None:                 # zero rows matched → insufficient credits
        raise InsufficientCreditsError()
    await db.commit()
```
**Reasoning:** two things make the fix correct. `credits=User.credits - amount` is a *SQL expression*, so the arithmetic happens in the database against the current value, not against a stale Python value. And the `credits >= amount` guard lives in the `WHERE` clause, so the check and the update are one atomic statement — there is no window between them. Zero rows affected is how you learn the check failed. This pattern (guard in WHERE, expression in SET, check the row count) is the standard answer for any concurrent counter, quota, or balance.

## 10.17 Mini Project — An Async Document Ingestion Pipeline

**Goal.** Ingest 1,000 PDFs into a vector store, correctly and fast.

**The pipeline:**
```
   download (I/O)  →  parse (CPU)  →  chunk (CPU, cheap)  →
   embed (I/O, batchable)  →  upsert (I/O)
```

**Requirements:**
1. Download concurrently with a semaphore (max 20) and per-file timeouts.
2. Parse PDFs in a `ProcessPoolExecutor` (CPU-bound, GIL-bound).
3. Chunk synchronously (pure, fast).
4. Embed via `BatchedEmbedder` with a 50 ms window and 100-item batches.
5. Upsert to the vector store in batches of 500.
6. A `TokenBucket` respecting the provider's RPM and TPM limits.
7. Progress reporting via an async queue consumed by a status endpoint.
8. Per-item failure isolation — one bad PDF must not abort the run.
9. Graceful cancellation: SIGTERM stops cleanly and records what completed.
10. Event-loop lag monitored throughout.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- 1,000 PDFs (avg 2 MB, 20 pages) ingest in under 5 minutes.
- Event-loop lag p99 stays under 50 ms during the entire run (proves CPU work is properly offloaded).
- Zero 429s from the embedding provider.
- A corrupt PDF is recorded as failed; the other 999 succeed.
- Cancelling at 50% leaves a consistent state and an accurate progress record.
- Database connections never exceed the configured pool size.

## Chapter 10 Summary

| Idea | The one-line version |
|---|---|
| One thread, many waits | the event loop makes waiting free, not computation fast |
| `await` is the only yield point | between awaits, nothing else on the worker runs |
| Blocking freezes everything | including `/health`, which gets your pod restarted |
| The GIL is irrelevant for I/O | released during syscalls; but it kills CPU parallelism |
| Coroutine ≠ task | tasks are scheduled and run concurrently; coroutines wait to be awaited |
| `TaskGroup` over `gather` | no orphans, sibling cancellation, ExceptionGroups |
| Bound every fan-out | unbounded concurrency causes 429s and pool exhaustion |
| Timeouts on every network await | one hung upstream otherwise fills every worker |
| Re-raise `CancelledError` | swallowing it makes the task uncancellable |
| Single-threaded ≠ atomic | anything spanning an `await` can interleave |
| Monitor event-loop lag | the single most diagnostic metric in an async service |

### Cheat Sheet

```python
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:  t = tg.create_task(coro())    # preferred
await asyncio.gather(*coros, return_exceptions=True)
async with asyncio.timeout(30): ...              # 3.11+
await asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout=30)
done, pending = await asyncio.wait(tasks, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)
for c in asyncio.as_completed(coros): r = await c

await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_fn, arg)                  # blocking I/O
await loop.run_in_executor(process_pool, cpu_fn, arg)      # CPU-bound

sem = asyncio.Semaphore(20)
async with sem: ...

try: await work()
except asyncio.CancelledError: await cleanup(); raise      # ALWAYS re-raise
await asyncio.shield(critical_cleanup())
```

### Production Checklist
- [ ] No blocking calls in any `async def` (grep: requests, psycopg2, time.sleep, boto3, open)
- [ ] Event-loop lag monitored and alerted on
- [ ] One shared HTTP client and DB engine per process, from lifespan
- [ ] All fan-outs semaphore-bounded
- [ ] Timeouts on every network await
- [ ] `TaskGroup` used; no bare `create_task`
- [ ] Connection pool math verified against `max_connections`
- [ ] CPU work in a process pool or a task queue
- [ ] Load tested at realistic concurrency; p99 reported

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Input list sizes capped *and* concurrency bounded
- [ ] Every outbound call has a deadline
- [ ] Billing/audit cleanup shielded from cancellation
- [ ] Read-modify-write replaced with atomic operations
- [ ] `asyncio` primitives used (not `threading`) in async code

### Performance Checklist
- [ ] Independent I/O parallelised, not sequentially awaited
- [ ] Batch APIs used where available (embeddings especially)
- [ ] `uvloop` installed
- [ ] Client and pool reuse verified (no per-request construction)
- [ ] Thread pool size tuned only after measuring saturation
- [ ] Eager loading on all ORM relationships used in async paths
