# Chapter 17 — Caching

> In an ordinary backend, caching saves milliseconds. In an AI backend, caching saves **seconds and money** — an LLM call is 4,000 ms and costs real currency per request. A cache hit rate of 30% on a $50,000/month inference bill is $15,000/month, recovered by a component you can build in an afternoon. No other optimisation in this guide has that return.

## 17.1 Concept Overview

**What it is.** Storing the result of an expensive operation so subsequent identical requests can skip it.

```
   THE CACHE HIERARCHY IN AN AI BACKEND

   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ LAYER              LATENCY   SCOPE          TYPICAL USE              │
   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ CDN / edge         5–50 ms   global         static assets, public    │
   │                                             GET responses            │
   │ HTTP (browser)     0 ms      one user       ETag / Cache-Control     │
   │ Application memory 0.001 ms  one process    settings, prompt         │
   │ (lru_cache)                                 templates, tokenizers    │
   │ Redis              0.2 ms    all pods       sessions, rate limits,   │
   │                                             LLM responses, embeddings│
   │ Database           1–5 ms    all pods       materialised views       │
   │ PROVIDER PROMPT    n/a       your account   OpenAI/Anthropic prompt   │
   │ CACHE                                       caching — 50–90% cheaper │
   │                                             on repeated prefixes     │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**The four things worth caching in an AI system, in order of value:**

```
 ① LLM COMPLETIONS       4,000 ms + $0.01–0.50 per call    ← highest value
 ② EMBEDDINGS            40 ms + $0.0001, but called constantly and
                         DETERMINISTIC — the easiest big win
 ③ RETRIEVAL RESULTS     30 ms, and lets you skip embedding too
 ④ ORDINARY DB QUERIES   1–5 ms — the thing most tutorials focus on,
                         and the least valuable here
```

**The one hard problem.** As Phil Karlton put it: *"There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things."* Everything difficult about caching is invalidation — knowing when a cached value has become wrong. The rest is a dictionary.

## 17.2 Historical Background

```
 1960s ─ CPU caches. The original: SRAM between the processor and main memory.
 1994 ─ HTTP/1.0 Expires header. The web's first caching mechanism.
 1996 ─ Squid: the reverse proxy cache.
 1999 ─ HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2616): Cache-Control, ETag, conditional requests.
        Still the foundation of web caching today.
 2003 ─ Memcached (LiveJournal): distributed in-memory caching. Facebook,
        Twitter, YouTube all run on it.
 2009 ─ Redis: memcached plus data structures, persistence, and pub/sub.
 2010s ─ CDNs become universal; edge caching moves content next to users.
 2020s ─ AI changes the economics entirely: caching stops being about latency
         and becomes about COST.
 2023 ─ SEMANTIC CACHING — matching on meaning rather than exact text —
        becomes viable because embeddings are cheap.
 2024 ─ Providers ship PROMPT CACHING: Anthropic (up to 90% cost reduction on
        cached prefix tokens), OpenAI (automatic 50% discount), Google.
        Prompt structure becomes a cost-engineering decision.
```

## 17.3 Internal Working

### 17.3.1 Cache-aside (the pattern you will use)

```
   READ                                    WRITE
   ────                                    ─────
   1. check cache                          1. write to database
      ├─ HIT  → return                     2. INVALIDATE the cache key
      └─ MISS →                               (do NOT write to the cache)
   2. read from source
   3. write to cache with a TTL
   4. return
```

```python
async def get_document(doc_id: UUID, org_id: UUID) -> Document | None:
    key = f"doc:v1:{org_id}:{doc_id}"

    if cached := await redis.get(key):
        CACHE_HITS.labels(type="document").inc()
        return Document.model_validate_json(cached)

    CACHE_MISSES.labels(type="document").inc()
    doc = await repo.get(doc_id, org_id=org_id)
    if doc is not None:
        await redis.setex(key, 300, doc.model_dump_json())
    return doc
```

**Why invalidate rather than update on write** (write-through)? Because updating the cache on write means two systems must agree, and under concurrency they will not:

```
   THE WRITE-THROUGH RACE

   T1: read DB → v1
   T2: write DB → v2
   T2: write cache → v2
   T1: write cache → v1        ← STALE VALUE WINS, and it wins for the full TTL

   Deleting the key is idempotent and cannot lose a race in this way.
   Both writers delete; the next read repopulates from the source of truth.
```

### 17.3.2 The three classic failure modes

```
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ ① CACHE STAMPEDE (thundering herd)                                        │
 │    A hot key expires. 1,000 concurrent requests all miss, all hit the      │
 │    database or the LLM simultaneously, and the source of truth falls over. │
 │    → FIX: a lock so one request recomputes while others wait or serve      │
 │      stale; plus probabilistic early expiry to desynchronise.              │
 ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ ② CACHE PENETRATION                                                        │
 │    Requests for keys that DON'T EXIST always miss and always hit the       │
 │    database. An attacker requesting random IDs bypasses your cache         │
 │    entirely and DDoSes the database through it.                            │
 │    → FIX: cache negative results with a short TTL; or a Bloom filter.      │
 ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │ ③ CACHE AVALANCHE                                                          │
 │    Many keys were written at the same moment (a deploy, a warmup) and      │
 │    therefore expire at the same moment. Everything misses at once.         │
 │    → FIX: jittered TTLs — `ttl + random.randint(0, ttl // 10)`.            │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 17.3.3 Stampede protection

```python
async def get_or_compute(
    key: str, compute: Callable[[], Awaitable[T]], *,
    ttl_s: int = 300, lock_timeout_s: int = 30, stale_ttl_s: int = 3600,
) -> T:
    """Single-flight with stale-while-revalidate.
    Guarantees at most ONE concurrent computation per key across all pods."""

    if cached := await redis.get(key):
        return deserialize(cached)

    lock_key = f"lock:{key}"
    lock_token = secrets.token_urlsafe(16)
    # SET NX is atomic: exactly one caller across the whole fleet wins.
    acquired = await redis.set(lock_key, lock_token, nx=True, ex=lock_timeout_s)

    if not acquired:
        # Someone else is computing. Prefer STALE DATA over waiting.
        if stale := await redis.get(f"stale:{key}"):
            CACHE_STALE_SERVED.inc()
            return deserialize(stale)
        # No stale value — wait briefly for the winner to finish.
        for _ in range(50):                       # up to ~5 seconds
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
            if cached := await redis.get(key):
                return deserialize(cached)
        # The winner died or is slow. Compute anyway rather than fail.
        CACHE_LOCK_TIMEOUT.inc()
        return await compute()

    try:
        value = await compute()
        payload = serialize(value)
        jitter = random.randint(0, max(1, ttl_s // 10))
        pipe = redis.pipeline()
        pipe.setex(key, ttl_s + jitter, payload)
        pipe.setex(f"stale:{key}", stale_ttl_s, payload)   # for the next stampede
        await pipe.execute()
        return value
    finally:
        # Release ONLY if we still hold it — a Lua CAS prevents deleting
        # a lock that expired and was re-acquired by someone else.
        await redis.eval(
            "if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then "
            "return redis.call('del', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end",
            1, lock_key, lock_token)
```

**The Lua compare-and-delete matters more than it looks.** Without it: your computation takes 35 seconds, the 30-second lock expires, another pod acquires it, and then your `finally` deletes *their* lock — allowing a third pod in. Now two computations run concurrently and the whole mechanism has silently failed. This is the standard distributed-lock correctness problem, and the CAS is the standard answer.

### 17.3.4 Cache key design

```python
def cache_key(namespace: str, version: int, **parts: Any) -> str:
    """Keys must be: deterministic, collision-free, versioned, and tenant-scoped."""
    ordered = "|".join(f"{k}={parts[k]}" for k in sorted(parts))
    if len(ordered) > 200:
        ordered = hashlib.sha256(ordered.encode()).hexdigest()
    return f"{namespace}:v{version}:{ordered}"

# Examples
cache_key("doc", 1, org="abc", id="123")
# → "doc:v1:id=123|org=abc"

cache_key("llm", 2, model="gpt-4o-mini", prompt_hash=sha256(prompt), temp=0.0)
# → "llm:v2:model=gpt-4o-mini|prompt_hash=8f3a...|temp=0.0"
```

**Four rules, each preventing a specific production bug:**

1. **Version the namespace.** Changing your serialisation format with old keys live means deserialisation errors on every hit. Bumping `v1` → `v2` invalidates everything atomically, for free.
2. **Include the tenant.** A cache key without `org_id` is a cross-tenant data leak — and unlike a database query, it bypasses every authorization check you wrote.
3. **Include every input that affects the output.** Model, temperature, system prompt version, retrieval parameters. A missing input means returning a result computed with different settings.
4. **Hash long keys.** Redis keys over a few hundred bytes waste memory and slow lookups.

## 17.4 Syntax

```python
import redis.asyncio as redis

r = redis.from_url(settings.REDIS_URL, decode_responses=False,
                   max_connections=50, socket_timeout=1.0,
                   socket_connect_timeout=1.0, retry_on_timeout=True)

# ── strings ──
await r.set(key, value, ex=300)          # with TTL
await r.set(key, value, nx=True, ex=30)  # only if absent (locks)
await r.setex(key, 300, value)
await r.get(key)
await r.getdel(key)                       # atomic read + delete (tickets)
await r.delete(key1, key2)
await r.exists(key)
await r.expire(key, 300)
await r.ttl(key)

# ── counters (atomic — the basis of rate limiting and quotas) ──
await r.incr(key); await r.incrby(key, 10); await r.decr(key)

# ── hashes (structured objects; update one field without rewriting) ──
await r.hset(key, mapping={"a": 1, "b": 2})
await r.hgetall(key); await r.hincrby(key, "tokens", 150)

# ── sets and sorted sets ──
await r.sadd(key, *members); await r.smembers(key)
await r.zadd(key, {"member": score}); await r.zrangebyscore(key, 0, 100)

# ── pipelines: N operations, ONE round trip ──
pipe = r.pipeline()
pipe.get("a"); pipe.get("b"); pipe.incr("c")
a, b, c = await pipe.execute()

# ── scanning (NEVER use KEYS in production — it blocks the whole server) ──
async for key in r.scan_iter(match="doc:v1:org123:*", count=500):
    await r.delete(key)
```

**`KEYS *` blocks Redis for the duration of a full keyspace scan.** On a 10-million-key instance that is seconds of total unavailability for every client. `SCAN` iterates incrementally. This is the single most common way to take down a shared Redis.

## 17.5 Beginner Examples

```python
from functools import lru_cache

# ── In-process caching for pure, process-scoped values ──
@lru_cache(maxsize=1)
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()

@lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def get_prompt_template(name: str, version: int) -> str:
    return (TEMPLATES_DIR / f"{name}_v{version}.jinja").read_text()

@lru_cache(maxsize=8)
def get_tokenizer(model: str):
    return tiktoken.encoding_for_model(model)     # ~200 ms to build; reuse it
```

**When `lru_cache` is right:** pure functions, process-scoped, bounded key space, and it's acceptable for each worker to have its own copy. **When it's wrong:** anything needing invalidation across pods, anything user-specific (unbounded keys → memory leak), and anything async (`lru_cache` on an `async def` caches the *coroutine object*, which can only be awaited once — a genuinely confusing bug).

```python
# ❌ Caches a coroutine; the second await raises RuntimeError
@lru_cache
async def fetch(x): ...

# ✔ Use an async-aware cache, or cache the result explicitly
from async_lru import alru_cache
@alru_cache(maxsize=128)
async def fetch(x): ...
```

## 17.6 Intermediate Examples

### HTTP caching with ETags

Free bandwidth savings, handled entirely by the browser and CDN.

```python
@router.get("/documents/{doc_id}", response_model=DocumentOut)
async def get_document(doc_id: UUID, response: Response, org: CurrentOrg,
                       repo: DocRepo,
                       if_none_match: Annotated[str | None, Header()] = None):
    doc = await repo.get(doc_id)
    if doc is None:
        raise HTTPException(404, "Document not found")

    etag = f'W/"{doc.updated_at.timestamp()}-{doc.version}"'
    if if_none_match == etag:
        # 304: no body at all. The client uses its cached copy.
        return Response(status_code=304, headers={"ETag": etag})

    response.headers["ETag"] = etag
    # `private` — a per-user response must NEVER be cached by a shared proxy.
    response.headers["Cache-Control"] = "private, max-age=60, must-revalidate"
    return doc
```

```
 Cache-Control DIRECTIVES THAT MATTER

 public              any cache may store it (CDNs, proxies)
 private             ONLY the end user's browser        ← authenticated responses
 no-cache            store it, but revalidate before each use
 no-store            never store it anywhere            ← secrets, PII
 max-age=N           fresh for N seconds
 s-maxage=N          fresh for N seconds in SHARED caches (overrides max-age)
 must-revalidate     once stale, do not serve without revalidating
 stale-while-revalidate=N   serve stale for N s while refreshing in background
 immutable           never revalidate (for content-hashed asset URLs)
```

**The mistake that causes cross-user data leaks:** `Cache-Control: public` on an authenticated response. A shared CDN or corporate proxy caches user A's response and serves it to user B. **Every authenticated endpoint must be `private` or `no-store`.** Make it a default in your security-headers middleware (Chapter 4) and opt in to `public` deliberately.

### Redis caching with a decorator

```python
def cached(ttl_s: int = 300, namespace: str = "default", version: int = 1,
           key_builder: Callable[..., str] | None = None):
    def decorator(fn):
        @functools.wraps(fn)                     # ⚠ required (Ch. 12 §12.7)
        async def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            key = (key_builder(*args, **kwargs) if key_builder
                   else cache_key(namespace, version,
                                  fn=fn.__name__,
                                  args=hashlib.sha256(
                                      repr((args, sorted(kwargs.items()))).encode()
                                  ).hexdigest()[:16]))
            redis_client = get_redis()
            try:
                if raw := await redis_client.get(key):
                    CACHE_HITS.labels(namespace=namespace).inc()
                    return pickle.loads(raw)      # ⚠ see the security note below
            except RedisError:
                CACHE_ERRORS.inc()                # FAIL OPEN: degrade, don't break

            CACHE_MISSES.labels(namespace=namespace).inc()
            result = await fn(*args, **kwargs)
            with contextlib.suppress(RedisError):
                await redis_client.setex(
                    key, ttl_s + random.randint(0, ttl_s // 10), pickle.dumps(result))
            return result
        return wrapper
    return decorator
```

**⚠ On `pickle`:** it is convenient and fast, but deserialising a pickle from a compromised Redis is arbitrary code execution. If your Redis is shared, network-exposed, or multi-tenant, use JSON or msgpack instead. The performance difference is small; the blast radius difference is total.

**Note `FAIL OPEN` on Redis errors.** A cache is an optimisation. If Redis is down, requests should be slower, not broken. Contrast with quota checks (Chapter 2), which must fail *closed* because failing open costs money.

### Tag-based invalidation

Deleting one key is easy. Invalidating "everything related to this document" is the actual problem.

```python
class TaggedCache:
    """Associate keys with tags so a domain event can invalidate a whole set."""

    async def set(self, key: str, value: Any, ttl_s: int, tags: list[str]) -> None:
        pipe = self._redis.pipeline()
        pipe.setex(key, ttl_s, serialize(value))
        for tag in tags:
            pipe.sadd(f"tag:{tag}", key)
            pipe.expire(f"tag:{tag}", ttl_s + 3600)   # outlive the keys
        await pipe.execute()

    async def invalidate_tag(self, tag: str) -> int:
        keys = await self._redis.smembers(f"tag:{tag}")
        if not keys:
            return 0
        pipe = self._redis.pipeline()
        pipe.delete(*keys)
        pipe.delete(f"tag:{tag}")
        await pipe.execute()
        CACHE_INVALIDATIONS.labels(tag=tag.split(":")[0]).inc(len(keys))
        return len(keys)

# Usage
await cache.set(f"kb:{kb_id}:documents", docs, ttl_s=300,
                tags=[f"kb:{kb_id}", f"org:{org_id}"])
await cache.set(f"doc:{doc_id}", doc, ttl_s=300,
                tags=[f"doc:{doc_id}", f"kb:{kb_id}", f"org:{org_id}"])

# One document changes → invalidate everything that could contain it
await cache.invalidate_tag(f"doc:{doc_id}")
await cache.invalidate_tag(f"kb:{kb_id}")
```

**The alternative — version stamping — is often simpler and always safer:**

```python
async def get_kb_version(kb_id: UUID) -> int:
    return int(await redis.get(f"kbver:{kb_id}") or 0)

async def bump_kb_version(kb_id: UUID) -> None:
    await redis.incr(f"kbver:{kb_id}")        # ← ONE atomic op invalidates everything

# Keys embed the version, so a bump orphans every old key at once.
version = await get_kb_version(kb_id)
key = f"kb:{kb_id}:v{version}:documents"
```

**Version stamping cannot leave stragglers.** Tag sets can drift out of sync with reality (a crashed process between `setex` and `sadd`); a version counter cannot. Orphaned keys simply expire on their TTL. Prefer it unless you specifically need to enumerate cached keys.

## 17.7 Production Example — A Complete Caching Layer

```python
# app/core/cache.py
class CacheLayer:
    """Two-tier: in-process L1 (microseconds, per-pod) over Redis L2
    (sub-millisecond, shared)."""

    def __init__(self, redis: Redis, l1_maxsize: int = 1000, l1_ttl_s: int = 5):
        self._redis = redis
        self._l1: TTLCache = TTLCache(maxsize=l1_maxsize, ttl=l1_ttl_s)

    async def get(self, key: str) -> Any | None:
        if (value := self._l1.get(key)) is not None:
            CACHE_HITS.labels(tier="l1").inc()
            return value
        try:
            if raw := await self._redis.get(key):
                value = deserialize(raw)
                self._l1[key] = value
                CACHE_HITS.labels(tier="l2").inc()
                return value
        except RedisError:
            CACHE_ERRORS.inc()
        CACHE_MISSES.inc()
        return None

    async def set(self, key: str, value: Any, ttl_s: int) -> None:
        self._l1[key] = value
        with contextlib.suppress(RedisError):
            await self._redis.setex(key, ttl_s + random.randint(0, ttl_s // 10),
                                    serialize(value))

    async def delete(self, *keys: str) -> None:
        for k in keys:
            self._l1.pop(k, None)
        with contextlib.suppress(RedisError):
            await self._redis.delete(*keys)
```

**⚠ The L1 tier's honest trade-off.** A per-pod in-memory cache cannot be invalidated from another pod. With a 5-second TTL you accept up to 5 seconds of staleness after a write, in exchange for eliminating a network round trip on hot keys. **That is the right trade for read-heavy, tolerant data (settings, feature flags, model catalogues) and completely wrong for anything where staleness is a correctness or security problem** (permissions, quotas, tenant membership). Decide per data type, not globally.

If you need cross-pod L1 invalidation, add a Redis pub/sub channel that broadcasts invalidations — but note that this reintroduces the delivery-guarantee problem from Chapter 13: a pod disconnected from Redis misses the message and serves stale data until its TTL expires. Keep the TTL short regardless.

### What to cache, and for how long

```python
CACHE_POLICIES = {
    # key namespace        ttl_s    reason
    "settings":            3600,    # changes on deploy only
    "model_catalogue":     600,     # rarely changes
    "user":                60,      # ⚠ short — deactivation must take effect
    "org_membership":      30,      # ⚠ very short — it's an authz input
    "plan_limits":         300,
    "document_metadata":   300,
    "kb_document_list":    60,
    "embedding":           604800,  # 7 days — DETERMINISTIC, never invalidates
    "retrieval_result":    300,     # the corpus changes
    "llm_completion":      3600,    # only for temperature=0
    "usage_summary":       60,
}
```

**The rule for security-relevant data: TTL is your exposure window.** A 5-minute cache on org membership means a removed employee retains access for 5 minutes. Either make it very short *and* invalidate explicitly on change, or don't cache it.

## 17.8 AI Engineering Perspective

### Embedding cache — the easiest big win

```python
class EmbeddingCache:
    """Embeddings are DETERMINISTIC: the same text and model always produce
    the same vector. This is the ideal cache — it never invalidates."""

    def __init__(self, redis: Redis, client: EmbeddingClient, model: str):
        self._redis, self._client, self._model = redis, client, model

    def _key(self, text: str) -> str:
        return f"emb:{self._model}:{hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()}"

    async def embed_many(self, texts: list[str]) -> list[list[float]]:
        keys = [self._key(t) for t in texts]

        # ONE round trip for all lookups.
        cached = await self._redis.mget(keys)
        results: list[list[float] | None] = [
            np.frombuffer(c, dtype=np.float32).tolist() if c else None
            for c in cached
        ]
        missing = [i for i, r in enumerate(results) if r is None]
        CACHE_HITS.labels(type="embedding").inc(len(texts) - len(missing))

        if missing:
            fresh = await self._client.embed_batch([texts[i] for i in missing])
            pipe = self._redis.pipeline()
            for idx, vector in zip(missing, fresh):
                results[idx] = vector
                # float32 binary: 1536 dims = 6 KB vs ~30 KB as JSON.
                pipe.setex(keys[idx], 604800,
                           np.asarray(vector, dtype=np.float32).tobytes())
            await pipe.execute()
        return results                                    # type: ignore[return-value]
```

**Why this is the first cache to build:**
- Embeddings are perfectly deterministic — no invalidation logic at all.
- Real workloads re-embed the same text constantly: repeated queries, re-ingested documents, evaluation runs, retries.
- Typical hit rates in production: **40–70%** for queries, higher for document re-ingestion.
- `mget` + pipeline means one round trip regardless of batch size.
- float32 binary storage is 5× smaller than JSON, which matters at millions of vectors.

### Exact-match LLM response cache

```python
class LLMCache:
    async def get_or_complete(self, request: ChatRequest,
                              complete: Callable) -> tuple[ChatResponse, bool]:
        # ⚠ Only cache DETERMINISTIC requests. temperature > 0 means the user
        # asked for variety; returning an identical answer defeats the purpose.
        if request.temperature > 0:
            return await complete(request), False

        key = self._key(request)
        if raw := await self._redis.get(key):
            response = ChatResponse.model_validate_json(raw)
            response.cached = True                    # tell the client
            LLM_CACHE_HITS.labels(model=request.model).inc()
            COST_SAVED.labels(model=request.model).inc(
                estimate_cost(response.usage, request.model))
            return response, True

        response = await complete(request)
        await self._redis.setex(key, 3600, response.model_dump_json())
        return response, False

    def _key(self, request: ChatRequest) -> str:
        # EVERY input that affects the output must be in the key.
        material = json.dumps({
            "model": request.model,
            "messages": [m.model_dump() for m in request.messages],
            "temperature": request.temperature,
            "max_tokens": request.max_tokens,
            "system_prompt_version": SYSTEM_PROMPT_VERSION,   # ← easy to forget
            "tools": sorted(t["function"]["name"] for t in (request.tools or [])),
        }, sort_keys=True)
        return f"llm:v3:{hashlib.sha256(material.encode()).hexdigest()}"
```

**`system_prompt_version` in the key is the field teams forget.** You improve the system prompt, deploy, and every cached response still reflects the old one — for an hour, invisibly. Include it, and bump it whenever the prompt changes.

### Semantic caching — matching on meaning

```python
class SemanticCache:
    """Exact-match caching misses 'What is your refund policy?' vs
    'How do refunds work?' — semantically identical, textually different.
    Semantic caching matches by embedding similarity."""

    def __init__(self, vector_store, embedder, threshold: float = 0.95):
        self._store, self._embedder, self._threshold = vector_store, embedder, threshold

    async def get(self, query: str, org_id: UUID) -> CachedAnswer | None:
        embedding = await self._embedder.embed(query)     # itself cached!
        hits = await self._store.search(
            embedding, collection="semantic_cache",
            filters={"org_id": str(org_id)},              # ⚠ TENANT SCOPED
            top_k=1)
        if hits and hits[0].score >= self._threshold:
            SEMANTIC_CACHE_HITS.inc()
            return CachedAnswer(**hits[0].payload, similarity=hits[0].score)
        return None

    async def put(self, query: str, answer: str, org_id: UUID,
                  sources: list[str], ttl_s: int = 86400) -> None:
        embedding = await self._embedder.embed(query)
        await self._store.upsert(
            collection="semantic_cache",
            points=[{"id": str(uuid4()), "vector": embedding,
                     "payload": {"query": query, "answer": answer,
                                 "org_id": str(org_id), "sources": sources,
                                 "created_at": utcnow().isoformat(),
                                 "expires_at": (utcnow() +
                                                timedelta(seconds=ttl_s)).isoformat()}}])
```

**Semantic caching is powerful and genuinely dangerous. Three rules:**

```
 ① THE THRESHOLD IS EVERYTHING
    0.95+  conservative — near-paraphrases only. Start here.
    0.90   moderate — noticeably more hits, occasional wrong answers.
    < 0.85 reckless — "What is our refund policy?" matches
           "What is our return policy?" and returns the wrong one.

    ⚠ Similarity does not distinguish NEGATION. "Is X covered?" and
      "Is X not covered?" are ~0.97 similar and have opposite answers.
      This alone justifies a high threshold.

 ② TENANT SCOPING IS MANDATORY
    An unscoped semantic cache serves org A's answer to org B — the exact
    breach Chapter 6 §6.8 describes, arriving through a different door.

 ③ NEVER SEMANTICALLY CACHE PERSONALISED OR TIME-SENSITIVE ANSWERS
    "What's my account balance?" and "What is my balance?" match at 0.98
    and must never share a cached answer.
```

```python
NEVER_SEMANTIC_CACHE = [
    r"\bmy\b", r"\bmine\b", r"\bour\b",           # personalised
    r"\btoday\b", r"\bnow\b", r"\bcurrent\b", r"\blatest\b",   # time-sensitive
    r"\b(balance|invoice|usage|quota|bill)\b",     # account-specific
]

def is_semantically_cacheable(query: str) -> bool:
    return not any(re.search(p, query, re.IGNORECASE) for p in NEVER_SEMANTIC_CACHE)
```

### Provider prompt caching — the highest-leverage cost optimisation

```python
# Anthropic: mark a stable prefix as cacheable. Cached tokens cost ~10% of normal.
messages = [{
    "role": "user",
    "content": [
        {"type": "text",
         "text": LONG_SYSTEM_PROMPT + KNOWLEDGE_BASE_CONTEXT,   # 50,000 tokens
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},               # ← cache this prefix
        {"type": "text", "text": user_question},                # varies per request
    ],
}]

# OpenAI: automatic for prompts over 1,024 tokens with a matching prefix.
# You don't opt in — you just have to STRUCTURE the prompt correctly.
```

```
   PROMPT STRUCTURE IS NOW A COST DECISION

   ❌ VARIABLE CONTENT FIRST — nothing can be cached
      [user question] [system prompt] [knowledge base]
       ↑ changes every request, so the entire prefix differs

   ✔ STABLE CONTENT FIRST — the long prefix is cached
      [system prompt] [knowledge base] [conversation history] [user question]
       └────────── cached (90% cheaper) ──────────┘  └── fresh ──┘

   For a 50,000-token context at $3/M input tokens:
     without prefix caching:  $0.15 per request
     with prefix caching:     $0.015 per request     ← 10× cheaper
   At 100,000 requests/month: $15,000 → $1,500.
```

**This is the single highest-return line item in this chapter**, and it costs nothing but reordering your prompt. Put stable content first, always.

## 17.9 Backend Engineering Perspective

**Redis operational concerns:**

```
 EVICTION POLICY (maxmemory-policy)
   allkeys-lru      evict least-recently-used     ← the right default for a cache
   allkeys-lfu      evict least-frequently-used   ← better for skewed access
   volatile-lru     only evict keys with a TTL
   noeviction       return errors when full       ← right for a QUEUE, wrong
                                                    for a cache

 ⚠ If Redis serves BOTH cache and queue duty, `allkeys-lru` will happily
   evict your job queue. Use separate Redis instances or separate databases
   with different policies. This has caused real, expensive incidents.

 PERSISTENCE
   RDB   periodic snapshots — fast restart, loses recent writes
   AOF   append-only log — durable, slower
   none  pure cache — correct for a cache-only instance

 HIGH AVAILABILITY
   Sentinel   automatic failover for a single primary
   Cluster    sharding + failover; needed above ~25 GB or high throughput
              ⚠ multi-key operations require keys in the same hash slot
```

**Monitoring — the metrics that matter:**

```python
CACHE_HITS = Counter("cache_hits_total", "Hits", ["namespace", "tier"])
CACHE_MISSES = Counter("cache_misses_total", "Misses", ["namespace"])
CACHE_ERRORS = Counter("cache_errors_total", "Backend errors")
CACHE_LATENCY = Histogram("cache_operation_seconds", "Latency", ["operation"])
COST_SAVED = Counter("llm_cost_saved_usd_total", "USD saved", ["model"])
```

```
 hit rate < 50%           → your TTLs are too short, or your keys are too specific
 hit rate > 99%           → suspicious: are you caching something that should be
                            invalidated? Check for stale-data bugs.
 rising eviction rate     → Redis is undersized; keys are evicted before expiry
 rising latency           → Redis is CPU-bound (often from KEYS or large values)
 memory near maxmemory    → evictions are about to start silently degrading you
```

## 17.10 Performance

```
 lru_cache hit                     ~0.1 µs
 Local dict (TTLCache) hit         ~0.5 µs
 Redis GET (same DC)               ~200 µs
 Redis MGET, 100 keys              ~500 µs   ← one round trip, not 100
 Redis pipeline, 100 ops           ~600 µs
 Postgres indexed SELECT           ~1,000 µs
 Embedding API call                ~40,000 µs
 LLM completion                    ~4,000,000 µs

 CACHE HIT vs MISS, by layer:
   Redis vs DB           5×
   Redis vs embedding    200×
   Redis vs LLM          20,000×
```

**Optimisations:**

1. **`MGET`/pipeline for batches.** 100 individual `GET`s = 20 ms; one `MGET` = 0.5 ms.
2. **Compress large values.** `zstd` on a 100 KB JSON blob: 10× smaller, ~1 ms CPU. Worth it above ~10 KB.
3. **Binary formats for vectors.** float32 bytes vs JSON: 5× smaller.
4. **An L1 tier for hot keys**, with the staleness caveat from §17.7.
5. **Jittered TTLs**, always — avalanche prevention costs one line.
6. **Cache the *right* thing.** Caching a 1 ms database query saves 0.8 ms. Caching a 4,000 ms LLM call saves 4 seconds and money. Spend your effort proportionally.
7. **Cap value sizes.** A 10 MB value in Redis blocks the server during serialisation and transfer; Redis is single-threaded for command execution.

## 17.11 Security

```python
# ❌ 1. Missing tenant scope in the cache key → cross-tenant data leak
key = f"doc:{doc_id}"                        # org B reads org A's cached document
# ✔ key = f"doc:v1:{org_id}:{doc_id}"

# ❌ 2. Caching authorization decisions too long
await redis.setex(f"perms:{user_id}", 3600, perms)   # a revoked admin keeps
                                                      # access for an hour
# ✔ TTL ≤ 30 s AND explicit invalidation on any role or membership change

# ❌ 3. `Cache-Control: public` on an authenticated response
#    A shared CDN or corporate proxy serves user A's data to user B.
# ✔ `private` or `no-store` on everything authenticated

# ❌ 4. Caching secrets
await redis.setex(f"key:{id}", 3600, api_key_plaintext)
# ✔ Never. If Redis is dumped, so are your credentials.

# ❌ 5. Unscoped semantic cache → org B receives org A's answer
# ✔ Filter by org_id inside the vector search, plus a redundant assertion

# ❌ 6. `pickle` deserialisation from a shared Redis → RCE
# ✔ JSON or msgpack when the Redis instance isn't fully trusted

# ❌ 7. Cache penetration as a DoS
#    An attacker requests random UUIDs; every one misses and hits the database.
# ✔ Cache negative results briefly:
if doc is None:
    await redis.setex(key, 30, b"__NULL__")     # short TTL — it may be created
# ✔ Or a Bloom filter of existing IDs for very high-volume endpoints

# ❌ 8. Unbounded in-process caches keyed by user → a slow memory leak
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def get_user_permissions(user_id): ...          # grows forever
# ✔ maxsize bounded, or use Redis

# ❌ 9. KEYS in production → blocks Redis for seconds
# ✔ SCAN, or maintain your own index set
```

**Cache poisoning** deserves a note. If any cache key is derived from unvalidated client input — a header, a query parameter, a `Vary` value — an attacker can store a chosen response under a key that legitimate users will hit. Validate everything that enters a key, and never include a raw client-supplied string without normalising it.

## 17.12 Best Practices

```
✔ Cache-aside with invalidate-on-write (never write-through)
✔ Version and tenant-scope every key
✔ Include EVERY input that affects the output — especially prompt versions
✔ Jitter every TTL
✔ Single-flight locking on expensive keys, with a Lua compare-and-delete release
✔ Serve stale while revalidating
✔ Cache negative results briefly (penetration defence)
✔ Fail OPEN on cache errors — a cache outage should slow you, not break you
✔ Short TTLs on authorization data, plus explicit invalidation
✔ `private`/`no-store` on all authenticated HTTP responses
✔ Embedding cache first — deterministic, high hit rate, trivial
✔ LLM cache only at temperature=0
✔ Semantic cache at ≥0.95 similarity, tenant-scoped, never for personalised queries
✔ Structure prompts with stable content FIRST for provider prompt caching
✔ MGET/pipeline for batches; SCAN never KEYS
✔ Track hit rate, cost saved, and evictions
✔ Separate Redis instances (or eviction policies) for cache and queue
```

## 17.13 Common Mistakes

```python
# ❌ 1. No tenant in the key → cross-tenant leak
# ❌ 2. Write-through instead of invalidate → stale value wins a race
# ❌ 3. No stampede protection → a hot key expiring takes down the database
# ❌ 4. No TTL jitter → avalanche after a deploy
# ❌ 5. Caching temperature>0 completions → the user asked for variety
# ❌ 6. Missing prompt version in the key → old answers after a prompt change
# ❌ 7. Semantic cache threshold too low → confidently wrong answers
# ❌ 8. Semantic caching personalised queries → "my balance" served to everyone
# ❌ 9. Long TTL on permissions → a revoked user keeps access
# ❌ 10. `Cache-Control: public` on authenticated responses
# ❌ 11. KEYS in production → seconds of total Redis unavailability
# ❌ 12. Failing closed on cache errors → a Redis blip becomes an outage
# ❌ 13. Unbounded lru_cache keyed by user → memory leak
# ❌ 14. No hit-rate monitoring → you don't know whether the cache works
# ❌ 15. Variable content first in the prompt → provider caching never engages
# ❌ 16. allkeys-lru on a Redis that also holds your job queue
```

## 17.14 Interview Questions

1. **What is cache-aside?** Read: check cache, on miss read the source and populate. Write: update the source and *delete* the key. It's the default pattern because deletion is idempotent and race-safe.

2. **Why invalidate rather than update on write?** Updating races: a slow reader can write a stale value after a fast writer wrote the fresh one, and the stale value persists for the whole TTL. Deletion cannot lose that race.

3. **What is a cache stampede?** A hot key expires and every concurrent request misses simultaneously, hammering the source. Fix with single-flight locking plus stale-while-revalidate and probabilistic early expiry.

4. **How do you implement single-flight across pods?** `SET NX` with a TTL as a distributed lock; losers serve stale data or wait; release with a Lua compare-and-delete so you never delete a lock you no longer hold.

5. **Why does the Lua CAS release matter?** If your computation outlives the lock TTL, another pod acquires it. A plain `DEL` would delete *their* lock, letting a third pod in — silently defeating the entire mechanism.

6. **What is cache penetration?** Repeated requests for non-existent keys always miss and always hit the source, letting an attacker DDoS your database through your cache. Fix by caching negative results briefly, or a Bloom filter.

7. **What is cache avalanche?** Many keys written together expire together, causing a mass miss. Fix with jittered TTLs.

8. **What must be in a cache key?** Namespace, version, tenant, and every input affecting the output — model, temperature, prompt version, retrieval parameters.

9. **Why version the key namespace?** Changing the stored format with old keys live causes deserialisation errors on every hit. A version bump invalidates everything atomically for free.

10. **What's the risk of caching without a tenant scope?** A cross-tenant data leak that bypasses every authorization check, because the cache lookup never touches your authz layer.

11. **How long should you cache authorization data?** Very briefly (≤30 s), with explicit invalidation on change. The TTL is literally your exposure window after revoking access.

12. **Why is `Cache-Control: public` dangerous on authenticated responses?** Shared caches — CDNs, corporate proxies — will store one user's response and serve it to another.

13. **What is an ETag and how does it help?** A version identifier for a resource. The client sends `If-None-Match`; if it matches, you return 304 with no body, saving bandwidth and serialisation.

14. **Why is caching embeddings the best first cache?** They're deterministic, so there's no invalidation logic at all; the same texts recur constantly; and hit rates of 40–70% are typical.

15. **When can you cache an LLM completion?** Only at temperature 0, where output is (approximately) deterministic. Above 0 the user asked for variety, and a cached identical response defeats the request.

16. **What is semantic caching and what makes it risky?** Matching queries by embedding similarity rather than exact text. Risky because similarity doesn't capture negation ("is X covered" ≈ "is X *not* covered" at 0.97) and personalised queries match across users. Use a high threshold, tenant scoping, and an exclusion list.

17. **What threshold would you use for semantic caching?** 0.95 or higher to start, measured against a labelled set of query pairs. Lower thresholds increase hit rate and increase wrong answers; the trade is rarely worth it below 0.90.

18. **What is provider prompt caching and how do you exploit it?** Providers cache stable prompt prefixes and charge ~10% for cached tokens. You exploit it by putting stable content (system prompt, knowledge base) *first* and variable content last — a pure reordering that can cut costs 10×.

19. **Should a cache failure fail open or closed?** Open. A cache is an optimisation; a Redis outage should make requests slower, not fail. Contrast with quota checks, which must fail closed because failing open costs money.

20. **Why never use `KEYS` in production?** It scans the entire keyspace while blocking Redis's single command thread — seconds of total unavailability for all clients. Use `SCAN`.

21. **What's wrong with sharing a Redis between cache and queue?** `allkeys-lru` eviction will evict queue entries under memory pressure. Use separate instances or separate databases with different eviction policies.

22. **How do you decide between tag-based invalidation and version stamping?** Version stamping is one atomic increment and cannot leave stragglers; tag sets can drift out of sync with reality. Prefer versions unless you need to enumerate cached keys.

23. **What are the risks of an in-process L1 cache?** It can't be invalidated from other pods, so writes elsewhere are invisible until the TTL expires. Acceptable for tolerant read-heavy data with a very short TTL; unacceptable for permissions and quotas.

24. **How do you measure whether caching is working?** Hit rate per namespace, cost saved (for LLM caches), eviction rate, and cache operation latency. A hit rate above 99% is as suspicious as one below 50% — it may indicate missing invalidation.

25. **Design the caching strategy for a RAG platform.** Provider prompt caching via stable-prefix-first prompt structure (biggest cost win); a 7-day embedding cache with `mget` batching and float32 storage; a 5-minute retrieval cache keyed by query hash plus knowledge-base version; an exact-match LLM cache at temperature 0 including prompt version in the key; an optional tenant-scoped semantic cache at 0.95 with a personalisation exclusion list; a short-TTL L1 for settings and catalogues; ETags on document reads; single-flight locking with stale-while-revalidate on all expensive keys; version stamping for invalidation; jittered TTLs; fail-open on Redis errors; and hit-rate plus cost-saved dashboards.

## 17.15 Exercises

**Easy**
1. Add `lru_cache` to a settings loader and prove it executes once.
2. Implement cache-aside for a document read with Redis; measure hit vs miss latency.
3. Add ETag support and verify a 304 response with `curl -H 'If-None-Match: ...'`.

**Medium**
4. Implement `get_or_compute` with single-flight locking; prove with 100 concurrent requests that the expensive function runs exactly once.
5. Implement the embedding cache with `mget` and float32 storage; measure the hit rate on a realistic query set.
6. Implement version-stamped invalidation for a knowledge base; prove one increment invalidates every related key.
7. Add jittered TTLs and demonstrate the difference in expiry distribution.

**Hard**
8. Implement the semantic cache with tenant scoping and an exclusion list; measure hit rate and false-positive rate at thresholds 0.85, 0.90, 0.95 on a labelled query set.
9. Implement the two-tier cache with L1 TTL and Redis pub/sub invalidation; measure staleness under concurrent writes.
10. Restructure a RAG prompt for provider prompt caching and measure the actual cost difference on a real provider.

**Production**
11. Build a complete caching layer: embedding cache, retrieval cache, LLM cache, semantic cache, HTTP caching, single-flight, version-stamped invalidation, fail-open behaviour, and a dashboard showing hit rates and dollars saved — with a load test proving no stampede when a hot key expires under 1,000 rps.

## 17.16 Solutions

**Solution 4 — proving single-flight.**
```python
async def test_single_flight_under_concurrency(redis_client):
    call_count = 0

    async def expensive():
        nonlocal call_count
        call_count += 1
        await asyncio.sleep(0.5)                  # simulate a slow source
        return {"value": "computed"}

    results = await asyncio.gather(
        *[get_or_compute("test:key", expensive, ttl_s=60) for _ in range(100)])

    assert all(r == {"value": "computed"} for r in results)
    assert call_count == 1, f"expensive() ran {call_count} times — stampede"
```
**Reasoning:** without the lock this asserts `call_count == 100`. The test is only meaningful because `expensive()` sleeps: with an instant function, the first caller populates the cache before the others check, and even a broken implementation passes. **Concurrency tests need the operation to be slow enough that the race window actually opens** — a general principle worth remembering when testing anything lock-related.

**Solution 8 — measuring the semantic cache trade-off.**
```python
# A labelled dataset is the only honest way to choose a threshold.
QUERY_PAIRS = [
    ("What is your refund policy?", "How do refunds work?", True),
    ("What is your refund policy?", "What is your return policy?", False),
    ("Is damage covered?", "Is damage not covered?", False),        # ← negation
    ("How do I reset my password?", "Password reset instructions", True),
    ("What is my balance?", "What's my current balance?", False),   # personalised
]

@pytest.mark.parametrize("threshold", [0.85, 0.90, 0.95, 0.98])
async def test_semantic_cache_precision(embedder, threshold):
    tp = fp = fn = 0
    for q1, q2, should_match in QUERY_PAIRS:
        v1, v2 = await embedder.embed(q1), await embedder.embed(q2)
        similarity = cosine(v1, v2)
        matched = similarity >= threshold
        if matched and should_match:      tp += 1
        elif matched and not should_match: fp += 1
        elif not matched and should_match: fn += 1

    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if (tp + fp) else 1.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) else 1.0
    print(f"threshold={threshold}: precision={precision:.2f} recall={recall:.2f}")

    # A false positive means serving a WRONG ANSWER. That is worse than a
    # cache miss by orders of magnitude — precision is non-negotiable.
    assert precision >= 0.99, f"threshold {threshold} serves wrong answers"
```
**Reasoning:** the asymmetry is the whole point. A cache miss costs 4 seconds and a few cents. A false positive returns a confidently wrong answer to a user, which is a product failure and potentially a compliance one. Optimising for hit rate is the wrong objective; optimise for precision and accept whatever hit rate that yields. The negation pair in the dataset is deliberately included because it is the failure mode most teams don't anticipate.

## 17.17 Mini Project — A Multi-Layer AI Cache

**Goal.** Cut inference cost by 40%+ without degrading answer quality.

**Requirements:**
1. Embedding cache: 7-day TTL, `mget` batching, float32 binary storage.
2. Retrieval cache: keyed by query hash + KB version, 5-minute TTL.
3. Exact LLM cache: temperature-0 only, prompt version in the key.
4. Semantic cache: tenant-scoped, 0.95 threshold, exclusion list, TTL.
5. Provider prompt caching: prompts restructured stable-first, with cache_control markers.
6. HTTP: ETags on document reads, correct `private`/`no-store` headers.
7. Single-flight with stale-while-revalidate on every expensive key.
8. Version-stamped invalidation on document create/update/delete.
9. Fail-open behaviour on all Redis errors.
10. Two-tier L1/L2 for settings and catalogues, with documented staleness bounds.
11. Metrics: hit rate per layer, dollars saved, eviction rate, latency.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- Overall LLM cost reduced ≥40% on a replayed production traffic sample.
- Embedding cache hit rate ≥50%.
- Semantic cache precision ≥0.99 on a labelled evaluation set.
- No stampede: 1,000 concurrent requests for an expired hot key produce exactly one upstream call.
- Redis down → all endpoints still work, with degraded latency and an alert.
- A cross-tenant cache test proves no key is reachable from another org.
- A document update invalidates all derived caches within one request.

## Chapter 17 Summary

| Idea | The one-line version |
|---|---|
| Caching in AI is about cost, not latency | 30% hit rate on a $50k bill is $15k/month |
| Cache-aside + invalidate on write | write-through loses races and persists stale data |
| Version and tenant-scope every key | one missing `org_id` is a cross-tenant leak |
| Stampede, penetration, avalanche | single-flight, negative caching, jitter |
| Lua CAS on lock release | otherwise you delete someone else's lock |
| Fail open | a cache outage should slow you, not break you |
| Embeddings are the easiest win | deterministic, high hit rate, no invalidation |
| LLM caching only at temperature 0 | above that the user asked for variety |
| Semantic caching: precision over hit rate | a false positive is a wrong answer |
| Prompt structure is a cost decision | stable content first → 10× cheaper prefixes |
| Short TTLs on authz data | the TTL is your post-revocation exposure window |

### Cheat Sheet

```python
# Cache-aside
if v := await r.get(key): return deserialize(v)
v = await compute()
await r.setex(key, ttl + random.randint(0, ttl//10), serialize(v))

# Single-flight
if await r.set(f"lock:{key}", token, nx=True, ex=30):
    try: ... finally: await r.eval(CAS_DEL, 1, f"lock:{key}", token)

# Batch
values = await r.mget(keys)                # ONE round trip
pipe = r.pipeline(); pipe.get(a); pipe.incr(b); await pipe.execute()

# Invalidate
await r.delete(key)                        # single
await r.incr(f"ver:{entity_id}")           # version stamp: invalidates all

# HTTP
response.headers["ETag"] = etag
response.headers["Cache-Control"] = "private, max-age=60, must-revalidate"

# NEVER: await r.keys("*")   →  use scan_iter
```

### Production Checklist
- [ ] Every key namespaced, versioned, and tenant-scoped
- [ ] TTLs jittered
- [ ] Single-flight on all expensive keys, with CAS release
- [ ] Negative results cached briefly
- [ ] Fail-open on cache backend errors, with an alert
- [ ] Invalidation on every write path (version stamps preferred)
- [ ] Separate Redis (or policy) for cache vs queue
- [ ] `maxmemory-policy` set deliberately
- [ ] Hit rate, cost saved, and eviction dashboards

### Security Checklist
- [ ] Tenant ID in every key; a cross-tenant test in CI
- [ ] Authorization data cached ≤30 s with explicit invalidation
- [ ] `private`/`no-store` on all authenticated responses
- [ ] No secrets cached
- [ ] Semantic cache tenant-scoped, high threshold, personalisation excluded
- [ ] JSON/msgpack rather than pickle on shared Redis
- [ ] Cache keys never built from unvalidated client input

### Performance Checklist
- [ ] `MGET`/pipeline for batch lookups
- [ ] Binary formats for vectors; compression above ~10 KB
- [ ] Provider prompt caching engaged (stable content first)
- [ ] Embedding cache before anything else
- [ ] Effort proportional to what's being saved (LLM ≫ database)
- [ ] Value sizes capped

# Chapter 18 — Testing

> Testing an AI backend has one problem no other backend has: **the core component is non-deterministic, slow, and costs money per invocation.** Everything in this chapter follows from managing that fact without giving up on correctness.

## 18.1 Concept Overview

**The testing pyramid, adapted for AI systems:**

```
                    ╱╲
                   ╱  ╲     EVALS (10s–hours, $$$, non-deterministic)
                  ╱ E  ╲    "is the model's OUTPUT good?"
                 ╱──────╲   nightly / pre-release, scored not asserted
                ╱        ╲
               ╱   E2E    ╲  (seconds, real infrastructure)
              ╱  10–30     ╲ "does the whole system work?"
             ╱──────────────╲
            ╱                ╲
           ╱   INTEGRATION    ╲ (100ms, real DB + Redis, STUBBED LLM)
          ╱      100–300       ╲ "do the layers work together?"
         ╱──────────────────────╲
        ╱                        ╲
       ╱          UNIT            ╲ (1ms, no I/O at all)
      ╱          500–2000          ╲ "is the logic correct?"
     ╱──────────────────────────────╲

  ⚠ THE CRITICAL SPLIT: evals are NOT tests. Tests assert; evals SCORE.
    A test either passes or fails. An eval produces a number you track
    over time. Mixing them gives you a flaky CI and no quality signal.
```

**The four rules that make an AI backend testable:**

```
 ① NEVER call a real LLM in CI. Slow, costly, non-deterministic, and it
    fails when the provider has an incident — which is not your bug.
 ② EVERY external system behind ONE dependency, so it can be overridden (Ch. 2).
 ③ Test YOUR logic, not the model's. That prompts produce good answers is an
    eval question; that your retry logic works is a test question.
 ④ Evals run on a schedule against a fixed dataset, producing tracked scores —
    never as a pass/fail gate in a pull-request pipeline.
```

## 18.2 Historical Background

```
 1999 ─ Extreme Programming popularises test-first development.
 2004 ─ JUnit-style frameworks everywhere; unittest ships with Python.
 2004 ─ pytest: fixtures, plain asserts, and plugins. Becomes the standard.
 2010 ─ Mocking libraries mature; over-mocking becomes a recognised anti-pattern.
 2013 ─ Docker makes real dependencies in tests practical.
 2015 ─ Testcontainers: spin up real Postgres/Redis per test session.
 2018 ─ FastAPI ships TestClient and dependency_overrides — testability
        designed in rather than bolted on.
 2020 ─ Property-based testing (Hypothesis) gains traction in Python.
 2023 ─ LLM evaluation becomes a discipline: golden datasets, LLM-as-judge,
        regression tracking. Tools: promptfoo, DeepEval, Langfuse, Braintrust.
 2024+ ─ The consensus settles: deterministic tests for code, scored evals for
         model behaviour, and never confuse the two.
```

## 18.3 Internal Working

### 18.3.1 `TestClient` vs `httpx.AsyncClient`

```python
# ── TestClient: synchronous, wraps the app with an ASGI transport ──
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

def test_health():
    with TestClient(app) as client:          # `with` TRIGGERS LIFESPAN
        response = client.get("/health/live")
        assert response.status_code == 200
```

**⚠ The `with` block matters.** Without it, `lifespan` never runs, so `app.state.redis`, `app.state.http`, and your model are all missing — and you get `AttributeError` in confusing places. `TestClient(app)` without the context manager is the most common FastAPI testing mistake.

```python
# ── httpx.AsyncClient: async-native, needed to await in your test body ──
import pytest
from httpx import AsyncClient, ASGITransport

@pytest.fixture
async def client(app):
    async with LifespanManager(app):          # from asgi-lifespan
        transport = ASGITransport(app=app)
        async with AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="http://test") as c:
            yield c

@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_chat(client, auth_headers):
    response = await client.post("/v1/chat", json={...}, headers=auth_headers)
    assert response.status_code == 200
```

**Which to use:** `AsyncClient` if your test needs to `await` anything (database setup, concurrent requests, streaming). `TestClient` for simple synchronous assertions. In an async codebase, standardise on `AsyncClient` — mixing them creates event-loop confusion.

```
   NEITHER makes a real network call. Both use an ASGI transport that calls
   your app directly:
       client.get("/x") → app(scope, receive, send) → your handler
   So you skip the socket, HTTP parsing, and Uvicorn — which is fast, but
   means these tests do NOT cover Uvicorn behaviour, proxy buffering, or
   real timeouts. Those need a live server (§18.6).
```

### 18.3.2 `dependency_overrides`

```python
app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: test_session
app.dependency_overrides[get_llm] = lambda: StubLLM()
app.dependency_overrides.clear()             # ALWAYS, in teardown
```

Covered mechanically in Chapter 12 §12.6. The three gotchas, restated because they cost hours:

1. **Overrides match by callable identity** — a factory-produced dependency needs a module-level name to be overridable.
2. **Overriding a sub-dependency doesn't skip its parent** — override `get_db` and `current_user` still runs, just with the fake session.
3. **They persist across tests** — a plain dict on the app object. Always clear in a fixture teardown, never inline.

### 18.3.3 The `anyio` / `asyncio` fixture problem

```python
# conftest.py
import pytest

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def anyio_backend():
    return "asyncio"           # tells anyio which backend to use

# Every async test needs a marker
@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_something(): ...

# Or apply it globally in pyproject.toml:
# [tool.pytest.ini_options]
# asyncio_mode = "auto"        # pytest-asyncio: no marker needed
```

**⚠ The event-loop scope trap.** By default `pytest-asyncio` creates a *new event loop per test*. A session-scoped fixture that creates an async resource (a database engine, a Redis pool) binds to the loop that existed when it was created — and then fails in every subsequent test with `RuntimeError: attached to a different loop` or `Event loop is closed`.

```python
# ✔ Match the fixture scope to the loop scope
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def event_loop():                        # pytest-asyncio < 0.23
    loop = asyncio.new_event_loop()
    yield loop
    loop.close()

# pytest-asyncio >= 0.23:
# [tool.pytest.ini_options]
# asyncio_default_fixture_loop_scope = "session"
```

This one error accounts for a large share of "my async tests are mysteriously broken" reports.

## 18.4 Syntax — pytest Essentials

```python
# ── fixtures ──
@pytest.fixture                       # function scope (default)
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")      # once per test run
@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)         # applied to every test automatically
@pytest.fixture(params=[1, 2, 3])     # runs the test once per param

# ── parametrisation ──
@pytest.mark.parametrize("value,expected", [(1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6)])
def test_double(value, expected):
    assert double(value) == expected

@pytest.mark.parametrize("case", CASES, ids=lambda c: c.name)   # readable IDs

# ── exceptions ──
with pytest.raises(HTTPException) as exc_info:
    await service.run()
assert exc_info.value.status_code == 402
assert "quota" in str(exc_info.value.detail).lower()

# ── markers ──
@pytest.mark.slow
@pytest.mark.integration
@pytest.mark.skipif(not settings.OPENAI_API_KEY, reason="no API key")
@pytest.mark.xfail(reason="known bug #1234", strict=True)

# ── running ──
pytest -x                    # stop at the first failure
pytest -k "chat and not slow"
pytest -m "not integration"
pytest --lf                  # last failed
pytest -n auto               # parallel (pytest-xdist)
pytest --cov=app --cov-report=term-missing
```

## 18.6 Intermediate Examples — The Test Suite Architecture

### `conftest.py` — the foundation

```python
# tests/conftest.py
import pytest
from httpx import AsyncClient, ASGITransport
from asgi_lifespan import LifespanManager
from testcontainers.postgres import PostgresContainer
from testcontainers.redis import RedisContainer

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def anyio_backend():
    return "asyncio"

# ── REAL infrastructure, once per session ──
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def postgres_url() -> str:
    with PostgresContainer("postgres:16") as pg:
        yield pg.get_connection_url().replace("psycopg2", "asyncpg")

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def redis_url() -> str:
    with RedisContainer("redis:7-alpine") as r:
        yield f"redis://{r.get_container_host_ip()}:{r.get_exposed_port(6379)}"

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
async def engine(postgres_url):
    engine = create_async_engine(postgres_url, poolclass=NullPool)
    async with engine.begin() as conn:
        await conn.run_sync(Base.metadata.create_all)
    yield engine
    await engine.dispose()

# ── A transaction-rollback session: perfect isolation, no truncation ──
@pytest.fixture
async def db(engine) -> AsyncGenerator[AsyncSession, None]:
    """Each test runs inside a transaction that is ROLLED BACK afterwards.
    Fast (no table truncation) and perfectly isolated (no cross-test leakage)."""
    async with engine.connect() as connection:
        transaction = await connection.begin()
        session = AsyncSession(bind=connection, expire_on_commit=False)
        # Nested transactions so service-layer commit() doesn't end the outer one.
        await connection.begin_nested()

        @event.listens_for(session.sync_session, "after_transaction_end")
        def restart_savepoint(sess, trans):
            if trans.nested and not trans._parent.nested:
                connection.sync_connection.begin_nested()

        yield session
        await session.close()
        await transaction.rollback()          # ← everything disappears

# ── Stubs for external services ──
@pytest.fixture
def stub_llm() -> StubLLMClient:
    return StubLLMClient()

@pytest.fixture
def stub_vector_store() -> InMemoryVectorStore:
    return InMemoryVectorStore()

# ── The app, fully wired with overrides ──
@pytest.fixture
async def app(db, redis_url, stub_llm, stub_vector_store):
    from app.main import create_app
    application = create_app(settings_override={"REDIS_URL": redis_url})
    application.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: db
    application.dependency_overrides[get_llm] = lambda: stub_llm
    application.dependency_overrides[get_vector_store] = lambda: stub_vector_store
    yield application
    application.dependency_overrides.clear()      # ← always

@pytest.fixture
async def client(app) -> AsyncGenerator[AsyncClient, None]:
    async with LifespanManager(app):
        async with AsyncClient(transport=ASGITransport(app=app),
                               base_url="http://test") as c:
            yield c

# ── Identity fixtures ──
@pytest.fixture
async def org(db) -> Organization:
    o = Organization(id=uuid4(), name="Test Org", plan=Plan.PRO)
    db.add(o); await db.flush()
    return o

@pytest.fixture
async def user(db, org) -> User:
    u = User(id=uuid4(), email="test@example.com", org_id=org.id,
             role=Role.MEMBER, is_active=True)
    db.add(u); await db.flush()
    return u

@pytest.fixture
def auth_headers(user) -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"Authorization": f"Bearer {create_access_token(user)}"}
```

**Why real Postgres and Redis but a stubbed LLM.** Databases have behaviour that SQLite and mocks do not reproduce: constraint violations, transaction isolation, JSONB operators, row-level security, index behaviour. Testing against SQLite means your constraint-violation handling (Chapter 8 §8.6) is never exercised. Redis has atomic semantics (`SET NX`, `INCR`) that a dict cannot reproduce. **The LLM is different**: it's slow, costly, non-deterministic, and its behaviour is an eval concern, not a test concern.

### The stub LLM

```python
# tests/stubs/llm.py
class StubLLMClient:
    """Deterministic, configurable, and RECORDING. The recording part is what
    makes it useful: you assert on how your code CALLED the LLM."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.calls: list[ChatRequest] = []
        self.responses: list[ChatResponse | Exception] = []
        self.default_response = ChatResponse(
            id="stub-1", content="stub answer", model="stub",
            usage=Usage(prompt_tokens=10, completion_tokens=5, total_tokens=15))
        self.stream_tokens: list[str] = ["stub", " ", "answer"]
        self.latency_s: float = 0.0

    def queue(self, *responses: ChatResponse | Exception) -> None:
        self.responses.extend(responses)

    async def complete(self, request: ChatRequest, **kw) -> ChatResponse:
        self.calls.append(request)
        if self.latency_s:
            await asyncio.sleep(self.latency_s)
        if self.responses:
            result = self.responses.pop(0)
            if isinstance(result, Exception):
                raise result
            return result
        return self.default_response

    async def stream(self, request: ChatRequest, **kw) -> AsyncIterator[StreamEvent]:
        self.calls.append(request)
        for token in self.stream_tokens:
            await asyncio.sleep(self.latency_s / max(len(self.stream_tokens), 1))
            yield StreamEvent(type="token", text=token)
        yield StreamEvent(type="usage", prompt_tokens=10, completion_tokens=3)

    # ── assertions ──
    @property
    def call_count(self) -> int:
        return len(self.calls)

    def assert_called_with_system_prompt_containing(self, text: str) -> None:
        system = next((m for m in self.calls[-1].messages if m.role == "system"), None)
        assert system is not None, "no system message was sent"
        assert text in system.content, f"{text!r} not in the system prompt"

    def assert_context_includes(self, snippet: str) -> None:
        combined = "\n".join(m.content for m in self.calls[-1].messages)
        assert snippet in combined, f"retrieved context missing {snippet!r}"
```

**The `queue()` method is what makes failure-path testing possible:**

```python
async def test_falls_back_to_secondary_provider(client, stub_llm, auth_headers):
    stub_llm.queue(UpstreamError("primary down"), CANNED_GOOD_RESPONSE)
    response = await client.post("/v1/chat", json=BODY, headers=auth_headers)
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert stub_llm.call_count == 2                # tried primary, then secondary

async def test_does_not_fall_back_on_content_filter(client, stub_llm, auth_headers):
    stub_llm.queue(ContentFilteredError())
    response = await client.post("/v1/chat", json=BODY, headers=auth_headers)
    assert response.status_code == 400
    assert stub_llm.call_count == 1                # ← the important assertion:
                                                   # no wasted money on a retry
```

That second test encodes the rule from Chapter 8: fall back on 5xx/429, never on 4xx. The `call_count == 1` assertion is what stops someone "improving" the fallback logic into a money-wasting one.

### Testing streaming endpoints

```python
@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_stream_delivers_incrementally(client, stub_llm, auth_headers):
    """Assert on TIMING, not just content. A content-only test passes even
    when a middleware has buffered the whole response (Ch. 9 §9.16)."""
    stub_llm.stream_tokens = ["one", "two", "three", "four", "five"]
    stub_llm.latency_s = 0.5                         # 0.1 s between tokens

    timings: list[tuple[float, str]] = []
    start = time.perf_counter()
    async with client.stream("POST", "/v1/chat/stream",
                             json=BODY, headers=auth_headers) as response:
        assert response.status_code == 200
        assert response.headers["content-type"].startswith("text/event-stream")
        assert response.headers.get("x-accel-buffering") == "no"
        async for line in response.aiter_lines():
            if line.startswith("data: "):
                timings.append((time.perf_counter() - start, line))

    assert len(timings) >= 5
    assert timings[0][0] < 0.3, "first event was slow — buffered?"
    assert timings[-1][0] - timings[0][0] > 0.2, "all events arrived at once"
    assert timings[-1][1] == "data: [DONE]"
```

### Testing security properties

```python
# tests/security/test_authz.py
RESOURCE_ENDPOINTS = [
    ("GET",    "/v1/documents/{id}"),
    ("PATCH",  "/v1/documents/{id}"),
    ("DELETE", "/v1/documents/{id}"),
    ("GET",    "/v1/conversations/{id}"),
    ("GET",    "/v1/jobs/{id}"),
    ("GET",    "/v1/api-keys/{id}"),
]

@pytest.mark.parametrize("method,template", RESOURCE_ENDPOINTS)
async def test_cross_tenant_access_returns_404(client, method, template,
                                                org_a_headers, org_b_resources):
    """OWASP API1 — the #1 API vulnerability. Automated, for every endpoint."""
    resource_id = org_b_resources[template]
    response = await client.request(method, template.format(id=resource_id),
                                    headers=org_a_headers)
    assert response.status_code == 404, (
        f"BOLA: {method} {template} returned {response.status_code} "
        f"for another tenant's resource")

async def test_every_route_has_an_auth_dependency(app):
    """Structural: a new endpoint without auth fails CI (Ch. 12 §12.7)."""
    PUBLIC = ("/health", "/v1/auth", "/docs", "/openapi", "/redoc", "/metrics")
    unprotected = []
    for route in app.routes:
        if not isinstance(route, APIRoute) or route.path.startswith(PUBLIC):
            continue
        names = collect_dependency_names(route.dependant)
        if not any("current_" in n or "verify_api_key" in n for n in names):
            unprotected.append(f"{sorted(route.methods)} {route.path}")
    assert not unprotected, "Unprotected endpoints:\n" + "\n".join(unprotected)

async def test_no_secrets_in_any_error_response(client, auth_headers, monkeypatch):
    """No 500 may leak internals (Ch. 8 §8.11)."""
    monkeypatch.setattr("app.services.chat.ChatService.complete",
                        AsyncMock(side_effect=RuntimeError(
                            "connection to postgres://user:hunter2@db failed")))
    response = await client.post("/v1/chat", json=BODY, headers=auth_headers)
    assert response.status_code == 500
    body = response.text.lower()
    for forbidden in ("hunter2", "postgres://", "traceback", "runtimeerror",
                      "/app/", "line "):
        assert forbidden not in body, f"error response leaked {forbidden!r}"
```
