## A.13 The Numbers

```
 LATENCY (order of magnitude)
   Pydantic v2 validate, 1 KB      ~8 µs        FastAPI framework overhead  ~200 µs
   Redis GET                       ~0.2 ms      Postgres indexed SELECT     ~1 ms
   Vector search, 1M, HNSW         5–30 ms      Embedding API call          20–80 ms
   LLM TTFT                        0.3–0.8 s    LLM full response           4–15 s

 CONCURRENCY
   asyncio task switch  ~0.1 µs    OS thread switch     ~1–10 µs
   coroutine memory     ~1–3 KB    thread stack         ~8 MB virtual
   threadpool (def endpoints)      40 slots by default

 MIDDLEWARE
   pure ASGI  ~10 µs               BaseHTTPMiddleware  ~300–1000 µs (breaks streaming)

 CACHE HIT vs MISS
   vs database  5×                 vs embedding  200×      vs LLM  20,000×
```

## A.14 The Non-Negotiables

```
 ⚠ Never block the event loop. Monitor event_loop_lag.
 ⚠ Never construct clients, pools, or models per request — lifespan owns them.
 ⚠ Never return an ORM object without a response_model.
 ⚠ Never trust filename, Content-Type, X-Forwarded-For, or an LLM's tool choice.
 ⚠ Never cache without a tenant in the key.
 ⚠ Never paginate with OFFSET on an unbounded table.
 ⚠ Never omit a timeout on an outbound call.
 ⚠ Never retry a 4xx across providers.
 ⚠ Never put `input` (the failing value) in a validation error response.
 ⚠ Never gzip or buffer a stream.
 ⚠ Never run a container as root, or deploy a `latest` tag.
 ⚠ Never point production at a floating model alias.
 ⚠ Always record usage in `finally`.
 ⚠ Always return 404 (not 403) for another tenant's resource.
```

# Appendix B — Capstone Project: A Complete AI SaaS Backend

> Reading backend engineering teaches recognition. Running a system under load teaches everything else. This appendix specifies one complete product — a multi-tenant RAG platform — that exercises all 22 chapters. Build it over six to eight weeks and you will have done the work this guide describes.

---

## B.1 The Product

**"Cortex"** — a document-intelligence API. Organisations upload documents, then query them in natural language and receive grounded, cited answers. Programmatic access via API keys; a web app via JWTs.

**Why this product.** It is the smallest system that genuinely requires everything: multi-tenancy, async fan-out, streaming, background processing, vector search, cost control, and rate limiting. A to-do API teaches CRUD; this teaches AI backend engineering.

---

**Row-level security on every tenant table** (Chapter 6 §6.16):

```sql
ALTER TABLE documents ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE documents FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON documents
  USING (org_id = current_setting('app.current_org_id')::uuid);
```

## B.6 Build Order

Build it in this sequence. Each phase produces something that works, and each depends only on what came before.

### Phase 1 — Foundations (week 1)
```
 [ ] Repo, pyproject, ruff, mypy, pre-commit
 [ ] Settings with production-safety validators                    [Ch 7,21]
 [ ] docker-compose: Postgres, Redis, Qdrant, MinIO
 [ ] FastAPI app, lifespan, split health probes                    [Ch 1]
 [ ] Structured logging with request IDs                           [Ch 4,21]
 [ ] Error hierarchy + handlers, one response shape                [Ch 8]
 [ ] Alembic; first migration
 [ ] tests/conftest.py: testcontainers, transaction rollback       [Ch 18]
 ✓ MILESTONE: /health/ready returns 200 with dependency checks; tests run.
```

### Phase 2 — Identity (week 2)
```
 [ ] User, Organization, Membership models + RLS                   [Ch 6]
 [ ] Argon2 hashing, offloaded from the loop                       [Ch 5]
 [ ] JWT with RS256, kid, JWKS endpoint
 [ ] Refresh rotation with families and reuse detection
 [ ] The dependency vocabulary in deps.py                          [Ch 2]
 [ ] current_org with membership verification in ONE query         [Ch 12]
 [ ] API keys: prefixed, hashed, lookup ID, scopes, spend limits
 [ ] Rate limiting (Redis sliding window) + quota gates
 [ ] Middleware stack, correctly ordered                           [Ch 4]
 [ ] Security tests: BOLA suite, escalation, algorithm confusion   [Ch 18]
 ✓ MILESTONE: cross-tenant access returns 404 for every endpoint, proven in CI.
```

### Phase 3 — Documents (week 3)
```
 [ ] KnowledgeBase, Document models; tenant-scoped repositories
 [ ] Direct multipart upload with magic-number validation          [Ch 15]
 [ ] Presigned uploads with content_length_range + verification
 [ ] Content-addressed storage; checksum deduplication
 [ ] ARQ workers, four queues; Job model; outbox pattern           [Ch 11]
 [ ] Isolated parsing: process pool, timeout, memory cap, no network
 [ ] Zip bomb / Zip Slip / XXE protections; EXIF stripping
 [ ] Chunking with overlap and sentence boundaries
 [ ] Embedding with batching + 7-day cache                         [Ch 17]
 [ ] Qdrant per-tenant collections; in-search filters + assertion  [Ch 6]
 [ ] Cursor pagination with signed cursors                         [Ch 16]
 ✓ MILESTONE: upload a PDF → job progresses → chunks searchable, tenant-isolated.
```

### Phase 4 — Intelligence (week 4)
```
 [ ] Provider adapters (OpenAI, Anthropic) with full error mapping [Ch 8]
 [ ] LLMRouter: fallback on 5xx/429, never on 4xx; circuit breakers
 [ ] Retry with full jitter and a total-time budget
 [ ] Token counting; context-budget validation BEFORE the call
 [ ] Hybrid retrieval (dense + BM25) fanned out with TaskGroup     [Ch 10]
 [ ] Reranking
 [ ] Prompt builder: stable content FIRST, trust delimiters        [Ch 15,17]
 [ ] OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions                        [Ch 3]
 [ ] RAG queries with citations
 [ ] Three-level cost guard with a global backstop                 [Ch 21]
 ✓ MILESTONE: the real openai SDK works against your endpoint, unmodified.
```

### Phase 5 — Real-time (week 5)
```
 [ ] SSE framing, keep-alives, disconnect detection                [Ch 9,14]
 [ ] Typed event protocol; published in the docs
 [ ] Streaming RAG: status → citations → tokens → usage → done
 [ ] Usage recorded in `finally` on every exit path
 [ ] Resumption via id: / Last-Event-ID / Redis Streams
 [ ] Per-user concurrent-stream limits, released in `finally`
 [ ] Nginx: proxy_buffering off, long read timeouts, HTTP/2
 [ ] Timing-based streaming tests                                  [Ch 18]
 ✓ MILESTONE: TTFT p95 < 1 s; killing a client stops billing within one token.
```

### Phase 6 — Production (weeks 6–7)
```
 [ ] Multi-stage non-root image, SHA-tagged, scanned, signed       [Ch 21]
 [ ] Kubernetes: Deployment, HPA on in-flight, PDB, zone spread
 [ ] Graceful shutdown: preStop, drain, 180 s grace
 [ ] Prometheus RED + AI metrics; Grafana dashboards
 [ ] OpenTelemetry with parent-based + forced-error sampling
 [ ] Alerts with runbooks: errors, loop lag, pool, circuits, cost
 [ ] Migrations as a Job; expand/contract; CONCURRENTLY indexes
 [ ] CI/CD: test → build → scan → migrate → canary → production
 [ ] Enriched OpenAPI; SDK generation; docs portal                 [Ch 19,20]
 ✓ MILESTONE: rolling restart under load loses zero requests.
```

### Phase 7 — Hardening (week 8)
```
 [ ] Game day: provider outage, DB failover, pod eviction, cost spike
 [ ] Load test at 200 concurrent; find and fix the first bottleneck
 [ ] Eval harness: golden dataset with adversarial cases           [Ch 18]
 [ ] Semantic cache with measured precision
 [ ] Prompt-injection scanning + hidden-text detection             [Ch 15]
 [ ] Full security review against the OWASP API Top 10
 ✓ MILESTONE: every failure mode has a documented, tested response.
```

## B.7 The Twelve Acceptance Criteria

These are the tests that prove the system is real. Each maps to a chapter's hardest lesson.

```
 ① TENANT ISOLATION                                                    [Ch 6]
    A parametrised suite hits every resource endpoint as org A with org B's
    ID and asserts 404. A separate test runs 1,000 semantically similar
    cross-tenant RAG queries and asserts zero foreign chunks are ever
    returned. Deleting the vector filter must make a test fail loudly.

 ② NO BLOCKING                                                        [Ch 10]
    Under 200 concurrent chat requests, /health/live p99 stays under 50 ms
    and event_loop_lag p99 under 50 ms.

 ③ STREAMING IS REAL                                                   [Ch 9]
    A timing test through the FULL production middleware stack asserts the
    first SSE event arrives under 500 ms and events are spread over time.
    Adding any buffering middleware must fail it.

 ④ BILLING IS COMPLETE                                                 [Ch 9]
    Usage is recorded identically on normal completion, on error, and on
    client disconnect. A disconnect at token 300 records 300 tokens.

 ⑤ IDEMPOTENCY                                                        [Ch 11]
    Every worker task, run twice, produces identical end state: same chunk
    count, no duplicate vectors, exactly one billing record.

 ⑥ ZERO-DOWNTIME DEPLOY                                               [Ch 21]
    A rolling restart under 20 rps of continuous traffic produces zero
    failed requests. A column rename via expand/contract works with old
    and new code running simultaneously.

 ⑦ GRACEFUL DEGRADATION                                                [Ch 8]
    Primary provider down → fallback, error rate under 0.1%.
    All providers down → retrieval-only mode, clearly labelled.
    Redis down → requests succeed, slower, with an alert.
    Database down → clean 503, never a stack trace.

 ⑧ COST CONTROL                                                       [Ch 21]
    A simulated prompt loop trips the global budget guard and pages within
    30 minutes. Per-org daily budgets refund correctly on rejection.

 ⑨ PAGINATION AT SCALE                                                [Ch 16]
    Page 500,000 of a 50M-row table responds within 3× page-1 latency.
    Concurrent inserts during pagination produce no duplicates or skips.

 ⑩ CACHE EFFECTIVENESS                                                [Ch 17]
    Embedding cache hit rate ≥50% on replayed traffic. Overall LLM cost
    reduced ≥40%. 1,000 concurrent requests for an expired hot key produce
    exactly one upstream call.

 ⑪ NO INFORMATION LEAKAGE                                              [Ch 8]
    Forced exceptions containing fake credentials produce responses with no
    secrets, connection strings, tracebacks, file paths, or class names.
    No secret appears in any captured log line.

 ⑫ DEVELOPER EXPERIENCE                                            [Ch 19,20]
    The official openai SDK works with only a base_url change. A developer
    who has never seen the API makes a successful call in under five
    minutes. Every documentation example passes in CI.
```

## B.9 What You Should Be Able to Answer at the End

If you have built this, these questions have concrete answers drawn from your own system rather than from theory:

```
 • What is your p99 latency, and which component dominates it?
 • What happens when OpenAI returns 500s for ten minutes?
 • How much does one RAG query cost, and what fraction is cached?
 • How many concurrent streams can one pod hold before it degrades?
 • What breaks first when traffic increases 10×?
 • How long does a deploy take, and how many requests does it drop?
 • If a customer reports a wrong answer at 14:32 yesterday, how do you
   reconstruct exactly what happened?
 • Which of your endpoints could leak another tenant's data if a single
   line were deleted, and what test catches that?
```

The last one is the real test. In a well-built system, the answer is *"none — the repositories require a tenant, RLS enforces it at the database, the vector store filters in-search, and there is a CI test for every endpoint."*

# Appendix C — System Design Interview Pack

> Backend interviews for AI roles have converged on a small set of questions. This appendix gives you the frameworks and the numbers. Everything here is drawn from the chapters; this is the compressed, whiteboard-ready version.

---

## C.1 The Framework

Forty-five minutes, five phases. Interviewers score you on *process* as much as on the answer.

```
 ① CLARIFY (5 min)          Do NOT start drawing.
    Who uses it? How many? What's the read/write ratio?
    Which parts are latency-critical vs throughput-critical?
    What's the budget? What must NOT fail?
    Is this a new build or a migration?

 ② SCOPE & ESTIMATE (5 min) Numbers first — they drive every later decision.
    DAU → requests/second → storage → cost per month.
    State your assumptions out loud and write them down.

 ③ HIGH-LEVEL DESIGN (10 min)
    Boxes and arrows. Client → LB → API → data stores → workers.
    Name the technology and say WHY in one clause.

 ④ DEEP DIVE (20 min)       The interviewer picks. Be ready for any of:
    data model · API contract · the hot path · scaling · failure modes ·
    consistency · cost.

 ⑤ TRADE-OFFS & GAPS (5 min)
    "Here's what I'd measure first, here's what I'd do differently at 10×,
     and here's what I've deliberately left out."
```

**What separates a strong answer from an average one** is almost never the architecture — most candidates draw a similar diagram. It is: correct back-of-envelope numbers, naming the specific failure modes, and saying what you would *measure* rather than asserting what would happen.

---

## C.2 The Numbers to Memorise

```
 LATENCY
   Redis GET                 0.2 ms      Postgres indexed SELECT   1 ms
   Vector search (1M, HNSW)  5–30 ms     Embedding API call        40 ms
   Cross-region RTT          80 ms       LLM TTFT                  0.5 s
   LLM full (500 tok)        4–15 s      Reranker (cross-encoder)  50 ms

 CAPACITY (per API pod, 2 workers, async)
   Simple JSON endpoint      ~2,000 rps
   LLM-backed endpoint       ~250 concurrent in-flight
   Concurrent SSE streams    ~5,000 (memory-bound, ~30 KB each)
   WebSocket connections     ~10,000 (fd-bound; raise ulimit -n)

 STORAGE
   Text document (10 pages)  ~30 KB
   Chunks per document       ~20 (at 512 tokens with overlap)
   Embedding (1536-d fp32)   6 KB   →  a 10-page doc costs ~120 KB of vectors
   1M documents              ~30 GB text + ~120 GB vectors

 COST (order of magnitude — verify current pricing)
   GPT-4o-mini               ~$0.15 / $0.60 per 1M in/out tokens
   GPT-4o class              ~$2.50 / $10 per 1M
   Claude Sonnet class       ~$3 / $15 per 1M
   Embeddings (small)        ~$0.02 per 1M tokens
   → A typical RAG query: 2k prompt + 500 completion on a mini model ≈ $0.0006
   → 1M queries/month ≈ $600 on mini, ≈ $10,000 on a frontier model
   → Prompt caching cuts the prefix cost ~10× (Ch 17)

 RULES OF THUMB
   1 DAU ≈ 1–10 requests/day for a normal app; 50–200 for a chat product
   peak rps ≈ 3–5 × average rps
   p99 ≈ 3–10 × p50 for network-bound work
```

---

## C.3 Question 1 — "Design ChatGPT's backend"

**Clarify:** 100M MAU? Free and paid tiers? Conversation history retained? Which modalities? Are we designing the inference layer too, or consuming a model service?

**Estimate:**
```
 100M MAU → ~20M DAU → ~15 messages/day → 300M messages/day
 → 3,500 messages/s average → ~15,000/s peak
 Each message: ~5 s generation → 75,000 CONCURRENT streams at peak
 Storage: 300M msgs/day × 1 KB = 300 GB/day = 110 TB/year
```

**Design:**
```
   Client ─► CDN/WAF ─► LB (HTTP/2, least-conn) ─► API pods (stateless)
                                                        │
        ┌───────────────┬────────────────┬──────────────┼──────────────┐
        ▼               ▼                ▼              ▼              ▼
   Postgres         Redis            S3            Inference      Queue
   users, convos    session,         attachments   fleet          (titles,
   (SHARDED by      rate limits,                   (vLLM,         embeddings,
    user_id)        prompt cache,                  continuous     moderation,
                    stream buffers                 batching)      analytics)
```

**Deep dives to be ready for:**

*Streaming.* SSE, not WebSockets — one-directional (Ch 14). Typed events. `id:` on each for resumption via Redis Streams. Capacity planned in *concurrent connections*, not rps. Nginx `proxy_buffering off`. Graceful drain on deploy with resume tokens.

*Conversation storage.* Shard Postgres by `user_id` (all reads are user-scoped, so no cross-shard queries). Messages are append-only; keyset pagination backward from newest (Ch 16). Archive conversations older than N months to object storage.

*Inference tier.* Separate from the API. Continuous batching gives 10–20× throughput over naive serving. Route by model and by tier. Queue with per-user fairness so one user's 50 tabs don't starve everyone (Ch 11).

*Cost control.* Per-tier token quotas; `max_tokens` ceilings; prompt caching with stable-prefix-first structure; a semantic cache for common questions; a global daily budget circuit breaker.

*The hardest question they'll ask:* **"A user sends a message, gets 400 tokens, then their phone loses signal. What happens?"**
> The generator's `is_disconnected()` check breaks the loop within one token, stopping provider billing. The `finally` block records the 400 tokens actually generated — we were charged for them, so the user is too, and abandonment shows in our metrics. Events are buffered in a Redis Stream keyed by stream ID with a 1-hour TTL. When the phone reconnects, `EventSource` sends `Last-Event-ID: 399` and any pod replays from 400 and tails the stream. If generation completed while they were offline, they get the remainder immediately.

---

## C.4 Question 2 — "Design a RAG system for enterprise documents"

**Clarify:** How many tenants and documents each? Do permissions vary *within* a tenant? Latency target? Data residency requirements? Update frequency?

**Estimate:**
```
 1,000 tenants × 100k documents × 20 chunks = 2 BILLION vectors
 At 1536-d fp32: 12 TB.  → quantise to int8: 3 TB. Or per-tenant indexes.
 Queries: 1,000 tenants × 500/day = 500k/day ≈ 6/s average, 30/s peak
```

**Design:**
```
   INGESTION (async)                    QUERY (synchronous, streamed)
   upload → validate → parse            embed query (cached)
   → chunk → embed (batched)                 │
   → upsert to TENANT COLLECTION        ├─► dense search  ┐
                                        ├─► BM25 search   ├─ TaskGroup, parallel
                                        └─► metadata      ┘
                                             │  fuse (RRF)
                                             ▼
                                        rerank (cross-encoder, top 20 → 5)
                                             ▼
                                        prompt (stable prefix FIRST)
                                             ▼
                                        stream tokens + citations
```

**The deep dive they always pick: tenant isolation.**
> Four layers. Per-tenant Qdrant collections (physical isolation). Metadata filters applied *during* the ANN traversal, not after. ACL group IDs in the vector payload for intra-tenant document permissions, so filtering scales without materialising ID lists. And a redundant post-check that raises a P0 alert if any returned chunk has the wrong `org_id` — if that ever fires, the isolation above has failed. Application repositories require `org_id` in their constructor so an unscoped query isn't expressible, and Postgres RLS is the backstop.
>
> The test that matters: 1,000 semantically similar cross-tenant queries, asserting zero foreign chunks. And a test that deleting the filter *fails loudly*.

**Second-favourite dive: chunking strategy.**
```
 Fixed-size (512 tokens, 64 overlap)   simple, predictable, splits mid-idea
 Sentence-aware                        better boundaries, variable size
 Semantic (embedding-similarity based) best quality, 10× ingestion cost
 Hierarchical (parent-child)           retrieve small, expand to the parent —
                                       best precision/context trade-off
 → Say: "start fixed-size, measure recall@5 on a golden set, then invest
   in hierarchical if retrieval quality is the bottleneck rather than
   generation quality."
```

**Cost question:** *"Reduce inference cost by 50% without hurting quality."*
> In order of return: (1) restructure prompts stable-content-first so provider prefix caching engages — up to 10× on the prefix, and it's a pure reordering; (2) embedding cache, 7-day TTL, deterministic so it never invalidates, typically 40–70% hit rate; (3) route by difficulty — a small model for extraction and summarisation, a frontier model only for complex reasoning; (4) rerank aggressively so you send 5 chunks instead of 20, cutting prompt tokens 4×; (5) a semantic cache at ≥0.95 similarity, tenant-scoped, excluding personalised queries. I'd measure each independently against replayed production traffic.

---

## C.5 Question 3 — "Design a multi-tenant AI API platform"

**The framing that scores well:** this is a *metering and isolation* problem more than a serving problem.

```
 THE FOUR HARD PARTS

 ① ISOLATION      data, compute, and noisy-neighbour
 ② METERING       accurate token accounting across streaming, retries,
                  failures, and caches
 ③ FAIRNESS       one tenant's 10,000-document import must not delay
                  another tenant's single interactive query
 ④ COST ATTRIBUTION  per-tenant, per-model, per-endpoint — in real time
```

**Metering is where candidates fail.** Be specific:
> Usage is recorded in a `finally` block on every exit path — success, error, and client disconnect — because a stream abandoned at token 300 still cost 300 tokens. Cached responses are recorded with `cached=true` and zero provider cost, so the customer sees the request but isn't billed for tokens we didn't buy. Retries that succeed on the second provider record one usage row, not two, but the failed attempt's tokens are recorded as internal cost. The billing source of truth is a `UsageRecord` row per call in Postgres; Redis holds a fast counter for quota checks, reconciled nightly against the rows.

**Fairness:** per-tenant concurrency caps with round-robin dequeue (Ch 11 §11.16), separate queues by resource profile, and an overflow queue rather than rejection so a bulk import degrades to slow rather than failing.

**Rate limiting layers:** IP at the edge (unauthenticated abuse), per-key requests/minute, per-org tokens/month, per-org daily spend, and a global spend circuit breaker as the anomaly backstop.

---

## C.6 Question 4 — "Design an AI agent platform"

**Clarify:** How long do agent runs take? Do they call external tools? Human-in-the-loop? Must a run survive a deploy?

**The key insight to state early:** *"If runs are long and multi-step and must survive deploys, this is a durable workflow problem, not a task queue problem."*

```
   Client ──SSE/WS──► API ──► Workflow engine (Temporal) ──► Activities
                                     │                          │
                                     │ state persisted          ├─ LLM call
                                     │ after EVERY step         ├─ tool call
                                     │                          └─ human approval
                                     ▼                             (sleeps for
                              survives crashes,                     days, free)
                              deploys, and restarts
```

**The security answer they're testing for:**
> The model *proposes* tool calls; the authorization layer *decides*. An agent grant is a strict subset of the user's permissions — effective authority is the intersection, never a union. Destructive tools require explicit human confirmation. Every tool call is schema-validated with the same Pydantic model that generated its definition, so a hallucinated argument is rejected before execution. And retrieved document content can contain instructions — that's prompt injection — so the defence that actually holds is authorization, not prompt engineering. An audit log records both the principal and the acting agent.

**Interruption:** generation runs in its own `asyncio.Task` so a WebSocket `interrupt` message can cancel it within 100 ms. `CancelledError` is re-raised, and usage is recorded in `finally`.

---

## C.7 Question 5 — "Your API is slow. Debug it."

This is a *process* question. The wrong answer is a list of optimisations.

```
 ① WHAT does "slow" mean? p50 or p99? Which endpoints? Since when?
    Correlated with a deploy, a traffic change, or a dependency?

 ② LOOK AT THE DATA before theorising.
    Grafana: latency percentiles by route, error rate, in-flight,
    event_loop_lag, DB pool utilisation, queue depth.

 ③ NARROW IT.
    All endpoints slow → infrastructure (loop blocked, pool exhausted,
                          noisy neighbour, network)
    One endpoint slow  → that code path or its dependency
    p99 only           → tail: GC, lock contention, a slow tenant, CFS throttling
    p50 too            → something systemically slower

 ④ TRACE ONE SLOW REQUEST.
    OpenTelemetry waterfall: which span dominates? An unexpectedly deep
    span usually IS the answer.

 ⑤ THE USUAL SUSPECTS, in the order I'd check them:
    • event_loop_lag > 50 ms → a blocking call (Ch 10) — the #1 cause
    • DB pool at 100% → too few connections, or a leak, or N+1
    • Sequential awaits that should be a TaskGroup
    • A missing index (EXPLAIN the slow query)
    • Cache hit rate dropped (a deploy changed a key?)
    • A provider is slow (their status page, our TTFT metric)
    • CFS throttling from a CPU limit
    • Middleware added recently (BaseHTTPMiddleware buffering?)

 ⑥ FIX ONE THING. MEASURE. Repeat.
```

**The senior signal:** saying "I'd look at event-loop lag first, because in an async Python service it's the metric that explains the most symptoms with one number."

---

## C.8 Rapid-Fire Questions

```
 Q: Why is my FastAPI app slow under load but fast in tests?
 A: A blocking call in an async handler. Invisible at concurrency 1,
    catastrophic at 100. Check event_loop_lag; grep for requests/time.sleep/
    psycopg2/boto3 inside `async def`.

 Q: 500 errors after scaling from 5 to 50 pods. Why?
 A: pool_size × workers × pods exceeded Postgres max_connections.
    Shrink the pool or add PgBouncer in transaction mode.

 Q: Streaming works locally, arrives all at once in production.
 A: Nginx proxy_buffering (default on). Fix with proxy_buffering off or
    the X-Accel-Buffering: no header.

 Q: Users report being logged out randomly.
 A: Refresh-token reuse detection revoking the family — usually caused by
    a client racing two refresh requests. Add client-side single-flight.

 Q: Costs doubled overnight with flat traffic.
 A: A prompt change broke prefix caching, a retry loop, a leaked key, or
    a model alias silently upgraded. Check cost per request by model, and
    pin your model versions.

 Q: How do you migrate a column with zero downtime?
 A: Expand/contract in three deploys — add nullable, write both, backfill
    in batches, switch reads, drop old. Old and new code run simultaneously
    during a rollout.

 Q: 403 or 404 for another tenant's resource?
 A: 404. A 403 confirms existence and enables ID enumeration.

 Q: How do you make LLM calls idempotent?
 A: Client sends Idempotency-Key; SET NX in Redis atomically; store the
    response; replays return it. Without it, a retry after a network blip
    charges twice.

 Q: Semantic cache returned a wrong answer. What went wrong?
 A: Threshold too low. Similarity doesn't capture negation — "is X covered"
    and "is X NOT covered" are ~0.97 similar. Optimise for precision, not
    hit rate, and exclude personalised queries.

 Q: Why did a database blip restart every pod?
 A: The liveness probe checks the database. Liveness must touch nothing —
    only readiness may check dependencies.
```

---

## C.9 What Interviewers Are Actually Scoring

```
 ✔ You asked clarifying questions before designing
 ✔ Your numbers are within an order of magnitude, and you said your assumptions
 ✔ You named specific technologies with a one-clause reason
 ✔ You identified failure modes unprompted
 ✔ You discussed cost — most candidates never mention it
 ✔ You said what you'd MEASURE, not just what you'd build
 ✔ You acknowledged trade-offs rather than claiming a design is optimal
 ✔ You said "I don't know, here's how I'd find out" when you didn't know

 ✘ Jumping straight to a diagram
 ✘ Naming technologies without reasons ("we'll use Kafka")
 ✘ Only the happy path
 ✘ No numbers at all
 ✘ Over-engineering for scale nobody asked for
 ✘ Defending a choice after the interviewer raises a real problem with it
```

---
---

# Appendix D — Where To Go Next

## D.1 The Honest Assessment

If you have read this guide and built the capstone, you can design, build, secure, and operate the backend of a real AI product. That is a genuinely valuable and reasonably rare skill set.

What you have *not* yet done, and what separates competence from depth:

```
 • Operated a system through a real incident at 3 a.m.
 • Had a design decision proven wrong by production, six months later
 • Debugged something where every layer's explanation was plausible and wrong
 • Made a cost/quality trade-off with real money and real users attached
 • Maintained a system built by someone else, under constraints you'd have
   chosen differently
```

None of that comes from reading. It comes from running things. The fastest way to get it is to put something small in front of real users and keep it up.

---

## D.2 The Ordered Roadmap

### Immediate — deepen what you've built

```
 DATABASES        Use The Index, Luke (use-the-index-luke.com) — free, and the
                  single highest-return resource for a backend engineer.
                  Then: query plans, isolation levels, lock contention,
                  connection pooling internals.
                  → You will hit these before you hit anything else.

 DISTRIBUTED      Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann). The one
 SYSTEMS          book everyone recommends, and correctly. Read chapters 5–9
                  slowly: replication, partitioning, transactions, consistency.

 PYTHON DEPTH     CPython internals: the GIL, reference counting, generators,
                  and how asyncio is built from them. Read the asyncio source —
                  it's ~10k lines and clearer than most explanations of it.

 OBSERVABILITY    Observability Engineering (Majors, Fong-Jones, Miranda).
                  The distinction between monitoring (known unknowns) and
                  observability (unknown unknowns) is the one that changes
                  how you build.
```

### Next six months — broaden

```
 SYSTEMS          Go or Rust. Not to switch languages, but because writing a
                  service without a GIL and without a garbage collector changes
                  how you think about the Python one.

 INFRASTRUCTURE   Kubernetes beyond deployments: operators, CRDs, the
                  scheduler, network policies. Terraform for real.
                  → The goal is being able to reason about why a pod is
                    behaving strangely, not to become a platform engineer.

 SECURITY         OWASP API Security Top 10, in depth. Then: a CTF or two.
                  Attacking systems teaches defence faster than reading about it.

 ML SYSTEMS       Designing Machine Learning Systems (Chip Huyen).
                  Understand what happens on the other side of your API:
                  training, evaluation, drift, feedback loops.
```

### Ongoing — stay current

```
 PRIMARY SOURCES  Provider docs and changelogs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google).
                  Read the actual API reference, not summaries of it —
                  the details that matter are never in the summaries.

 ENGINEERING      Papers and posts from teams operating at scale: Stripe,
 BLOGS            Cloudflare, Netflix, Discord, Figma. Read postmortems
                  especially — public incident reports are the densest
                  engineering writing available.

 SPECIFICATIONS   Read RFCs when a detail matters: 9110 (HTTP semantics),
                  6749/9700 (OAuth), 7519 (JWT), 8288 (Link), 9457 (Problem
                  Details). They are shorter and clearer than most blog posts
                  about them.

 SOURCE CODE      Read FastAPI's `routing.py` and `dependencies/utils.py`.
                  Read Starlette in full — it's small. Read vLLM's API server.
                  Reading production code you depend on is undervalued.
```

---

## D.3 What Not To Chase

```
 ✘ Every new framework. The ASGI + Pydantic paradigm is settled. Litestar
   and Robyn are fine; learning them teaches you almost nothing new.

 ✘ Every new vector database. They differ in operations, not in concepts.
   Learn one deeply; the second takes an afternoon.

 ✘ Every new agent framework. The underlying loop is: prompt → tool call →
   validate → authorize → execute → repeat. Frameworks wrap it differently.
   Understand the loop and the frameworks become optional.

 ✘ Microservices before you need them. A well-layered monolith with clean
   domain boundaries (Chapter 1 §1.7) splits easily when it must. A premature
   split gives you distributed-systems problems with none of the benefits.

 ✘ Kubernetes for three services. Cloud Run, Fly, Railway, or ECS will serve
   you well past the point where you think you've outgrown them.
```

---

## D.4 The Principles That Outlive the Tools

FastAPI will be replaced. Pydantic will be replaced. The models in this guide will be obsolete within two years. These will not be:

```
 ① VALIDATE AT THE BOUNDARY
    One place where untrusted data becomes trusted objects. Everything
    inside can then assume correctness.

 ② MAKE ILLEGAL STATES UNREPRESENTABLE
    A repository that requires a tenant ID beats remembering to filter.
    Structure beats discipline, every time.

 ③ EXPENSIVE THINGS HAPPEN ONCE
    Connections, models, compiled schemas, and cached results are built
    once and reused. Per-request construction is the most common
    performance bug there is.

 ④ NEVER BLOCK THE SHARED RESOURCE
    The event loop, the database pool, the GPU. One consumer holding a
    shared resource degrades everyone.

 ⑤ FAIL FAST, FAIL LOUD, FAIL SAFE
    Crash at startup on misconfiguration. Log with enough context to fix it.
    Deny by default when the security layer is uncertain.

 ⑥ EVERY EXTERNAL CALL CAN FAIL, HANG, OR LIE
    Timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breakers, and a degraded mode —
    for every dependency, decided before the incident.

 ⑦ IDEMPOTENCY IS THE PRICE OF DURABILITY
    At-least-once delivery is the only guarantee you get. Design every
    operation so running it twice is harmless.

 ⑧ MEASURE THE THING USERS FEEL
    TTFT, not CPU. Error rate, not memory. Abandonment, not throughput.

 ⑨ THE MODEL IS AN UNTRUSTED CLIENT
    It is influenced by data you did not write. Validate its output;
    authorize its actions; never let it be the security boundary.

 ⑩ COST IS A FIRST-CLASS CONSTRAINT
    In AI backends, a correctness bug and a cost bug can be the same bug.
    Instrument spend like you instrument latency.
```

---

## D.5 A Closing Note

The chapters in this guide describe a large amount of machinery. It is easy to read it and conclude that a production AI backend requires all of it on day one. It does not.

**What you actually need on day one:** validated input, a database session per request, authentication, one timeout, structured logs with a request ID, and a health check. That is a real service, and it will serve real users.

Everything else in this guide is a response to a specific problem you will meet *later* — usually at a specific scale, or after a specific incident. Circuit breakers matter when a provider has its first bad day. Cursor pagination matters when a table passes a million rows. Cost guards matter the first time someone writes a loop. Semantic caching matters when the bill gets large enough to notice.

**Build the simple version. Instrument it well enough to see what breaks. Then reach for the chapter that addresses what broke.**

That sequence — build, measure, learn, fix — is the actual skill. The chapters are just a reference for step four.

*End of guide.*
